items.explanation_markdown:
You get home, keys still in your hand, and call out ただいま — but nobody answers right away. Everyone in the house is already mid-task, and you can hear it before you even reach the living room: something's cooking, someone's humming along to a song. Nobody planned any of this for you, and none of it is a habit you could look up on a schedule — it's just what's happening in the house at this exact second, and that's precisely the gap ている exists to fill.

You open the door and look around.

```jp
{{chichi||父[ちち]}}は{{shinbun||新[しん]聞[ぶん]}}を{{yomu|te|読[よ]んで}}{{iru-exist||いる}}。
```

*My father is reading the newspaper.*

```jp
{{haha||母[はは]}}は{{ryouri||料[りょう]理[り]}}を{{suru|te|して}}いる。
```

*My mother is cooking.*

```jp
妹[いもうと]は歌[うた]を歌[うた]っている。
```

*My little sister is singing.*

None of that is what your family generally does. Your father doesn't spend his life reading the newspaper, and your sister isn't a professional singer — this is just what each of them happens to be doing at this exact second, and freezing an action mid-swing like that is the entire job of ている.

Japanese doesn't mark this the way English bolts -ing onto a verb. It literally glues "exist" onto the action, so a sentence like this says something closer to "reading, existing" — reading is the state your father exists in right now. Once that clicks, the whole pattern stops feeling like a separate tense and starts feeling like exactly what it is: one verb sitting on top of another. You already know {{iru-exist||いる}} as a standalone word meaning "to exist" for people and animals; this is that exact same {{iru-exist||いる}}, just borrowed to describe existing in the middle of doing something instead of existing in a place.

## How ている Works

The shape is simple once you already have the te-form — the て／で shape you use to connect actions and ask for things. Take a verb's te-form and add {{iru-exist||いる}} right after it. That's the whole rule: ている isn't a separate conjugation with its own quirks, it's always somebody's te-form plus this one extra verb sitting on top of it.

```jp
{{ryouri||料[りょう]理[り]}}{{suru||する}} → {{ryouri||料[りょう]理[り]}}{{suru|te|して}} → {{ryouri||料[りょう]理[り]}}{{suru|te|して}}いる
```

*to cook → te-form → is cooking*

```jp
歌[うた]う → 歌[うた]って → 歌[うた]っている
```

*to sing → te-form → is singing*

```jp
泣[な]く → 泣[な]いて → 泣[な]いている
```

*to cry → te-form → is crying*

Whatever sound change the te-form already goes through — {{suru||する}} becoming {{suru|te|して}}, う becoming って, く becoming {{iru-exist|te|いて}} — just rides along into ている unchanged. There's nothing new to memorize about the verb itself here; you're gluing a familiar shape onto a form you can already build with your eyes closed.

It also helps to notice what ている is replacing. The plain form {{yomu||読[よ]む}} on its own usually points at something general — a habit, a fact, a plan already on the calendar — not something unfolding this second. That gap between "reads" and "is reading" is exactly the space ている exists to fill, and every ている sentence is quietly doing two things at once: naming the base action, and timestamping it to right now.

Context carries some of that weight too. {{ima||今[いま]}} (right now) often shows up right next to ている specifically to nail the timing down, because the same shape can also describe something a person does repeatedly over a stretch of time, not only this literal second. Nothing in the grammar itself decides which reading is meant — the sentence around it does that work.

## Rules and Exceptions

> ている always sits on top of the te-form, never the plain dictionary form. There's no such word as `泣くいる` — it has to be 泣[な]いている.

This mix-up is common in the first few weeks, because {{iru-exist||いる}} by itself just means "to exist" (for people and animals), and it's tempting to tack it straight onto the dictionary form the way you'd add any second verb. It doesn't work like that — {{iru-exist||いる}} leans entirely on the te-form underneath it.

> {{aru||ある}} and {{iru-exist||いる}} already describe a state on their own, so they never take ている. There's no `あっている` or `いている` — the plain forms already do that job.

This one trips people up precisely because ている usually signals "something is happening," and existing feels like the most basic kind of happening there is. But existing isn't an action you can catch someone partway through — a thing either exists right now or it doesn't — so the plain forms already carry that meaning without any help from ている.

One more thing worth knowing: every example above is in plain form, which is exactly how you'd talk to family or close friends. Swap {{iru-exist||いる}} for {{iru-exist|masu|います}} and you get the polite version instead — {{yomu|te|読[よ]んで}}{{iru-exist|masu|います}}, 歌[うた]っています — for anyone you'd normally address politely. The rule underneath doesn't change at all; only the last piece does. Nothing else in the sentence moves around for any of this, either — particles, time words, and objects all stay exactly where they already were, since ている is simply replacing the verb's ending, not rearranging anything around it.

## Casual Speech

In fast, everyday speech, ている often loses its い entirely and shrinks down to てる. You'll hear this constantly between friends and family members — it isn't sloppy Japanese, it's just how the spoken language moves once nobody's being careful about it.

```jp
妹[いもうと]は{{ima||今[いま]}}、宿[しゅく]題[だい]を{{suru|stem|し}}てる。
```

*My little sister's doing her homework right now.*

```jp
{{chichi||父[ちち]}}も{{ima||今[いま]}}、{{terebi||テレビ}}を{{miru-v|stem|見[み]}}てる。
```

*My father's watching TV right now too.*

The dropped い isn't random, either — casual spoken Japanese regularly thins out a weak, unstressed vowel sitting in the middle of a word, and ている's い is a textbook case of exactly that. You'll notice the same instinct at work elsewhere the further you get into casual speech.

Keep the full ている for anything even slightly formal — a note to a teacher, a conversation with someone you've just met, anything written carefully — and save てる for the people you're already relaxed around. Nobody will misunderstand you either way; it's a register choice, not a correctness one.

## Contrast: ている vs らしい

You've already met らしい for reporting something you picked up from evidence or heard secondhand rather than confirmed yourself. ている and らしい aren't fighting over the same job — they actually stack — but the difference between using one alone and adding the other on top is worth feeling out carefully.

```jp
妹[いもうと]が泣[な]いている。
```

*My little sister is crying.*

```jp
妹[いもうと]が泣[な]いているらしい。
```

*Sounds like my little sister is crying.*

The first sentence is something you're witnessing directly — you're in the room, you can hear it and see it happening. The second is something you're relaying secondhand — a phone call, a message, a closed door you haven't opened yet. ている states the moment as a plain fact you're standing right in front of; stacking らしい on top of that same ている quietly tells the listener you weren't actually there to confirm it yourself. Swap one for the other and you've changed whether you're a witness or a messenger, even though the underlying event is identical.

ようだ and みたいだ can layer on top of ている the same way らしい does — the flavor of your evidence shifts a little between them, but the underlying move, adding a layer of distance on top of a plain fact, stays the same across all three.

This is worth sitting with, because it's easy to assume ている is only ever about certainty. It isn't — ている just states what's unfolding; how sure you are, or how you found out, is a separate layer you add or leave off on top of it.

ている is going to keep showing up for the rest of your Japanese, and it won't always be doing this exact job. Soon you'll run into verbs where this same shape describes a state that already happened rather than one still unfolding — but that's a story for another lesson, and nothing you need to worry about yet. For now, every time you catch somebody mid-action — reading, cooking, singing, crying — this is the shape that says so.
caution_notes: ている only attaches to the te-form, never to the plain dictionary form — there's no such word as 泣くいる, only 泣いている.
ある and いる already describe a state on their own, so they never take ている — there's no いている or あっている.
Casual speech drops the い in ている to give てる, but keep the full ている in polite contexts (います).
らしい layered onto ている adds hearsay or secondhand inference on top of the plain fact ている states — swapping them changes whether you saw it yourself or were told about it.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're at a friend's place in Tokyo, and the tea on the table smells amazing. You want a cup, but it's not yours to just grab. In English you'd ask "can I have some?" — in Japanese you reach for てもいい, the pattern that asks *is it okay if I…?*

```jp
{{kono||この}}{{ocha||お茶[ちゃ]}}を{{nomu-v|te|飲[の]んで}}も{{ii||いい}}ですか。
```

*Is it okay if I drink this tea?*

That's the whole job of てもいい: you describe an action, then ask whether doing it is permitted — or, without the question, you *grant* that permission to someone else. It's the polite handshake around "may I" and "you may."

## How it works

The build is simple because you already own the hard part. Take a verb, put it into its て-form (the same form you learned for てください and て{{iru-exist||いる}}), then bolt on も{{ii||いい}}.

```jp
{{taberu||食[た]べる}} → {{taberu|te|食[た]べて}} → {{taberu|te|食[た]べて}}もいい
```

*eat → eating(-form) → may eat*

The literal pieces are worth seeing once. も means *even*, and {{ii||いい}} means *good*. So {{taberu|te|食[た]べて}}もいい is *even if I eat, it's good* — "even doing this is fine," which is exactly how permission feels. That's your *why*: the も is what makes it *permission* rather than a command.

To make it polite, add です on the end. Both of these are correct; the first is plain, the second is the one you'll say to a stranger or a teacher.

```jp
{{koko||ここ}}に座[すわ]ってもいい。
{{koko||ここ}}に座[すわ]ってもいいですか。
```

*I may sit here. / Is it okay if I sit here?*

When you're the one *giving* permission, drop the question and just state it. A parent to a child, a host to a guest:

```jp
{{terebi||テレビ}}を{{miru-v|te|見[み]て}}もいいですよ。
```

*You may watch TV.*

There's also a more formal, more generous-sounding variant: てもかまいません, literally *even doing it, I don't mind*. Use it when you want to sound extra accommodating — a station attendant, say, telling you it's no trouble.

```jp
{{koko||ここ}}で待[ま]ってもかまいません。
```

*You may wait here (I don't mind at all).*

## Rules and exceptions

The most common early mistake is dropping the も. Learners hear that permission is "て + {{ii||いい}}" and write `食べていい` thinking that's the neutral form. In casual speech that contraction does happen (more on that below), but in careful, polite Japanese the も carries the *permission* meaning — leave it out in a formal setting and it sounds unfinished. When in doubt, keep the も.

> てもいい asks about *your own* action or grants one to someone else. It does **not** work as a general "is X allowed here?" sign-style rule. For that broader "is it forbidden?" feeling you'll want a different pattern (coming very soon).

Another sharp edge: adding か makes it a genuine request for permission, and the answer matters. If you ask {{nomu-v|te|飲[の]んで}}も{{ii||いい}}ですか and the host says だめ (no good), you don't drink. Without か, you're not asking — you're telling someone it's fine. Mixing those up can make you sound like you're granting yourself permission out loud, which is a little odd.

One more: because {{ii||いい}} is an adjective, some learners try to bend it like `食べてもいかった` for the past. Don't chase that at N5 — stick to the present *may / it's okay* meaning, which covers almost every situation you'll meet.

## Casual speech

Among friends, two things happen. First, the polite です falls away. Second — and this is the big one — the も itself often contracts out, so てもいい becomes て{{ii||いい}} in fast speech.

```jp
{{kore||これ}}{{taberu|te|食[た]べて}}もいい。
{{kore||これ}}{{taberu|te|食[た]べて}}{{ii||いい}}。
```

*Can I eat this? (both casual)*

Both are casual and both are fine between friends; the second, with the も gone, is the more relaxed of the two. The tone alone (a rising, questioning tone) does the work that か does in polite speech.

> Keep the も in anything written, formal, or spoken to someone above you. The dropped-も version is friends-and-family territory only.

## Contrast

You've met てください — *please do this* — and it lives right next door, because both attach to the て-form. But they point in opposite directions. てください *asks the other person to act*; てもいい asks whether *you* may act, or tells the other person they *may*.

```jp
窓[まど]を開[あ]けてください。
窓[まど]を開[あ]けてもいいですか。
```

*Please open the window. / Is it okay if I open the window?*

The first hands the job to your listener. The second keeps the action with you and just checks permission. Swap one for the other and you've flipped who's doing the opening — a real change in meaning, not just politeness.

It's also worth setting てもいい beside ませんか, the invitation you learned. ませんか pulls the other person into an activity with you — *won't you…?* — while てもいい is purely about whether an action is allowed.

```jp
一[いっ]緒[しょ]に{{iku-v|masu|行[い]きません}}か。
一[いっ]緒[しょ]に{{iku-v|te|行[い]って}}もいいですか。
```

*Won't you go together (with me)? / Is it okay if I come along?*

The first is a warm invitation you extend; the second is you asking to be let in. Same activity, completely different social move.

Here's the one-line recap: て-form + も{{ii||いい}} asks or grants permission — *may I / you may*. Hold onto the shape, because the moment you can say "you may," the natural next question is "and what may I *not* do?" — that's てはいけない, *must not*, waiting for you just around the corner.
caution_notes: In polite Japanese keep the も — dropping it (食べていい) is casual only and sounds unfinished in formal speech.
Add か to ask for permission; without か you are granting permission, not requesting it.
てもいい asks about your own action or grants one to someone else — it is not a general 'is X allowed here?' rule sign.
てください asks the other person to act; てもいい keeps the action with you or lets the listener act — don't swap them.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're standing in a quiet library, and your friend pulls out their phone to make a call. Before they even tap the screen, you want to stop them — not with a polite "please don't," but with the flat, no-exceptions "you can't do that here." That's the job of てはいけない.

This is the pattern for rules and prohibitions: the sign on the wall, the thing the teacher says, the line you don't cross. It's the mirror image of something you already know — ても{{ii||いい}}, which grants permission. Where ても{{ii||いい}} opens a door, てはいけない slams it shut.

```jp
{{koko||ここ}}で{{denwa||電[でん]話[わ]}}を使[つか]ってはいけません。
```

*You must not use the phone here.*

## How it works

The build is simple because you already own half of it. Take a verb, put it in its て-form (the same て-form you use for てください and ても{{ii||いい}}), and attach はいけない. That's the whole machine.

```jp
{{taberu||食[た]べる}} → {{taberu|te|食[た]べて}} → {{taberu|te|食[た]べて}}はいけない
{{nomu-v||飲[の]む}} → {{nomu-v|te|飲[の]んで}} → {{nomu-v|te|飲[の]んで}}はいけない
```

*eat → (te-form) → must not eat*
*drink → (te-form) → must not drink*

The polite version just swaps いけない for いけません. Same meaning, more formal register — the kind of thing you'd see on a posted notice or hear from station staff.

```jp
{{koko||ここ}}でお酒[さけ]を{{nomu-v|te|飲[の]んで}}はいけません。
```

*You must not drink alcohol here.*

Why はいけない? Literally いけない is a word meaning "it won't do" or "it's no good." So the whole thing reads like "doing X won't do." That's a useful intuition: you're not commanding a person directly, you're declaring that a certain *action* is not acceptable. The は in the middle is the topic particle — it's marking "as for doing this thing" — which is exactly why it's pronounced *wa*, not *ha*.

```jp
夜[よる]に{{koohii||コーヒー}}を{{nomu-v|te|飲[の]んで}}はいけない。
```

*You must not drink coffee at night.*

## Rules and exceptions

The て-form does the heavy lifting, so every irregular て-form you've already met carries straight over. {{iku-v||行[い]く}} becomes {{iku-v|te|行[い]って}} (not `行きて`), {{hanasu-v||話[はな]す}} becomes {{hanasu-v|te|話[はな]して}}, 待[ま]つ becomes 待[ま]って. If your て-form is right, the prohibition is right.

```jp
{{sono||その}}部屋[へや]に入[はい]ってはいけません。
```

*You must not enter that room.*

One thing to watch: because いけない ends like a negative, learners sometimes try to negate it again to say "don't have to." That's a different pattern entirely, and stacking negatives here just produces something broken. Don't reach for `食べてはいけなくない` — it isn't a thing.

> てはいけない is genuinely strong. It's the register of laws, safety signs, and adults laying down rules to children. Saying it to your host at a dinner party — even about something small — lands like scolding. For softening someone's behavior gently, this is the wrong tool.

The subject is usually left unspoken, because a prohibition tends to apply to everyone or to "you." But you can name who's bound by the rule with は or が when you need to be clear about it.

```jp
子[こ]供[ども]はお酒[さけ]を{{nomu-v|te|飲[の]んで}}はいけません。
```

*Children must not drink alcohol.*

## Casual speech

In real conversation, てはいけない contracts hard. The ては collapses into ちゃ, so {{taberu|te|食[た]べて}}はいけない becomes {{taberu|te|食[た]べちゃ}}いけない. This is everywhere in casual speech — friends, family, anyone you'd already be speaking plainly with.

```jp
{{sore||それ}}を{{taberu|te|食[た]べちゃ}}いけない。
```

*You can't eat that.*

The で-form verbs (the ones whose て-form is で, like {{nomu-v||飲[の]む}} → {{nomu-v|te|飲[の]んで}}) shift to じゃ instead: {{nomu-v|te|飲[の]んで}}はいけない → {{nomu-v|te|飲[の]んじゃ}}いけない. Same logic, just following the voicing of the sound before it.

```jp
{{ima||今[いま]}}、{{kaeru-v|te|帰[かえ]っちゃ}}いけない。
```

*You can't go home right now.*

Even the ending often gets trimmed — people drop off after ちゃ and just let the tone or a trailing だめ carry the "no good" meaning. But for now, ちゃいけない is the reliable casual form to lock in.

## Contrast

Line てはいけない up against ても{{ii||いい}}, the permission pattern you learned right before it. They share the て-form base and differ only in the tail, but they're opposites — and that's the cleanest way to feel the meaning.

```jp
{{koko||ここ}}で写[しゃ]真[しん]を{{miru-v|te|見[み]て}}はいけません。
```

*You must not look at photos here.*

```jp
{{koko||ここ}}で写[しゃ]真[しん]を{{miru-v|te|見[み]て}}も{{ii||いい}}です。
```

*You may look at photos here.*

One tail says "no," the other says "yes." If you can build one, you can build the other — same verb, same て-form, just choose the door.

It's also worth separating this from てください, your request pattern. てください asks someone to *do* something as a favor; てはいけない tells them an action is *off-limits* as a rule. "Please close the door" and "you must not close the door" are not two shades of the same idea — one is a polite ask, the other is a prohibition.

So: て-form plus はいけない is your "off-limits" stamp, softening to ちゃいけない among friends. When you later want to say "please *don't*" as a gentle request rather than a hard rule, you'll meet ないでください — a much softer way to hold someone back, and the natural next step from here.
caution_notes: Build it from the て-form: 行く → 行って → 行ってはいけない, never 行きて.
The は in てはいけない is pronounced wa, not ha, because it's the topic particle.
てはいけない is strong — the register of rules and signs; it lands as scolding in casual polite situations.
In casual speech ては contracts to ちゃ (食べちゃいけない) and で-verbs use じゃ (飲んじゃいけない).

items.explanation_markdown:
You just walked through the door. You are starving, but your hands are completely dirty from the train. You want to tell your family you are going to eat *after* you wash your hands.

```jp
{{te-v||手[て]}}を洗[あら]ってから、{{gohan||ご飯[はん]}}を{{taberu|masu|食[た]べます}}。
```
*After washing my hands, I will eat.*

## How it works

You already know the て-form (the versatile form that lets you link verbs and make requests). To say you will do something *after* doing something else, just take the て-form of the first action and attach から.

The action in the てから half of the sentence always happens first. The second half of the sentence is what happens next.

```jp
{{uchi||うち}}に{{kaeru-v|te|帰[かえ]って}}から、寝[ね]ます。
{{gohan||ご飯[はん]}}を{{taberu|te|食[た]べて}}から、映[えい]画[が]を{{miru-v|masu|見[み]ます}}。
```
*After returning home, I will sleep.*
*After eating a meal, we will watch a movie.*

## Controlling time

Here is a convenient trick: the てから part of your sentence does not have a tense of its own. It just locks the two events into a sequence.

To change the sentence from future to past, you only need to change the very last verb in the sentence.

```jp
{{hon||本[ほん]}}を{{yomu|te|読[よ]んで}}から、寝[ね]ました。
{{mado||窓[まど]}}を閉[し]めてから、出[で]ました。
```
*After reading a book, I slept.*
*After closing the window, I left.*

## The "because" trap

This trips everyone up the first week, so it is completely normal if it feels weird at first. You previously learned that から means "because." So why does it suddenly mean "after"?

It is all about what the particle attaches to. If から follows a plain verb or a polite `ます`, it gives a reason ("because"). But if it attaches *specifically* to a て-form, the meaning transforms into a strict sequence ("after").

Look at how swapping just the verb form completely flips the meaning of the sentence:

```jp
映[えい]画[が]を{{miru-v||見[み]る}}から、{{kaeru-v|masu|帰[かえ]ります}}。
映[えい]画[が]を{{miru-v|te|見[み]て}}から、{{kaeru-v|masu|帰[かえ]ります}}。
```
*Because I will watch a movie, I will go home.*
*After watching a movie, I will go home.*

## Casual speech

When speaking casually with friends, the pattern works exactly the same way. You just drop the polite `ます` on the final verb at the very end of the sentence.

```jp
{{te-v||手[て]}}を洗[あら]ってから、{{gohan||ご飯[はん]}}を{{taberu||食[た]べる}}。
```
*After washing my hands, I will eat.*

> You can only use てから with verbs, because nouns do not have a て-form. If you want to say something like "after the movie," you will need a different pattern called 後[あと]で that we will tackle a little later. For now, master your sequences!
caution_notes: The てから phrase has no tense of its own; you only change the final verb to make the sentence past tense.
Attaching から to a dictionary-form or polite verb means 'because', but attaching it to a て-form means 'after'.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're relaxing in your friend's living room. It's late, and you have a long day tomorrow. They ask if you want coffee. If you say {{koohii||コーヒー}}を{{nomu-v|masu|飲[の]みません}}, you sound perfectly polite, but maybe a little stiff for a late-night hangout. It sounds almost formal, like you're speaking to a waiter. How do you casually tell them "I won't drink it" without putting up that formal barrier? You need the plain negative: the ない form.

## Bending the verb

When you first learned to speak politely, you used ません to say you don't or won't do something. The ない form takes over that exact same job in casual speech. To make it, we just need to change the tail end of the verb.

Think of Japanese verbs as falling into a couple of main families. For the verbs that simply drop their final る sound when they conjugate (often called ru-verbs, like {{taberu||食[た]べる}} and {{miru-v||見[み]る}}), the rule is effortless. You just chop off that final る and replace it with ない.

```jp
肉[にく]を{{taberu|nai|食[た]べない}}。
{{terebi||テレビ}}を{{miru-v|nai|見[み]ない}}。
```
*I don't eat meat.*
*I don't watch TV.*

Now, for the other major family of verbs (often called u-verbs), it requires a slight vowel shift. You take the final syllable of the dictionary form, shift its vowel from an "u" sound to an "a" sound, and then attach ない. 

For example, {{nomu-v||飲[の]む}} ends in the syllable *mu*. Shift that to *ma*, and you get {{nomu-v|stem|飲[の]ま}}. Then add ない. {{iku-v||行[い]く}} ends in *ku*. Shift that to *ka*, and you get {{iku-v|stem|行[い]か}}.

```jp
{{koohii||コーヒー}}を{{nomu-v|nai|飲[の]まない}}。
{{kyou||今日[きょう]}}は学[がっ]校[こう]に{{iku-v|nai|行[い]かない}}。
```
*I won't drink coffee.*
*I won't go to school today.*

There is one special catch with this vowel shift. If your verb ends in the pure vowel う, like {{kau-v||買[か]う}} (to buy) or 会[あ]う (to meet), that final vowel shifts to a わ sound, not an あ sound. So {{kau-v||買[か]う}} becomes {{kau-v|nai|買[か]わない}}.

```jp
{{atarashii-adj||新[あたら]しい}}{{kutsu||靴[くつ]}}を{{kau-v|nai|買[か]わない}}。
友[とも]達[だち]に会[あ]わない。
```
*I won't buy new shoes.*
*I won't meet my friend.*

Finally, there are always irregulars that like to break the rules. The only one you need to worry about right now is {{kuru-v||来[く]る}} (to come). It completely changes its pronunciation at the beginning of the word, becoming {{kuru-v|nai|来[こ]ない}} (こない).

```jp
{{kare||彼[かれ]}}は{{kuru-v|nai|来[こ]ない}}。
```
*He will not come.*

## Talking about the past

How do you talk about the past? When you want to say you *didn't* do something, you already know to use ませんでした.

The casual ない form handles the past a bit differently. To make the casual past negative, you take the ない ending, drop the final い, and add かった. So, ない becomes なかった. 

If you want to casually say you didn't play, you conjugate 遊[あそ]ぶ to 遊[あそ]ばない, and then change it to 遊[あそ]ばなかった.

```jp
{{kinou||昨日[きのう]}}は遊[あそ]ばなかった。
```
*I didn't play yesterday.*

> **Watch out:** Don't try to mix politeness levels in a single verb. A sentence is either entirely polite (using ません) or entirely casual (using ない). Never say `見ませんない` or `飲まないません`. Choose the single level that matches your relationship with the listener.

## Distance and closeness

The difference between ません and ない isn't a change in dictionary meaning—it's a change in social distance.

```jp
{{watashi||私[わたし]}}は{{iku-v|masu|行[い]きません}}。
僕[ぼく]は{{iku-v|nai|行[い]かない}}。
```
*I will not go. (Polite)*
*I won't go. (Casual)*

The ません ending puts a respectful, safe buffer between you and the listener. It's the default choice for your teachers, station staff ({{ekiin||駅[えき]員[いん]}}), and people you just met. It shows you respect their boundaries.

The ない form deliberately removes that buffer. You use it with close friends, your immediate family like your siblings ({{kyoudai||兄[きょう]弟[だい]}}), and when you are just thinking out loud to yourself. In fact, if you insist on using polite forms with your best friend, it can actually sound cold, like you are intentionally pushing them away. Mastering these plain forms is crucial for building real, close relationships in Japanese.

Once you get comfortable using ない and なかった, you'll start to notice they both end in that trailing い sound. Hold onto that thought—because when you formally learn how い-adjectives (like {{ookii||大[おお]きい}} and {{chiisai||小[ちい]さい}}) conjugate later, you'll find they behave exactly the same way. The language is beautifully consistent once you know what to look for.
caution_notes: Never try to mix politeness levels in a single verb—choose either the polite ません or the casual ない, but never combine them.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're at home with a terrible cold, wrapped in a blanket. Your well-meaning friend walks in and goes straight for the window to let in some freezing winter air. You need to stop them politely but quickly.

You already know how to ask someone to do something using てください. Here is how you ask them *not* to.

```jp
{{mado||窓[まど]}}を開[あ]けないでください。
```
*Please don't open the window.*

## How it works

To make a negative request, you take the negative form of the verb (the *nai* form) and attach でください.

For a regular *ru*-verb, just drop the final る and add ない:

```jp
傘[かさ]を忘[わす]れないでください。
```
*Please don't forget your umbrella.*

For a *u*-verb, change the final *u* vowel sound to an *a* sound, then add ない. So {{nomu-v||飲[の]む}} (to drink) becomes {{nomu-v|nai|飲[の]まない}}:

```jp
{{sono||その}}{{mizu||水[みず]}}を{{nomu-v|nai|飲[の]まないで}}ください。
```
*Please don't drink that water.*

And for irregular verbs, you just have to remember their shapes. 心[しん]配[ぱい]{{suru||する}} (to worry) becomes 心[しん]配[ぱい]{{suru|nai|しない}}:

```jp
心[しん]配[ぱい]{{suru|nai|しないで}}ください。
```
*Please don't worry.*

## The missing joint

> A very common trap is forgetting the little で in the middle. It is never `飲まないください`. The で acts like a structural joint, basically meaning "in a state of not doing [verb], please exist."

Grammatically, this is still a polite request because of ください. But because you are directly telling someone what to do (or not do), it can feel a little heavy-handed if used with a boss or teacher. With friends, coworkers, or strangers on the street, it is perfectly fine.

## Casual speech

When you are talking to family or close friends, the full polite phrase often feels too stiff. In casual Japanese, you simply chop off the ください and end the sentence on で.

```jp
{{kyou||今日[きょう]}}は学[がっ]校[こう]に{{iku-v|nai|行[い]かないで}}。
```
*Don't go to school today.*

## Personal requests vs. Hard rules

You recently learned てはいけない (must not). They might seem like they do the same job, but they live in entirely different spaces.

てはいけない expresses a strict rule or prohibition. You use it to state a fact about what is forbidden.

```jp
{{koko||ここ}}に入[はい]ってはいけない。
```
*You must not enter here. (It is against the rules)*

ないでください is a personal favor. You are making a request of the person in front of you.

```jp
{{watashi||私[わたし]}}の部屋[へや]に入[はい]らないでください。
```
*Please don't enter my room. (I am asking you not to)*

Hold onto this negative *nai* form shape. Soon, we'll see how swapping out the でください for something else gives you the power to say what you *must* do.
caution_notes: Always include the particle で between the negative verb and ください; never attach ください directly to the nai-form.
While grammatically polite, this pattern is a direct command and can sound blunt if used with superiors.

items.explanation_markdown:
Your friend texts you: {{ashita||明日[あした]}}試[し]験[けん]が{{aru|masu|あります}}。There's a version of tonight where you watch TV until you fall asleep, and a version where you don't get to choose — because tomorrow's exam doesn't care how you feel about it. Japanese marks that second kind of night with a single ending: なければならない, "must / have to." It turns a plain verb into something you don't get to skip.

## How It Works

なければならない attaches to the same stem you already met in なくても{{ii||いい}} — the ない-stem, the shape a verb takes right before ない. You already know how to build it; this ending just replaces くても{{ii||いい}} with ければならない.

```jp
{{kyou||今日[きょう]}}は漢[かん]字[じ]を覚[おぼ]えなければならない。
```
*I have to memorize kanji today.*

覚[おぼ]える drops its る and takes the ない-stem 覚[おぼ]え, then ければならない tacks straight on. ならない is just the negative of なる (to become) — more on that shape in a moment.

```jp
{{hon||本[ほん]}}も{{yomu|stem|読[よ]ま}}なければならない。
```
*I also have to read the book.*

{{yomu||読[よ]む}} is a different kind of verb — its stem swaps む for ま before any ない-family ending, the same swap you'd make for なくても{{ii||いい}}. も here just means "also," stacking a second obligation on top of the first.

The same swap works for {{iku-v||行[い]く}}, which turns its く into か:

```jp
学[がっ]校[こう]に{{iku-v|stem|行[い]か}}なければならない。
```
*I have to go to school.*

## Rules and Exceptions

That なりません isn't a random polite tag — it's the negative of なる, "to become." Read the whole phrase literally and it says something like "if [this] doesn't happen, it won't become [okay]" — which is exactly the shape of an obligation: skip the verb, and things don't turn out right. Once you see that, なければならない stops looking like a memorized chunk and starts looking like ordinary grammar wearing a long coat.

> Don't split なければ off as its own negative clause. It's one fused ending, not "if not" plus a separate sentence — you can't remove ならない and still mean the same thing.

なければいけない means the same thing and swaps in freely; いけない reads as "it won't do," which lands in the same place as "won't become okay." Some verbs favor one variant over the other for no reason beyond habit, and native speakers mix both without thinking about it.

```jp
{{konshuu||今[こん]週[しゅう]}}、{{hon||本[ほん]}}を返[かえ]さなければいけません。
```
*I have to return the book this week.*

返[かえ]す swaps す for さ before this ending, same pattern as every verb so far.

## Casual Speech

In speech, なければ shrinks hard — down to なきゃ — and いけない often drops entirely, leaving a bare なきゃ standing in for the whole obligation.

```jp
宿[しゅく]題[だい]、{{suru|stem|し}}なきゃいけない。
```
*Gotta do the homework.*

You'll also hear just 宿[しゅく]題[だい]、{{suru|stem|し}}なきゃ。 with nothing after it — the いけない is implied, understood, gone. That's normal, not sloppy; write out the full form in anything that isn't a text message to a friend.

## Contrast

You already know なくても{{ii||いい}} from a few lessons back — it says a verb is optional, not required. Swap it in against なければならない and the meaning flips completely, not just softens.

```jp
音[おん]楽[がく]を聞[き]かなくても{{ii||いい}}です。
```
*I don't have to listen to music.*

Same ない-stem, opposite conclusion: なくても{{ii||いい}} clears the requirement; なければならない installs it. And てはいけない — "must not" — sits on the far side of なければならない, not next to it: one demands an action, the other forbids one.

```jp
{{osoi|stem|遅[おそ]く}}寝[ね]てはいけません。
```
*I must not go to bed late.*

Mixing these up is an easy early mistake: saying `寝なくてもいい` when you mean "you must not sleep late" tells someone the opposite of what you intended — that sleeping late is fine, just not required.

For a fast mental shortcut, the dictionary form and the obligation form line up directly:

```jp
{{iku-v||行[い]く}} → {{iku-v|stem|行[い]か}}なければならない
```
*to go → have to go*

That's the whole engine: find the ない-stem you already know, and decide whether you're forbidding it (てはいけない), excusing it (なくても{{ii||いい}}), or locking it in (なければならない). Later, when you meet ように{{suru||する}}, you'll see the same instinct pointed at habits instead of single obligations — making something happen on purpose, rather than being told it must.
caution_notes: なりません is the polite negative of なる, not a separate negation you can remove from the ending.
なくてもいい and なければならない use the identical ない-stem but land on opposite meanings, so double-check which one you actually wrote.
なきゃいけない and the even shorter なきゃ belong to speech and texts, not formal writing.
てはいけない forbids an action, while なければならない requires one — they are not two strengths of the same rule.

items.explanation_markdown:
It's the night before a test, and your desk is covered in 宿[しゅく]題[だい] you haven't touched. You message a classmate to panic together, and they text back something that stops you cold: not everything on that pile is actually due tomorrow.

```jp
{{kyou||今日[きょう]}}は宿[しゅく]題[だい]を全[ぜん]部[ぶ]{{suru|nai|しなくて}}もいい。
```

*You don't have to finish all the homework today.*

That's なくてもいい — "don't have to," "it's fine even without doing." It tells you a rule you assumed was strict actually has slack in it.

## How it works

Start from the plain negative (ない-form) of the verb, drop the final い, and add くても{{ii||いい}}. {{suru|nai|しない}} becomes {{suru|nai|しなくて}}, and も{{ii||いい}} tacks on the same "it's fine" feeling you already know from ても{{ii||いい}}.

```jp
{{iku-v||行[い]く}} → {{iku-v|nai|行[い]かなくて}}もいい
```

*to go → don't have to go*

```jp
{{taberu||食[た]べる}} → {{taberu|nai|食[た]べなくて}}もいい
```

*to eat → don't have to eat*

U-verbs like {{iku-v||行[い]く}} shift to the あ-row before ない ({{iku-v|stem|行[い]か}}-), and ru-verbs like {{taberu||食[た]べる}} just drop る and add ない — the same split you already learned for building the plain negative in the first place. なくてもいい just rides on top of a form you can already produce.

You'll also see です tacked on for politeness, and a slightly stiffer cousin, なくてもかまわない ("it doesn't matter if you don't"), which leans a little more formal but means the same thing.

```jp
{{ashita||明日[あした]}}は早[はや]く起[お]きなくてもいいです。
```

*You don't have to wake up early tomorrow.*

```jp
{{kyou||今日[きょう]}}は学[がっ]校[こう]へ{{iku-v|nai|行[い]かなくて}}もかまわない。
```

*It's fine even if you don't go to school today.*

## Rules and exceptions

The trap almost everyone falls into first: なくてもいい looks like it should mean "must not," because it has ない sitting right there next to a rule word. It doesn't. It means the opposite of forced — permission to skip, not a ban.

> Don't reach for なくてもいい when you mean "must not." That's a completely different pattern — てはいけない, which you already know — and mixing them up flips the meaning of your sentence.

There's no irregular twist here: any verb that has a plain negative can take なくてもいい, including {{suru||する}} and {{kuru-v||来[く]る}} once they're in their ない-forms ({{suru|nai|しない}}, {{kuru-v|nai|来[こ]ない}}). The pattern is mechanical once the ない-form is solid, which is exactly why it's worth double-checking that form first if a sentence feels off.

## Casual speech

In relaxed conversation, も{{ii||いい}} often just shrinks the sentence's weight rather than changing its wording — you'll hear なくてもいい said fast and clipped, sometimes with {{ii||いい}} swapped for a shrug-toned よ at the end for warmth.

```jp
{{sonna||そんな}}に急[いそ]がなくてもいいよ。
```

*You don't have to hurry that much.*

```jp
心[しん]配[ぱい]{{suru|nai|しなくて}}もいいよ。
```

*You don't have to worry.*

That よ isn't part of the grammar — it's the same softening particle you've seen elsewhere — but it shows up on this pattern constantly because なくてもいい is so often said to reassure someone.

## Contrast

You already have two close relatives of this pattern, and lining them up side by side is the fastest way to keep them separate.

ても{{ii||いい}} gives permission to do something; なくてもいい gives permission to skip it. Same も{{ii||いい}} ending, opposite verb form feeding into it.

```jp
宿[しゅく]題[だい]を{{suru|te|して}}も{{ii||いい}}ですか。
```

*Is it okay if I do the homework?*

Compare that to the very first example above — 宿[しゅく]題[だい]を全[ぜん]部[ぶ]{{suru|nai|しなくて}}もいい, "you don't have to do all the homework" — and the difference is entirely in that one syllable, ない, sitting in front of くても{{ii||いい}}.

てはいけない sits at the opposite end from both of them: it forbids, full stop.

```jp
{{kyou||今日[きょう]}}は宿[しゅく]題[だい]を{{suru|nai|しなくて}}はいけない。
```

*You have to do the homework today.*

Notice that sentence isn't even なくてもいい's opposite — {{suru|nai|しなくて}}はいけない ("must do") is built the same way as なくてもいい but swaps {{ii||いい}} for はいけない, and the meaning flips to an obligation instead of a release from one. Three patterns, three feelings: {{ii||いい}} lets you off the hook, はいけない locks you to it, and mixing up which one you reached for is the single most common mistake with this whole family.

Hold onto that hook feeling — it's the flip side of なければならない, which you'll meet soon and which says "you must" using the same ない-stem this pattern already taught you to build.
caution_notes: Don't confuse なくてもいい with てはいけない — one grants release from a rule, the other forbids the action entirely.
なくてもいい needs a correctly formed ない-stem underneath it, so double-check that form first if the sentence feels off.
なくてもかまわない means the same thing as なくてもいい but reads a little more formal.
The casual よ often tacked onto the end is a separate softening particle, not part of this pattern's grammar.

items.explanation_markdown:
You are at a friend's house. They point to an empty box and ask if you finished the sweets. You want to say "I ate it." If you say {{taberu|masu|食[た]べました}}, you will sound like you are giving a formal report to your boss. You need the casual past tense.

This is where the た形[かたち] (ta-form) comes in. It is the plain, casual equivalent of ました. But here is the best news you will hear all day: if you survived learning the て-form (the connective form), you already know exactly how to make the た-form.

## How it works

The rule is completely identical to the て-form. You just take the て-form of any verb and swap the final て for **た**. If the te-form ends in で, you swap it for **だ**. That is the entire rule.

```jp
{{taberu||食[た]べる}} → {{taberu|te|食[た]べて}} → {{taberu|ta|食[た]べた}}
{{nomu-v||飲[の]む}} → {{nomu-v|te|飲[の]んで}} → {{nomu-v|ta|飲[の]んだ}}
{{kau-v||買[か]う}} → {{kau-v|te|買[か]って}} → {{kau-v|ta|買[か]った}}
{{iku-v||行[い]く}} → {{iku-v|te|行[い]って}} → {{iku-v|ta|行[い]った}}
```
*Eat becomes ate.*
*Drink becomes drank.*
*Buy becomes bought.*
*Go becomes went.*

Let's look at how this sounds in a normal conversation when you are talking to a friend about what you did recently.

```jp
{{kinou||昨日[きのう]}}友[とも]達[だち]と{{hirugohan||昼[ひる]ご飯[はん]}}を{{taberu|ta|食[た]べた}}。
{{senshuu||先[せん]週[しゅう]}}海[かい]に{{iku-v|ta|行[い]った}}。
```
*Yesterday, I ate lunch with a friend.*
*Last week, I went to the sea.*

## Rules and exceptions

Because this is the plain form, it is strictly for casual speech. You use this with your friends, your family, or people younger than you.

> Do not use the plain た-form alone at the end of a sentence with a teacher, a boss, or a stranger. It strips away all the politeness and will sound overly familiar. Stick to ました for those situations.

Also, keep in mind that this is only for affirmative past actions ("I did"). The casual negative past ("I didn't do") is a completely different pattern that builds on the ない-form instead.

## Contrast: ました vs た

Both of these patterns tell the listener that an action is finished and in the past. The only difference is your relationship with the listener.

Notice how the exact same meaning changes its outfit depending on who you are talking to. If you are reporting to your teacher, you use ました. If you are chatting with a friend, you drop down to た.

```jp
{{kyou||今日[きょう]}}学[がっ]校[こう]で{{sensei||先[せん]生[せい]}}に会[あ]いました。
{{kyou||今日[きょう]}}学[がっ]校[こう]で友[とも]達[だち]に会[あ]った。
```
*Today I met my teacher at school.*
*Today I met my friend at school.*

You also already know the て-form, which looks incredibly similar and shares the exact same conjugation rules. Remember that て connects ideas, while た finishes a thought in the past. You will often see them working together in the same sentence.

```jp
{{tegami||手[て]紙[がみ]}}を{{kaku|te|書[か]いて}}、寝[ね]た。
```
*I wrote a letter, and went to sleep.*

Mastering the た-form unlocks a massive chunk of everyday, natural Japanese conversation. You will soon see that it isn't just for verbs, either — hold onto this concept, because we will soon see how adjectives have their own past tense rules to say things like "it *was* big". For now, get comfortable swapping your て for a た.
caution_notes: Do not use the plain た-form alone at the end of a sentence with a teacher, a boss, or a stranger, as it will sound too blunt and familiar.

items.explanation_markdown:
Your friend just got back from a trip and asks if you've ever eaten sushi. Not "do you eat sushi" — "have you ever, at any point in your life, eaten it." English handles this with "have" plus a past participle. Japanese handles it with a little noun, こと (the word that turns a whole action into "a thing" you can talk about), sitting after a verb in its past form, followed by {{aru||ある}} (to exist). Literally: "the thing of having eaten exists." That's the whole idea behind ことがある.

```jp
すしを{{taberu|ta|食[た]べた}}ことがありますか。
```

*Have you ever eaten sushi?*

## How it works

The recipe is simple: take a verb, put it in its plain past (た-form), and add ことがある after it.

```jp
{{hanasu-v||話[はな]す}} → {{hanasu-v|ta|話[はな]した}}
```

{{taberu||食[た]べる}} becomes {{taberu|ta|食[た]べた}}, {{iku-v||行[い]く}} becomes {{iku-v|ta|行[い]った}}, {{noru||乗[の]る}} becomes {{noru|ta|乗[の]った}} — whatever past form you already know, that's the piece that slots in front of こと. The {{aru||ある}} at the end conjugates like the plain "to exist" verb you already know: {{aru|masu|あります}} in polite speech, ない in the negative, {{aru|ta|あった}} if you're describing a past state of "having had that experience" (rare, but it shows up).

```jp
日本[にっぽん]語[ご]を勉[べん]強[きょう]{{suru|ta|した}}ことがあります。
```

*I have studied Japanese before.*

Notice what's *not* changing: the main verb stays frozen in its plain past form no matter how polite the sentence around it gets. You're not conjugating {{taberu||食[た]べる}} for politeness — you're conjugating {{aru||ある}}. That's the part that carries です/ます, and it's the part that turns negative when you want "never."

```jp
いいえ、{{taberu|ta|食[た]べた}}ことがありません。
```

*No, I've never eaten it.*

```jp
飛[ひ]行[こう]機[き]に{{noru|ta|乗[の]った}}ことがあります。
```

*I've been on a plane before.*

That last one is worth sitting with. In English you might say "I've flown before" or "I've been on a plane," and neither maps cleanly onto Japanese word order — but ことがある doesn't care about your English phrasing. It only asks one question: has this specific action, this specific verb, ever happened to you at least once? One time counts. A hundred times counts. The pattern is blind to frequency; it just confirms the experience exists somewhere in your past.

## Rules and exceptions

The biggest trap is reaching for ことがある when you actually mean "I did X yesterday" or "I did X once, at a specific known time." ことがある is for experience in the abstract — "at some point, ever" — not for narrating a specific past event. If your friend asks "what did you do last weekend," answering with a lifetime-experience statement sounds like you're dodging the question with a resume bullet point instead of just telling the story. For a one-off specific event, plain た-form alone does the job: 猫[ねこ]と一[いっ]緒[しょ]に{{oyogu|masu|泳[およ]ぎました}}.

```jp
猫[ねこ]と一[いっ]緒[しょ]に{{oyogu|ta|泳[およ]いだ}}ことがあります。
```

*I've swum together with a cat before.*

That sentence, said flatly, describes a fact about your life history — somewhere, at some point, a cat was involved in your swimming. It doesn't say when, doesn't say how many times, and doesn't say whether it was on purpose.

> Don't drop ことがある onto a dictionary-form verb expecting the same meaning. `食べることがある` is grammatical, but it means something completely different — "it sometimes happens that I eat [this]," a statement about habits, not history. Past tense + ことがある = experience. Dictionary form + ことがある = occasional occurrence. Same skeleton, opposite job, and mixing them up is one of the most common beginner slips with this pattern.

Another edge worth knowing: because {{aru||ある}} is the verb doing all the conjugating, questions form exactly the way you'd expect — swap ます for ますか, or drop the polite ending entirely in casual speech and just raise your voice at the end.

```jp
山[やま]に登[のぼ]ったことがありますか。
```

*Have you ever climbed a mountain?*

## Casual speech

In relaxed conversation, が often just disappears: ことがある becomes こと{{aru||ある}}, said quickly, almost like one word. {{aru|masu|あります}} shrinks the same way informal verbs always do — {{aru|masu|あります}} becomes {{aru||ある}}, {{aru|masu|ありません}} becomes ない. So a casual friend asking about your sushi history might say すし{{taberu|ta|食[た]べた}}こと{{aru||ある}}? instead of the full すしを{{taberu|ta|食[た]べた}}ことがありますか. Same question, same structure underneath, just worn down the way frequently used phrases always wear down in speech.

## Contrast

You've already met つもり for talking about the future — 日本[にっぽん]に{{iku-v||行[い]く}}つもりです, "I intend to go to Japan." ことがある lives in the opposite direction entirely: it only ever looks backward.

```jp
日本[にっぽん]に{{iku-v||行[い]く}}つもりです。
```

*I intend to go to Japan.*

Swap the tense and the verb form and the sentence flips its whole orientation. つもり sits on a dictionary-form verb and points forward, toward a plan that hasn't happened yet. ことがある sits on a た-form verb and points backward, toward something that's already settled into your history. Neither one can do the other's job — you can't use つもり to report an experience you already had, and you can't use ことがある to state an intention. If you're ever unsure which one you need, ask yourself: is this pointing at tomorrow, or at a memory?

Hold onto this shape, too — you're about to meet ことに{{suru||する}}, which reuses the same こと (turning an action into "a thing") but glues it to a completely different verb, and lands on "I've decided to." Same building block, new direction.
caution_notes: ことがある only attaches to a verb's plain past (た-form) — putting it on the dictionary form instead changes the meaning to an occasional habit, not a past experience.
Use ことがある for experience in general, not to narrate one specific known event from last week — plain past alone tells that kind of story.
In casual speech が can drop and あります can shrink to ある, but the underlying ことがある structure stays the same.
つもり points forward to an intention and ことがある points backward to an experience — they can never substitute for each other.

items.explanation_markdown:
Imagine you are catching up with a coworker on a Monday morning, and they ask what you did over the weekend. If you try to list out your actions strictly—saying, "I read a book, I watched TV, and I slept"—it can sound a bit like a police interrogation report. You are giving a rigid, step-by-step timeline of your weekend that feels almost too precise.

In real life, we usually want to give a more relaxed summary. You want to say, "Oh, you know, I did things like reading and watching TV." You aren't claiming that those two activities are the *only* things you did, nor are you saying you did them in a specific order. You are just pulling a couple of representative examples out of a hat to give a general vibe of how you spent your day.

To do this in Japanese, you use the `〜たり〜たりする` pattern. It is the absolute best tool for creating a relaxed, non-exhaustive list of actions, and mastering it will instantly make your Japanese sound more natural and less robotic.

## How it works

To build this pattern, you need the plain past tense form of your verb. You already know this form from when we learned how to talk about past experiences with `たことがある` (have done before). Because it always ends in a "ta" sound, teachers often just call it the "た-form".

Take your verb's た-form, and simply attach `り` to the very end.

- `読む` (to read) becomes `読んだ` (read), which becomes `読んだり`.
- `見る` (to watch) becomes `見た` (watched), which becomes `見たり`.
- `買う` (to buy) becomes `買った` (bought), which becomes `買ったり`.

Once you have your verbs ready, you string them together and finish the entire package with the verb `する` (to do).

```jp
週[しゅう]末[まつ]、{{hon||本[ほん]}}を{{yomu|stem|読[よ]ん}}だり、{{terebi||テレビ}}を{{miru-v|stem|見[み]}}たり{{suru|masu|しました}}。
```
*Over the weekend, I did things like read books and watch TV.*

Think of these `たり` verbs as floating ideas. By themselves, they do not carry any actual tense, and they aren't polite or casual. They are just raw, timeless concepts: "things like reading", "things like watching". 

It is that final `する` at the end of the sentence that acts as the engine. It grounds those floating ideas in time and determines exactly how polite you are being. In the example above, `する` becomes `しました` because the weekend is in the past, and you are speaking politely to your coworker.

If you are talking about a daily habit or something you do regularly, the final verb is just the present tense `します`.

```jp
{{mainichi||毎[まい]日[にち]}}、友[とも]達[だち]と{{hanasu-v|stem|話[はな]し}}たり、{{ocha||お茶[ちゃ]}}を{{nomu-v|stem|飲[の]ん}}だり{{suru|masu|します}}。
```
*Every day, I do things like talk with friends and drink tea.*

## Rules and exceptions

Because English speakers are used to assigning time to every single verb in a sentence ("Tomorrow I *will* go and I *will* buy"), this pattern holds a very common trap: trying to make the `たり` verbs match the time of the event.

If you are talking about your plans for tomorrow, you might feel a strong urge to use a future or present form for the list. Do not do this! The verbs inside the list are *always* frozen in the past `た` form, even if the action hasn't happened yet. Only the final `する` gets to change to show the future tense.

```jp
{{ashita||明日[あした]}}、町[まち]へ{{iku-v|stem|行[い]っ}}たり、服[ふく]を{{kau-v|stem|買[か]っ}}たり{{suru|masu|します}}。
```
*Tomorrow, I will do things like go to town and buy clothes.*

Notice how it is still `行ったり` and `買ったり`, even though the sentence is clearly about tomorrow (`明日`). The final `します` does all the heavy lifting to tell the listener this is a future plan. Never try to say something like `行くなり` or `買うたり`—the form is strictly locked to the past tense shape.

> **The phonetic shift:** Just like with the `て` and `た` forms, verbs that end in a voiced, heavy sound in their dictionary form (like `読む` or `遊ぶ`) carry that heaviness over. Because their た-form ends in `だ` instead of `た`, they take `だり` instead of `たり`.

For example, `遊ぶ` (to play) becomes `遊んだ`, which becomes `遊んだり`. `飲む` (to drink) becomes `飲んだ`, which becomes `飲んだり`.

```jp
公[こう]園[えん]で遊[あそ]んだり、{{mizu||水[みず]}}を{{nomu-v|stem|飲[の]ん}}だり{{suru|masu|しました}}。
```
*I did things like play in the park and drink water.*

Another massive feature of this grammar point: you do not actually have to list two things. You can absolutely use just a single `たり` to soften a statement. When you use it with just one verb, it implies, "I did this... among other things." It acts like a verbal shrug that keeps you from sounding overly declarative.

```jp
{{kinou||昨日[きのう]}}は、家[いえ]で寝[ね]たり{{suru|masu|しました}}。
```
*Yesterday, I did things like sleep at home.*

## Casual speech

When you are speaking casually with close friends or family members, you simply drop the polite `します` or `しました` and use the casual forms of `する`, which are `する` (for present/future) and `した` (for past).

In extremely casual, fast-paced Japanese, people sometimes drop the `する` completely if the context is totally obvious, leaving the sentence hanging on `〜たり`. However, as a learner, you should strongly stick to always including the final `する` or `した`. Leaving it off by accident in a polite conversation sounds abruptly unfinished and a bit rude, so build the muscle memory of attaching `する` every time first.

## Mixing menus and rules

You already know a few powerful rules for giving permission and setting boundaries. Let's look at how beautifully the `たり〜たり` list integrates with the grammar you already know. 

Think about the pattern `てもいい` (it's okay to / you may). If you say `テレビを見てもいいです` (you may watch TV), it is a specific green light for one single action.

But what if you are hosting a guest, and you want to offer them a menu of options? You just take your `たり` list and swap the final `する` engine for `してもいい`.

```jp
{{watashi||私[わたし]}}の部屋[へや]で、{{terebi||テレビ}}を{{miru-v|stem|見[み]}}たり、{{hon||本[ほん]}}を{{yomu|stem|読[よ]ん}}だり{{suru|te|して}}も{{ii||いい}}です。
```
*In my room, you may do things like watch TV or read a book.*

Suddenly, you aren't just granting rigid permission; you are being an accommodating host offering a variety of choices. The list provides the options, and the final `してもいい` grants the permission for all of them at once.

The exact same magic works in reverse with `てはいけない` (must not). A library doesn't just have one single rule; they have a blanket policy of disruptive behaviors to avoid. By changing the final `する` to `してはいけません` (the polite form of must not do), you create a comprehensive ban.

```jp
図[と]書[しょ]館[かん]で{{hanasu-v|stem|話[はな]し}}たり、{{denwa||電[でん]話[わ]}}を{{tsukau|stem|使[つか]っ}}たり{{suru|te|して}}はいけません。
```
*You must not do things like talk or use the phone in the library.*

And if you want to reassure someone that they have the day off and absolutely no obligations to worry about, you can plug in `なくてもいい` (don't have to).

```jp
{{ashita||明日[あした]}}、学[がっ]校[こう]へ{{iku-v|stem|行[い]っ}}たり、{{hon||本[ほん]}}を{{yomu|stem|読[よ]ん}}だり{{suru|nai|しなくて}}も{{ii||いい}}です。
```
*Tomorrow, you don't have to do things like go to school or read a book.*

The `たり〜たり` pattern turns rigid, singular actions into flexible, representative lists. Because it relies completely on that final `する` to decide the sentence's ultimate meaning, it is incredibly modular. Hold onto this concept of swapping the final engine. When we learn how to express personal desire with `たい` (want to do) later on, you will already know exactly how to say that you want to do things like watch a movie and sleep—you will just swap that hardworking `する` for a `したい`.
caution_notes: The verbs inside the list are always frozen in the past tense (た-form), even if you are talking about future plans.
Never forget to add the final する (or しました, します) at the very end of the sentence to establish the tense and politeness.
Verbs that end in a voiced sound (like 読む or 遊ぶ) take だり instead of たり.

items.explanation_markdown:
You've had a long week, and your friend asks what you're doing this weekend. You don't just plan to sleep—you actively crave it. To express what you want to do, you need a specific pattern.

## How it works

To build this pattern, take the stem of a verb (the part right before `ます`) and attach `たい`. The verb `寝ます` (sleep) becomes `寝` plus `たい`. Add `です` at the end to keep things polite.

```jp
週[しゅう]末[まつ]は寝[ね]たいです。
{{watashi||私[わたし]}}は日本[にっぽん]へ{{iku-v|stem|行[い]き}}たいです。
{{ano||あの}}映[えい]画[が]を{{miru-v|stem|見[み]}}たいです。
```
*I want to sleep on the weekend.*
*I want to go to Japan.*
*I want to watch that movie.*

### Shapeshifting like an adjective

The real magic of `たい` is that once you attach it, your verb transforms into an *i-adjective*. It ends in `い`, so it conjugates exactly like descriptive words you already know, such as `高い` (expensive) or `新しい` (new). 

To make it negative, drop the `い` and add `くない`. For the past tense, drop the `い` and add `かった`.

```jp
{{kyou||今日[きょう]}}は{{kaisha||会[かい]社[しゃ]}}へ{{iku-v|stem|行[い]き}}たくないです。
{{kinou||昨日[きのう]}}、{{ano||あの}}{{hon||本[ほん]}}を{{kau-v|stem|買[か]い}}たかったです。
```
*I don't want to go to the office today.*
*Yesterday, I wanted to buy that book.*

## The unwritten rules of desire

> You can only use `たい` to talk about your *own* desires, or to ask someone directly about theirs (like "Do you want to go?"). You cannot use this pattern to state "He wants to go" or "She wants to eat."

There is also a quirk with particles. When you use a verb that normally takes `を` (like drinking water), you will often hear Japanese speakers swap it for `が` when using `たい`.

Because `たい` acts like an adjective, "wanting to drink" becomes a descriptive state rather than a direct action. Both `を` and `が` are perfectly natural here.

```jp
{{mizu||水[みず]}}が{{nomu-v|stem|飲[の]み}}たいです。
```
*I want to drink water.*

## Keeping it casual

Because `たい` behaves exactly like an i-adjective, making it casual is as simple as dropping `です`. In questions, just use a rising intonation instead of adding `か`.

```jp
{{ima||今[いま]}}、{{kaeru-v|stem|帰[かえ]り}}たい。
{{ashita||明日[あした]}}、{{au|stem|会[あ]い}}たい？
```
*I want to go home now.*
*Do you want to meet tomorrow?*

## When desire meets obligation

Sometimes what you want to do and what you *must* do are entirely different things. You already know `なければならない` for obligations. Notice how these two patterns stack up against each other in real life.

```jp
{{byouin||病[びょう]院[いん]}}へ{{iku-v|stem|行[い]き}}たくないです。
{{byouin||病[びょう]院[いん]}}へ{{iku-v|stem|行[い]か}}なければ{{naru-become|masu|なりません}}。
```
*I don't want to go to the hospital.*
*I have to go to the hospital.*

We've spent this whole time talking about actions you want to *do*. If you just want a physical *thing*—like money or a new camera—you won't use `たい`. There is a different word for that coming right up.
caution_notes: You can only use たい to express your own desires, or to ask directly about the listener's desires.
Once you attach たい, the verb transforms into an i-adjective and conjugates exactly like one (たくない, たかった).

items.explanation_markdown:
You have been walking around town all afternoon in the summer heat. You walk into a convenience store, head straight for the cold drinks, and think: "I want water."

```jp
{{mizu||水[みず]}}がほしいです。
```
*I want water.*

When you want a physical object—something you can hold, buy, or point to—you use the word ほしい.

## The mechanics of wanting

The structure for expressing what you want is simple: **Noun + が + ほしい**.

Notice the particle が. In English, we say "I want a car", treating the car as the direct object of an action. But in Japanese, ほしい is actually an *i-adjective* (a descriptive word like {{ookii||大[おお]きい}} or {{atarashii-adj||新[あたら]しい}}). You are literally saying "to me, a car is desirable". That is why we usually use が to mark the thing you want, instead of the object particle を.

```jp
{{atarashii-adj||新[あたら]しい}}車[くるま]がほしいです。
```
*I want a new car.*

Because ほしい functions exactly like an adjective, it follows all the normal conjugation rules you already know. To make it negative, drop the い and add くない. To make it past tense, drop the い and add かった.

```jp
古[ふる]い服[ふく]はほしくないです。
```
*I don't want old clothes.*

```jp
去[きょ]年[ねん]、{{kamera||カメラ}}がほしかったです。
```
*Last year, I wanted a camera.*

## Reading minds

There is one major catch with ほしい. Because Japanese is culturally extremely careful about not claiming to know what other people are feeling inside, you can only use ほしい for **your own desires**, or when asking someone directly about theirs.

You can declare "I want a book" or ask your friend "Do you want a book?". But you cannot state as a plain fact that your friend wants a book.

> Saying `彼女は本がほしいです` sounds presumptuous, as if you are reading her mind. Later on, you will learn specific grammar to talk about what other people seem to want, but for now, keep ほしい limited to the first and second person.

## Casual speech

When you are talking with friends or family, you drop the です completely. In real casual speech, people also frequently drop the particle が, leaving just the noun and the adjective.

```jp
{{ocha||お茶[ちゃ]}}がほしいですか。
```
*Do you want some tea? (Polite)*

```jp
{{ocha||お茶[ちゃ]}}、ほしい？
```
*Want some tea? (Casual)*

## Things vs. Actions

This one trips everyone up the first week, so don't worry if it takes a moment to click. You already learned how to say you want to *do* something using たい. So when do you use ほしい, and when do you use たい?

It strictly comes down to nouns versus verbs.

If you want a **thing** (a noun), use ほしい. If you want to **do an action** (a verb), use たい. Look at how these two sentences feel different:

```jp
{{pasokon||パソコン}}がほしいです。
```
*I want a computer.*

```jp
{{pasokon||パソコン}}を{{kau-v|stem|買[か]い}}たいです。
```
*I want to buy a computer.*

You can never attach ほしい directly to a verb, and you can never attach たい directly to a noun. They each have their own strict territory.

Once you master asking for what you want, you will eventually want to rank those desires—hold onto this thought for when we meet 一[いち]番[ばん] (the most) to say what you want more than anything else in the world.
caution_notes: You can only use ほしい to state your own desires, not those of a third person like 'he' or 'she'.
Use ほしい for wanting nouns (things) and たい for wanting verbs (actions)—they cannot be swapped.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're making weekend plans and you want to tell a friend what you're up to. You know how to say "I'm going to the cinema" (映[えい]画[が]館[かん]に行[い]く) and you know how to say "I will watch a movie" (映[えい]画[が]を{{miru-v||見[み]る}}). But how do you combine them into a single, natural thought?

You need a way to say you are going *in order to* do something.

## How it works

You already know the particle に can mark a destination or a time. Here, it steps up to mark the **purpose** of your movement.

To build this pattern, take the verb for the action you want to do and chop off the ます. We call this the "verb stem." Then, attach に, and finish with a movement verb like {{iku-v||行[い]く}} (to go), {{kuru-v||来[く]る}} (to come), or {{kaeru-v||帰[かえ]る}} (to return).

- {{miru-v||見[み]る}} (to watch) becomes {{miru-v|stem|見[み]}}. Add に行[い]く and you get {{miru-v|stem|見[み]}}に行[い]く (go to watch).
- 遊[あそ]ぶ (to play/hang out) becomes `遊び`. Add に来[く]る and you get 遊[あそ]びに来[く]る (come to hang out).
- {{taberu||食[た]べる}} (to eat) becomes {{taberu|stem|食[た]べ}}. Add に帰[かえ]る and you get {{taberu|stem|食[た]べ}}に帰[かえ]る (return to eat).

Usually, you also want to say *where* you are going. You put the place at the beginning of the sentence.

```jp
映[えい]画[が]館[かん]へ映[えい]画[が]を{{miru-v|stem|見[み]}}に行[い]く。
```
*I'm going to the cinema to watch a movie.*

```jp
友[とも]達[だち]が{{uchi||うち}}へ遊[あそ]びに来[く]る。
```
*A friend is coming to my house to hang out.*

```jp
{{mainichi||毎[まい]日[にち]}}、学[がっ]校[こう]へ勉[べん]強[きょう]{{suru|stem|し}}に行[い]く。
```
*Every day, I go to school to study.*

> You might notice we used the direction particle へ for the destination (映[えい]画[が]館[かん]へ) instead of に. While you *can* say 映[えい]画[が]館[かん]に映[えい]画[が]を{{miru-v|stem|見[み]}}に行[い]く, using に twice in the same sentence feels repetitive. Many Japanese speakers prefer へ for the destination just to keep things sounding clean.

## Rules and exceptions

This pattern is incredibly strict about how it ends. The final verb **must** be a verb of physical movement. You can't use this grammar to say "I stood up to see" or "I sat down to eat." It exists exclusively for going, coming, or returning somewhere.

```jp
妹[いもうと]は{{maiban||毎[まい]晩[ばん]}}、{{bangohan||晩[ばん]ご飯[はん]}}を{{taberu|stem|食[た]べ}}に帰[かえ]る。
```
*Every night, my younger sister returns home to eat dinner.*

## Dropping it in casual speech

In fast, casual conversation, Japanese speakers often drop the purpose に entirely to save breath, smashing the two verbs straight together. You should stick to the full に行[い]く form for polite speech or any written tests, and only recognize the dropped version when you hear it.

## Stacking with what you know

Because {{iku-v||行[い]く}} is just a normal verb, you can plug it right into other grammar rules you've already learned, like combining it with a list of activities using たり〜たり{{suru||する}}.

```jp
週[しゅう]末[まつ]、友[とも]達[だち]と遊[あそ]びに行[い]く。
```
*This weekend, I'll go hang out with a friend.*

```jp
{{resutoran||レストラン}}へ{{oishii||おいしい}}{{gohan||ご飯[はん]}}を{{taberu|stem|食[た]べ}}に行[い]く。
```
*I go to a restaurant to eat delicious food.*

```jp
週[しゅう]末[まつ]は、{{hon||本[ほん]}}を{{kau-v|stem|買[か]っ}}たり、映[えい]画[が]を{{miru-v|stem|見[み]}}に{{iku-v|stem|行[い]っ}}たり{{suru||する}}。
```
*On the weekend, I do things like buy books and go watch movies.*

Now you can declare your own plans. But what if you want to invite someone else? "How about going to eat?" You'll need {{dou||どう}}ですか for that, which is coming up next.
caution_notes: This grammar pattern only works with verbs of physical movement like 行く, 来る, and 帰る at the end.
Using に twice in a sentence for both the destination and the purpose is grammatically fine, but many speakers prefer へ for the destination to avoid repeating it.

items.explanation_markdown:
Picture this. You just arrived at a friend's house. You can smell something amazing coming from the kitchen. They just finished cooking dinner, and the table is set. You are starving and ready to dig right in. You pull up a chair, but your friend points a stern finger toward the bathroom sink.

You need to wash your hands *before* you eat.

In English, "before" is a very simple word. You just slap it in front of a noun or a verb phrase and move on with your life. But to talk about the sequence of events in Japanese, you have to understand how the language treats time. It helps to think of time as a physical space.

## How it works

To say "before" in Japanese, we use the pattern `前に` (まえに). Let's break this down.

The word `前` translates directly to "front." Think of time as a road you are walking down. The things that haven't happened yet are physically in "front" of you.

Then we have the particle `に`. You already know that `に` is used to pin an action to a specific time on the clock. It works the exact same way here. By combining them, `前に` literally means "at the time in front of" or "at the point just before."

Let's look at how to attach it to the actions you want to take.

### Attaching to verbs

When you are attaching an action to `前に`, you must always use the verb's **dictionary form**. This is the plain, basic form of the verb you look up in the dictionary.

```jp
{{taberu||食[た]べる}}前[まえ]に{{te-v||手[て]}}を洗[あら]う。
```
*I wash my hands before eating.*

Why the dictionary form? This is where Japanese logic is incredibly consistent. The dictionary form is technically called the "non-past" or "incomplete" form.

Think about the exact moment you are standing at the sink washing your hands. Has the eating happened yet? No. The eating is still in the future. It is completely incomplete. Because the eating hasn't happened yet relative to washing your hands, it must stay in its basic, un-conjugated state.

### Attaching to nouns

What if you want to use a noun instead of a verb? Maybe you want to say "before class" or "before dinner."

Grammatically speaking, `前` is actually a noun itself. In Japanese, you cannot just smash two nouns together like building blocks. You need a way to link them. This is where your trusty noun-gluing particle `の` comes to the rescue.

The formula is straightforward: Noun + `の` + `前に`.

```jp
授[じゅ]業[ぎょう]の前[まえ]に{{koohii||コーヒー}}を{{nomu-v||飲[の]む}}。
```
*I drink coffee before class.*

```jp
{{bangohan||晩[ばん]ご飯[はん]}}の前[まえ]に{{terebi||テレビ}}を{{miru-v||見[み]る}}。
```
*I watch TV before dinner.*

You can use this structure with almost any "event" noun. It works perfectly for meals, school, work, or any scheduled block of time in your day.

## The past tense trap

Now we arrive at the single biggest trap for English speakers learning this pattern. This one trips almost everyone up the first week, so it is completely normal if it feels a little backwards at first.

What happens if you are telling a story about yesterday? In English, we say "Before I *slept*, I *read* a book." Both verbs are safely conjugated into the past tense.

Let's see how Japanese handles that exact same sentence.

```jp
寝[ね]る前[まえ]に{{hon||本[ほん]}}を{{yomu|ta|読[よ]んだ}}。
```
*I read a book before sleeping.*

Look closely at that first verb. `寝る` (to sleep) is still in the dictionary form! Even though you read the book last night—an action firmly in the past, shown by the past tense `読んだ` at the end of the sentence—the sleeping is not conjugated.

> **Never put the verb before 前[まえ]に in the past tense.** Even if your entire story happened ten years ago, `寝た前に` is always grammatically incorrect and will confuse the person you are talking to.

Why does Japanese do this? It comes back to that relative time logic we talked about earlier.

Japanese grammar doesn't care about the absolute time on the clock right now. It cares about the time *relative to the actions*. At the exact moment you were reading the book last night, the sleeping was still in your future.

The verb at the very end of the sentence acts like a time machine. That final verb (`読んだ`) is the anchor. It pulls the entire sentence into the past. Every other verb in the sentence just relates to that final anchor point. 

## Using it to say "ago"

There is a special, extremely useful shortcut you can take when dealing with exact numbers and time durations.

If you attach `前に` directly to a duration of time—like minutes, hours, or days—it translates to "ago." It literally means "at the time before this duration."

```jp
三[さん]時[じ]間[かん]前[まえ]に{{kuru-v|ta|来[き]た}}。
```
*I came three hours ago.*

Notice what is missing here? There is no `の`. When you use a specific time duration like "three hours" (`三時間`) or "five minutes" (`五分`), you attach it directly to the pattern. You do not say `三時間の前に`.

```jp
五[ご]分[ふん]前[まえ]に起[お]きた。
```
*I woke up five minutes ago.*

This is one of the most common and natural ways to answer the question "When did you get here?" or "When did that happen?"

## Casual speech drops

As you start listening to native speakers, you will notice that casual Japanese is all about efficiency. When speaking casually with friends, people love to drop particles to speed up their sentences.

The `に` in `前に` is a prime target for this. In casual, everyday speech, it is often dropped entirely, leaving just `前`.

```jp
友[とも]達[だち]が{{kuru-v||来[く]る}}前[まえ]、部屋[へや]を{{deru-v||出[で]る}}。
```
*Before my friend comes, I'll leave the room.*

This doesn't change the meaning at all. It just lowers the formality and makes the sentence flow a bit faster. You can safely use this shorter version around people you are close with.

## Contrast: Setting the sequence

You already know how to use `てから` to say "after doing" something. You use it to sequence events, like saying "After I wake up, I eat."

`てから` and `前に` live in the exact same grammatical space. They are two tools for the exact same job, but they are mirror images of each other. Knowing when to use which depends entirely on what part of the sequence you want to emphasize.

Let's say you have a movie you want to watch and you also want to get some sleep.

If you want to emphasize the first action, you use `てから`. Remember that `てから` requires the `て`-form of the verb.

```jp
映[えい]画[が]を{{miru-v|te|見[み]て}}から、寝[ね]る。
```
*After watching the movie, I sleep.*

If you want to emphasize the second action, you use `前に`. And as we just covered extensively, `前に` demands the dictionary form.

```jp
寝[ね]る前[まえ]に、映[えい]画[が]を{{miru-v||見[み]る}}。
```
*Before sleeping, I watch a movie.*

Notice how swapping from `てから` to `前に` means you have to physically flip the order of the actions in your sentence.

With `てから`, the first thing out of your mouth is the first thing you actually do. You watch the movie, then you sleep.

With `前に`, the first thing out of your mouth is the *second* thing you actually do. You mention sleeping first, but watching the movie is what actually happens first in reality.

It takes a little bit of mental gymnastics to flip these around on the fly. Don't worry if you have to pause for a second while speaking to line up your timeline. Everyone goes through that phase!

Mastering `前に` gives you immense control over telling stories and scheduling your day. Just remember the golden rule: lock that first verb in the dictionary form, and let the end of the sentence do all the time traveling for you. 

Hold onto this relative-time logic tightly. It's going to become incredibly important when we learn the exact opposite pattern—`後で` (after)—very soon!
caution_notes: Never use the past tense before 前に; the verb must always stay in the dictionary form, even if the sentence describes a past event.
When attaching a noun to 前に, you must always use the particle の (e.g., 授業の前に).

items.explanation_markdown:
You're wrapping up at the office, and a friend texts to ask if you want to hang out. You want to tell them you'll call them after work. You already know how to say "work" and "call", but you need the glue to stick them together.

In Japanese, to say "after doing X," you use 後[あと]で. It literally translates to "at the later (time)."

```jp
仕[し]事[ごと]の後[あと]で、{{denwa||電[でん]話[わ]}}{{suru|masu|します}}。
```
*After work, I will call.*

## How it works

If you want to place a noun on the timeline, you just connect it to 後[あと]で with the particle の.

```jp
授[じゅ]業[ぎょう]の後[あと]で、映[えい]画[が]を{{miru-v|masu|見[み]ます}}。
```
*After class, I will watch a movie.*

But when you want to say "after *doing* something," you have to attach a verb. Here is the golden rule: the verb before 後[あと]で must always be in its plain past form (the た-form).

```jp
{{gohan||ご飯[はん]}}を{{taberu|ta|食[た]べた}}後[あと]で、{{ocha||お茶[ちゃ]}}を{{nomu-v|masu|飲[の]みます}}。
```
*After eating a meal, I drink tea.*

Why the past tense? Because on your mental timeline, the eating has to be completely finished before the tea drinking can begin. You're saying "in the aftermath of having eaten." Do not use the dictionary form here — saying `食べる後で` is grammatically incorrect.

## Rules and exceptions

The most common trap here is overthinking the tense of your sentence. Remember that the verb before 後[あと]で is *always* locked into the past tense (た-form), even if the whole sentence is talking about your plans for tomorrow.

> The tense of the actual event is controlled entirely by the very last verb in the sentence.

If you did something yesterday, the ending verb is in the past tense. But the verb glued to 後[あと]で stays exactly the same.

```jp
{{hon||本[ほん]}}を{{yomu|ta|読[よ]んだ}}後[あと]で、寝[ね]ました。
```
*After I read a book, I went to sleep.*

## Casual speech

You will very often see this written entirely in hiragana as あとで. Both are perfectly normal, though the kanji is slightly more common in formal writing.

In casual speech, people sometimes drop the で entirely and just say あと. If you're talking to a friend, `食べたあと` (after I eat) sounds a bit more relaxed than `食べた後で`, but keeping the で is the safest habit to build right now.

## Wait, what about てから?

You already know `てから`, which also means "after doing." They feel similar, but they have a slightly different flavor.

`てから` is a tight, direct sequence. It implies "A finishes, and then B happens as the direct next step." `後で` is a looser timeline. It just means B happens at *some point* after A.

There's also a structural difference. You can use nouns directly with `後で` (like `仕事の後で`), but you cannot do that with `てから`.

And what about `前に` (before)? They work as exact opposites, but notice the verb forms. Since "before" means the action hasn't happened yet, `前に` takes the dictionary form. Since "after" means the action is finished, `後で` takes the た-form.

```jp
映[えい]画[が]を{{miru-v||見[み]る}}前[まえ]に、{{gohan||ご飯[はん]}}を{{taberu|masu|食[た]べます}}。
```
*Before watching a movie, I will eat a meal.*

```jp
映[えい]画[が]を{{miru-v|ta|見[み]た}}後[あと]で、{{gohan||ご飯[はん]}}を{{taberu|masu|食[た]べます}}。
```
*After watching a movie, I will eat a meal.*

Hold onto this sense of a mental timeline. Right now we're looking at things that happen clearly before or after each other. Later, at N4, we'll look at how to describe things happening at the exact same time when we meet `ながら`.
caution_notes: The verb before 後で is always in the past tense (た-form), even if the main event happens in the future.
The tense of the entire sentence is controlled by the final verb, not the verb attached to 後で.
