items.explanation_markdown:
You're at a friend's place for dinner, and they hand you a bowl of something they made themselves. It looks like an ordinary side dish — a little glossy, a little brown — nothing unusual on the surface. Then it hits your tongue and it's unmistakably sweet, like dessert wearing a dinner costume. You want to say something on the spot, casually, without stopping to construct a careful sentence first.

```jp
{{kono||この}}{{ryouri||料[りょう]理[り]}}は{{okashi||お菓[か]子[し]}}みたいだ。
```

*This dish tastes like candy.*

You could just say this is sweet — that's true, and it's simple — but that flattens the moment. What you actually want to report is the mismatch: it presents itself as one thing and turns out, as far as you can tell, to be another. English reaches for "seems like" or "tastes like" for exactly this job, and Japanese has a single, compact word that does the same work without any extra machinery.

That reaction — this looks, tastes, or feels like something else, going purely on your own impression in the moment — is exactly what みたいだ is built for. Attach it to the **plain form** (the casual, dictionary-style form you'd use with friends, not the polite -ます form) of almost anything, and an impression turns into a full sentence with barely any effort.

## How it works

みたいだ is easygoing about what it attaches to — nouns, na-adjectives, i-adjectives, and verbs all work, and for most of them the plain form is all you need, with nothing inserted in between.

With a noun, みたいだ just sits directly on top of it. {{okashi||お菓[か]子[し]}} (a sweet) plus みたいだ gives you exactly the sentence above — no connecting word, no extra syllable, nothing to remember except to keep them next to each other.

Na-adjectives lose something on the way in. Watch what happens to {{shizuka||静[しず]か}} (quiet):

```jp
{{shizuka||静[しず]か}} → {{shizuka||静[しず]か}}みたいだ
```

*quiet → seems quiet*

```jp
{{kono||この}}{{heya||部屋[へや]}}は{{shizuka||静[しず]か}}みたいだ。
```

*This room seems quiet.*

Notice what's missing: no な. A na-adjective normally needs that な right before a noun ({{shizuka||静[しず]か}}な{{heya||部屋[へや]}}, a quiet room), but in front of みたいだ it drops out completely — みたいだ treats the na-adjective's bare stem the same way it treats a noun, so nothing extra gets inserted.

I-adjectives don't change at all. The form you'd find in a dictionary is the exact form you use:

```jp
{{ano||あの}}{{ryouri||料[りょう]理[り]}}は{{karai||辛[から]い}}みたいだ。
```

*That dish looks spicy.*

Verbs behave the same way — plain form, completely untouched:

```jp
{{ani||兄[あに]}}は{{ban||晩[ばん]}}に{{deru-v||出[で]る}}みたいだ。
```

*My older brother seems to be going out in the evening.*

Line them up and the shape is consistent:

- noun — bare, no connector ({{okashi||お菓[か]子[し]}}みたいだ)
- na-adjective — bare stem, no な ({{shizuka||静[しず]か}}みたいだ)
- i-adjective — dictionary form, unchanged ({{karai||辛[から]い}}みたいだ)
- verb — plain form, unchanged ({{deru-v||出[で]る}}みたいだ)

One shape, four word types, nothing extra to memorize once you've seen it applied. For all four, swap だ for です whenever the company calls for it — {{ano||あの}}{{ryouri||料[りょう]理[り]}}は{{karai||辛[から]い}}みたいです instead, same meaning, just dressed up a little for someone you don't know well.

## Rules and exceptions

The な that na-adjectives usually carry is the single most common slip here. `静かなみたいだ` feels like it should be right, because that な shows up everywhere else {{shizuka||静[しず]か}} goes — but not in front of みたいだ. Only {{shizuka||静[しず]か}}みたいだ is correct; the な simply has no job to do there.

> The same instinct causes trouble with nouns, usually from learners who've already met ようだ, which does take の after a noun. That の doesn't carry over: `料理のみたいだ` is wrong. みたいだ never takes の, on nouns or anything else.

It's tempting to reach for はず here instead, since you already have it for "should be" — but はず is about logical expectation, not appearance. はず fits when you've worked something out and expect it to be true; みたいだ fits when you're going purely on what's in front of you right now, no working-out required. The two can even show up describing the same situation and still disagree, because they're reporting two different kinds of confidence.

Plain みたいだ is casual by nature — perfectly fine with friends and family, a little blunt for a stranger, a client, or your boss. Reach for みたいです the moment the conversation turns more formal, the same way you'd reach for です anywhere else in the sentence.

The textbook line between "my own impression right now" (みたいだ), "something I heard or read" (らしい), and "what the evidence suggests" (ようだ) is cleaner on paper than it is in an actual conversation. Plenty of native speakers reach for みたいだ in all three situations and let context sort out which one they mean; noticing the categories blur in real speech is a sign you're paying attention, not a sign you're doing something wrong.

One more edge worth knowing: once you've actually confirmed what's going on — you've tasted the dish, you already know for a fact it's sweet — the guess disappears, and so does みたいだ. You'd just state the fact plainly, the same way you would in English once you'd stopped guessing and started knowing.

## Casual speech

In relaxed spoken Japanese, だ often disappears right before ね, especially once a sentence is basically just confirming something out loud to whoever's standing next to you.

```jp
{{ame-v||雨[あめ]}}みたいだね。
```

*Looks like rain, doesn't it.*

```jp
{{ame-v||雨[あめ]}}みたいね。
```

*Looks like rain, doesn't it.*

Both get used constantly; dropping the だ just sounds a touch more offhand, a little quicker off the tongue. Keep the だ in writing, or anywhere you want the sentence to stand on its own as a complete thought.

## Contrast

ようだ covers almost identical ground — an impression based on what you can see, hear, or otherwise sense — but it asks for more scaffolding on nouns and na-adjectives, and it reads more neutral, closer to something you'd write in a report than blurt out over dinner.

```jp
{{kono||この}}{{ryouri||料[りょう]理[り]}}は{{okashi||お菓[か]子[し]}}のようだ。
```

*This dish is like candy.*

Same dish, same idea as the sentence you opened with, but notice the の holding {{okashi||お菓[か]子[し]}} and ようだ together. That の is required with ようだ and forbidden with みたいだ — the single biggest thing to keep straight between the two once you know both. You'll meet ようだ constantly in writing and in anything read aloud for an audience — a script, an announcement over a station platform speaker — anywhere a sentence needs to sound composed rather than tossed off between friends. みたいだ almost never shows up in that kind of formal delivery; it belongs to conversation, texts, anywhere you'd talk the way you actually talk.

らしい lives in a different lane entirely: it's for something you picked up secondhand — a forecast on the news, a rumor, something someone told you — not something you're sensing with your own eyes or ears right now.

```jp
{{ashita||明日[あした]}}は{{ame-v||雨[あめ]}}らしい。
```

*I heard it's going to rain tomorrow.*

Say that after checking the forecast. Look up at a darkening sky yourself and reach for みたいだ instead — same rain, but the confidence behind the sentence comes from a completely different place. らしい answers "where did you get this," while みたいだ answers "what does it look like to you, right now."

Once the shape settles in, みたいだ turns into one of the most-used sentence-enders you own, because most of what you notice about the world around you really is exactly that: a first impression, not a certified fact. Most of language learning early on is just this — noticing how often you're actually reporting an impression instead of a fact, and finally having a word ready for it. Hold onto that instinct: once て{{iru-exist||いる}} (marking something as ongoing) enters the picture, you'll be able to say what someone looks like they're doing, not just what they look like.
caution_notes: Don't add な before みたいだ after a na-adjective, like in 静かなみたいだ — go straight to 静かみたいだ.
Don't add の before みたいだ after a noun the way you would with ようだ, like in 料理のみたいだ — say 料理みたいだ instead.
みたいだ on its own is casual; switch to みたいです once the conversation turns formal.
らしい points to something you heard or read, while みたいだ points to your own impression right now — keep them apart.

items.explanation_markdown:
Your friend sends you a photo of their kitchen window with a crack running straight across it. You want to describe what you're looking at right now, not the moment it happened.

```jp
{{mado||窓[まど]}}が{{kowareru|te|壊[こわ]れて}}いる。
```

*The window is broken.*

That's the same て-form + {{iru-exist||いる}} you already used for progressive ている (something happening right now). Here it's doing a different job: it describes a resultant state — the lingering result of something that already happened, still true at this moment. The window broke at some point in the past; what you're reporting is the state it's in now.

## How it works

The shape is identical to progressive ている: take the て-form of the verb and add {{iru-exist||いる}}. What changes is the *kind* of verb you attach it to. With a verb that describes a one-time change — something flips from one state to another and stays there — ている points at the state left behind, not the flipping itself.

```jp
{{kowareru||壊[こわ]れる}} → {{kowareru|te|壊[こわ]れて}}
```

{{kowareru||壊[こわ]れる}} (to break) is exactly this kind of verb: a window can't be "in the middle of" breaking for very long, it either hasn't broken or it has. So {{kowareru|te|壊[こわ]れて}}いる can only mean *is broken*, never *is breaking*.

The same logic covers things left in a spot after arriving there.

```jp
{{hon||本[ほん]}}が{{tsukue||机[つくえ]}}の{{shita-v||下[した]}}に{{ochiru|te|落[お]ちて}}いる。
```

*The book has fallen and is under the desk.*

{{ochiru||落[お]ちる}} (to fall) is another one-shot change — the falling itself takes a second, but {{ochiru|te|落[お]ちて}}いる describes the much longer stretch afterward, where the book just sits there under the desk.

A handful of verbs use this same pattern to describe a state you're simply *in*, with no separate "event" moment you're picturing at all.

```jp
{{watashi||私[わたし]}}は{{sensei||先[せん]生[せい]}}を{{shiru|te|知[し]って}}いる。
```

*I know the teacher.*

{{shiru||知[し]る}} technically means "to come to know" — the moment information lands in your head. But {{watashi||私[わたし]}}は{{sensei||先[せん]生[せい]}}を{{shiru||知[し]る}} with no {{iru-exist||いる}} would sound like you're about to learn who your teacher is, right now, live. {{shiru|te|知[し]って}}いる is how you say you already have that knowledge and are holding onto it. {{motsu||持[も]つ}} (to hold) works the same way — 財[さい]布[ふ]を{{motsu|te|持[も]って}}いる is simply "I have a wallet," not "I am in the act of grabbing one."

```jp
{{kaigi||会[かい]議[ぎ]}}の{{jikan||時[じ]間[かん]}}は{{mou||もう}}{{kimaru|te|決[き]まって}}いる。
```

*The meeting time has already been decided.*

{{kimaru||決[き]まる}} (to be decided) flips once, from undecided to decided, and {{mou||もう}} (already) leans into exactly that: the decision landed at some point, and ている reports the settled state it left behind.

## Rules and exceptions

The test isn't the verb's meaning in English — it's whether the action is a one-time flip or something you can watch unfold second by second. {{hajimaru||始[はじ]まる}} (to begin) sounds like an instant, but it's used the same way once the event is underway:

```jp
授[じゅ]業[ぎょう]は{{mou||もう}}{{hajimaru|te|始[はじ]まって}}いる。
```

*Class has already started.*

The class began at a specific moment; ている covers the whole stretch of time you're now sitting inside, after that moment.

> 死[し]ぬ (to die) is the sharpest example of this. Death happens once and doesn't repeat, so 死[し]んで{{iru-exist||いる}} can only mean *is dead* — never *is dying*. English speakers reach for "is dying" instinctively and it trips people up the first week; that's normal.

```jp
{{neko||猫[ねこ]}}が死[し]んで{{iru-exist||いる}}。
```

*The cat is dead.*

One thing this pattern does *not* do: it doesn't reach back and describe someone actively doing the breaking, deciding, or dropping. `窓を壊している` with a direct object reads as someone breaking the window *right now*, live, because {{kowasu||壊[こわ]す}} (the transitive partner of {{kowareru||壊[こわ]れる}}) is a normal ongoing action when you're the one doing it. Resultant ている belongs to the intransitive side — the thing that changed, not the person who changed it.

## Casual speech

In relaxed spoken Japanese, ている often shrinks to てる, and this pattern is no exception.

- {{kowareru|te|壊[こわ]れて}}いる → `壊れてる`
- {{shiru|te|知[し]って}}いる → `知ってる`

Same meaning, just faster to say. You'll hear the contracted form constantly; write the full ている in anything formal.

## Contrast: the same ている, two different jobs

This is where {{mado||窓[まど]}}が{{kowareru|te|壊[こわ]れて}}いる and the progressive ている you already know split apart, even though they're built identically. With an ordinary ongoing action, ている still means "happening right now":

```jp
{{kare||彼[かれ]}}は{{ima||今[いま]}}{{tomodachi||友[とも]達[だち]}}と{{hanasu-v|te|話[はな]して}}いる。
```

*He is talking with a friend right now.*

{{hanasu-v||話[はな]す}} is a verb you can watch unfold — talking has duration, a beginning and an end you could interrupt. That's progressive ている, the one you already met. {{kimaru||決[き]まる}} and {{kowareru||壊[こわ]れる}} can't be interrupted mid-flip the same way, so the exact same grammar points at the aftermath instead.

A few verbs sit right on the border and genuinely go either way depending on context, which is honestly just messy — no clean rule saves you here, only the situation does.

```jp
{{kare||彼[かれ]}}は{{shatsu||シャツ}}を{{kiru-wear|te|着[き]て}}いる。
```

*He is wearing a shirt.*

{{kiru-wear||着[き]る}} (to put on) is momentary — the act of pulling a shirt over your head takes a couple of seconds. So {{kiru-wear|te|着[き]て}}いる almost always describes the state afterward, *wearing* it, the way you'd use it to describe someone across the room. Only in a scene where you're watching someone get dressed in real time would the same sentence mean "is putting on" instead.

One more state ている covers, that you'll want soon: this lesson stuck to verbs that already describe their own change, like {{kowareru||壊[こわ]れる}}. There's a separate pattern, て{{aru||ある}}, for describing a state that someone deliberately *set up* — a window someone left open on purpose, a table someone already set. Hold onto that distinction; it's the whole reason て{{aru||ある}} exists.

Same て-form + {{iru-exist||いる}} shape you already knew — the only new skill is checking whether the verb can be "in progress" at all before you decide what the sentence is reporting.
caution_notes: With one-time change verbs like 壊れる, 決まる, or 死ぬ, ている describes the state left behind, not the change happening live.
死んでいる can only mean 'is dead' — Japanese has no way to say 'is dying' with this pattern.
Resultant ている attaches to the intransitive verb (壊れる); the transitive partner (壊す) with ている describes someone doing the action right now instead.
Verbs like 着る can be read as either progressive or resultant depending on context — there is no clean rule, only the situation.

items.explanation_markdown:
You get home, and the bicycle that was leaning against the fence this morning is standing upright against the wall, chained in place. You didn't do that. Your roommate did, earlier, and now the state of it — parked, secured — is just sitting there as a fact about the world. That's the feeling てある captures: not someone doing something, but something someone did, on display.

## How it works

てある attaches to the te-form of a **transitive** verb (one that takes a direct object — the person doing the action acts *on* something) and adds {{aru||ある}}, the verb for existence of things. Together they describe a state that exists *because* someone deliberately set it up that way.

```jp
{{mado||窓[まど]}}が{{akeru|te|開[あ]けて}}ある。
```

*The window has been opened (and left that way).*

Notice the marker: it's が, not を, even though {{akeru||開[あ]ける}} is a transitive verb and {{mado||窓[まど]}} is what got opened. Once てある turns the sentence into a description of a state, が marks what that state belongs to — the same shift you'd expect from any sentence about how something *is*.

```jp
{{namae||名[な]前[まえ]}}が{{kaku|te|書[か]いて}}ある。
```

*A name is written (there).*

```jp
{{tsukue||机[つくえ]}}の{{ue||上[うえ]}}に{{tegami||手[て]紙[がみ]}}が置[お]いてある。
```

*There's a letter placed on the desk.*

The verb conjugates exactly like it does before {{iru-exist||いる}} in て{{iru-exist||いる}} — drop る, add て — then {{aru||ある}} just tacks on.

```jp
{{tomeru-stop||止[と]める}} → {{tomeru-stop|te|止[と]めて}}ある
```

## Rules and exceptions

The whole pattern depends on the verb being transitive. {{tomeru-stop||止[と]める}} (to stop something — a car, a machine) works because there's an agent doing the stopping. Its intransitive twin, {{tomaru||止[と]まる}} (to stop, on its own), can't take てある at all — there's no one whose deliberate setup you'd be describing.

> てある almost always implies a person set the state up on purpose. If nothing planted an intentional state, てある sounds wrong to a native ear — plain て{{iru-exist||いる}} is what you want for something that just happened on its own.

```jp
{{jitensha||自[じ]転[てん]車[しゃ]}}が{{tomeru-stop|te|止[と]めて}}ある。
```

*The bicycle has been parked.*

Because the emphasis is on the *result being ready for someone*, てある often shows up when the state matters to the speaker right now — a door left open for a guest, a seat saved, food set out. Simply stating that a transitive action happened isn't enough; you need the outcome to still be sitting there, relevant.

## Casual speech

In casual explanations, てある often picks up んだ instead of the more formal んです — you're not changing the pattern itself, just how you frame it as an aside. {{denki||電[でん]気[き]}}が{{tsukeru|te|つけて}}あるんだ ("the light's on, see" — someone left it on) reads far more natural in conversation than the plain sentence alone.

```jp
{{denki||電[でん]気[き]}}が{{tsukeru|te|つけて}}ある。
```

*The light has been left on.*

## Contrast

You already have て{{iru-exist||いる}} doing two jobs: progressive ("in the middle of") and resultant state for **intransitive** verbs. てある is the transitive half of that second job — same idea, "something is in a state," but now there's a person behind it.

```jp
{{jitensha||自[じ]転[てん]車[しゃ]}}が{{tomaru|te|止[と]まって}}{{iru-exist||いる}}。
```

*The bicycle is stopped (it's just sitting there, stopped).*

Line that up against {{jitensha||自[じ]転[てん]車[しゃ]}}が{{tomeru-stop|te|止[と]めて}}ある above: both describe a parked bike, but {{tomaru|te|止[と]まって}}{{iru-exist||いる}} only tells you the bike isn't moving — it says nothing about who parked it or why. {{tomeru-stop|te|止[と]めて}}ある insists someone put it there on purpose, and that fact is still true.

```jp
{{doa||ドア}}が{{shimeru|te|閉[し]めて}}ある。
```

*The door has been shut.*

Swap in {{doa||ドア}}が閉[し]まって{{iru-exist||いる}} and you'd only be reporting that the door is closed right now, no hint of intent behind it — useful if you don't know or don't care who closed it.

That distinction — a bare fact about how something is, versus a fact plus someone's fingerprints on it — is what you're listening for every time you meet these two side by side. Hold onto てある; you'll want it again soon when you learn ておく, which is the *moment before* this state gets set up on purpose.
caution_notes: てある needs a transitive verb behind it — an intransitive twin like 止まる can't take this pattern at all.
The object of the original action is marked with が, not を, once てある turns the sentence into a state description.
てある implies a person deliberately set the state up; don't reach for it when nothing and no one caused the state on purpose, like a flower blooming.

items.explanation_markdown:
Your friend is coming over tonight, and right now the room is a mess and the fridge is empty. You've got a couple of hours before they show up, which means everything you do now is really *for later* — you're not cleaning because someone's watching, you're cleaning so that later, when they arrive, it's already done.

Japanese has a dedicated way to mark that kind of action: te-form + おく.

```jp
{{heya||部屋[へや]}}を掃[そう]除[じ]{{suru|te|して}}おく。
```
*I'll clean the room ahead of time.*

The cleaning happens now, but the sentence's whole point is the *later* — you're doing it so that future-you doesn't have to.

## How it works

`おく` on its own is a normal verb meaning "to put / place" (置[お]く — you'll have seen 置[お]く with this exact kanji). Attach the te-form of any verb to it, and the meaning shifts from "put something down" to "do this now, for a reason that shows up later."

```jp
{{biiru||ビール}}を{{kau-v|te|買[か]って}}おく。
```
*I'll buy beer in advance.*

The structure is mechanical: take the te-form you already know, then add おく. {{kau-v||買[か]う}} → {{kau-v|te|買[か]って}} → {{kau-v|te|買[か]って}}おく. Nothing about the te-form itself changes — おく just rides on the back of it.

```jp
{{mado||窓[まど]}}を{{akeru|te|開[あ]けて}}おく。
```
*I'll leave the window open (ahead of time).*

Notice something here: with an already-open-ended verb like {{akeru||開[あ]ける}}, ておく can land on either of two related jobs — "do this in preparation" (I'll open it before the guests arrive) or "do this and then leave it that way" (I'm opening it and not touching it again). Context decides which one you're hearing; the grammar itself doesn't distinguish them.

```jp
{{okane||お金[かね]}}を{{motsu|te|持[も]って}}おく。
```
*I'll have money on me (just in case).*

That "just in case" flavor is common — ておく covers not just "prepare for a known event" but also "take care of this now so I'm not caught out later," a slightly broader net than "prepare" alone suggests.

## Rules and exceptions

おく conjugates exactly like the plain verb 置[お]く does, because that's what it is — a u-verb ending in く. So you get おく → おかない → おきます → おいて, all the ordinary patterns. The only thing special is that it's riding on a te-form host, not standing alone.

> A very common wrong guess is treating おく like an auxiliary that doesn't conjugate — writing something like `掃除しておくます` instead of 掃[そう]除[じ]{{suru|te|して}}おきます. おく still takes its own conjugation ending; only the verb in front of it stays frozen in te-form.

ておく wants a *deliberate* action with a *purpose* pointing forward. It's a poor fit for things that are simply true or that just happened to end up a certain way — for that job you already have て{{aru||ある}} and て{{iru-exist||いる}}, which we'll get to in the contrast section below.

## Casual speech

In relaxed spoken Japanese, ておく contracts hard — the て and おく fuse into とく. It's extremely common; you'll hear it constantly among friends and family.

```jp
{{mado||窓[まど]}}、{{akeru|stem|開[あ]け}}とく。
```
*I'll leave the window open.*

Same meaning as {{mado||窓[まど]}}を{{akeru|te|開[あ]けて}}おく, just faster and more casual — drop the と for です/ます-level speech, since とく reads as clearly informal.

## Contrast

You've met て{{aru||ある}} for "has been done, and the result is sitting there" — the difference is *whose intention the sentence is tracking*. て{{aru||ある}} describes the state as a fact you're reporting; ておく describes the deliberate act of setting that state up, with your reason for doing so implied.

```jp
{{mado||窓[まど]}}が{{akeru|te|開[あ]けて}}{{aru||ある}}。
```
*The window has been left open.*

Compare that to {{mado||窓[まど]}}を{{akeru|te|開[あ]けて}}おく from earlier — same window, same open state, but that version is about *you doing the opening on purpose, now, for later*. て{{aru||ある}} just notes that it's open; it doesn't care why or by whom.

て{{iru-exist||いる}} (progressive) is a different trap entirely — it's about an action unfolding in real time, not something staged for the future.

```jp
{{ima||今[いま]}}、{{heya||部屋[へや]}}を掃[そう]除[じ]{{suru|te|して}}{{iru-exist||いる}}。
```
*I'm cleaning the room right now.*

Swap {{suru|te|して}}おく in for {{suru|te|して}}{{iru-exist||いる}} here and the sentence stops describing what's happening this second — it starts describing something you're doing *because of what comes next*, which is a completely different scene.

ておく is the one you reach for whenever the real content of the sentence is "I'm doing this now so that later goes smoothly" — hold onto that shape, because てしまう later covers the flip side: doing something now and living with the consequences, whether you meant to or not.
caution_notes: おく still conjugates on its own as a regular u-verb (おかない, おきます, おいて) — only the verb in front of it stays frozen in te-form.
とく is the casual, spoken contraction of ておく; don't write it anywhere formal.
ておく needs a deliberate action aimed at a later purpose — for a state that simply exists or just happened, use てある or ている instead.
With verbs like 開ける, ておく can mean either 'do it now to prepare' or 'do it and leave it that way' — only context tells you which.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're describing your day to a friend, but every sentence carries a little sigh — you forgot the homework, you ate all the snacks you were supposed to save, you lost your wallet. In English you'd just say "I forgot" or "I ate it all," but Japanese has a whole grammar pattern built for that sigh: てしまう.

```jp
宿[しゅく]題[だい]を{{wasureru|te|忘[わす]れて}}しまう。
```
*I end up forgetting the homework.*

That しまう on the end isn't decoration — it's doing real work. It's telling the listener: this happened in full, and the speaker wishes it hadn't.

## How it works

てしまう attaches to the te-form of any verb, exactly like て{{iru-exist||いる}} or ておく do. Take the verb, drop it into its te-form, and add しまう.

```jp
{{taberu||食[た]べる}} → {{taberu|te|食[た]べて}}しまう
```
*to eat → to eat up / end up eating*

Once you've got te-form + しまう, that whole chunk conjugates like any regular verb: past, non-past, and so on, just like a normal verb.

```jp
{{okashi||お菓[か]子[し]}}を{{zenbu||全[ぜん]部[ぶ]}}{{taberu|te|食[た]べて}}しまう。
```
*I end up eating all the snacks.*

Notice what しまう adds that {{taberu|ta|食[た]べた}} alone wouldn't: it wasn't supposed to happen, or it happened faster or more thoroughly than intended. {{taberu|ta|食[た]べた}} is neutral. {{taberu|te|食[た]べて}}しまう has a story behind it.

```jp
財[さい]布[ふ]を{{nakusu|te|無[な]くして}}しまう。
```
*I end up losing my wallet.*

## Rules and exceptions

てしまう actually carries two related meanings, and context decides which one you're hearing:

1. **An unwanted result** — something went wrong, and you (or someone) is stuck with it. That's the wallet, the snacks, the homework you forgot.
2. **Emphatic completion** — the action ran all the way through, with no bad feeling at all, just emphasis that nothing was left undone.

```jp
宿[しゅく]題[だい]を{{zenbu||全[ぜん]部[ぶ]}}{{suru|te|して}}しまう。
```
*I get all the homework done.*

Same grammar, opposite mood — here it just means "done, every last bit of it," maybe even with relief. Which reading you get depends entirely on the situation and the speaker's tone, not on the grammar itself.

> てしまう attaches only to verbs — you can't put it on an adjective or a noun directly. `暑いてしまう` is not a sentence; there's no equivalent shortcut for adjectives. Keep it to the te-form of verbs.

A common beginner habit is reaching for てしまう every time something is simply "done," the way learners overuse plain past tense on its own. Save it for moments where thoroughness or an unwanted outcome is actually the point — otherwise plain past tense does the job.

## Casual speech

In fast, casual speech, てしまう almost always contracts. てしまう becomes ちゃう, and でしまう (after ん-stem verbs like {{asobu||遊[あそ]ぶ}}) becomes じゃう.

```jp
{{wasureru|stem|忘[わす]れ}}ちゃう。
```
*I totally forget.*

```jp
{{asobu|stem|遊[あそ]ん}}じゃう。
```
*I go and play (when I shouldn't).*

You'll hear ちゃう constantly between friends and almost never in polite writing — treat it like any other casual contraction: fine to recognize everywhere, risky to use with your teacher.

## Contrast

You've already met ておく — te-form + おく — for doing something *in advance*, so it's ready later. てしまう points the opposite direction: it looks *back* at something already fully done, often with a reaction attached.

```jp
{{ashita||明日[あした]}}の準[じゅん]備[び]を{{suru|te|して}}おきました。
```
*I got tomorrow's preparations done in advance.*

```jp
{{ashita||明日[あした]}}の準[じゅん]備[び]を{{suru|te|して}}しまう。
```
*I go and do tomorrow's preparations (before I meant to).*

Swap おく for しまう and the meaning shifts from "I set this up ahead of time, on purpose" to a completed action with a reaction attached — the forward-planning feel disappears entirely.

て{{iru-exist||いる}}, by contrast, marks something still in progress or a state that has settled in. てしまう marks a point where the action stops because there's nothing left to do.

Homework you've already turned in and can't get back, snacks you can't unsnack — that's the shape of てしまう. Hold onto that finality; you'll want the opposite feeling again once ていく and てくる show up, since those describe change that's still underway.
caution_notes: てしまう attaches only to verb te-forms — it cannot attach directly to an adjective or a noun.
The same grammar can read as either an unwanted result or plain emphatic completion — the feeling comes from context, not the words themselves.
ちゃう and じゃう are casual contractions of てしまう and でしまう — avoid them in polite or written Japanese.
Don't reach for てしまう for every finished action — plain past tense is usually enough unless thoroughness or an unwanted outcome is the point.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're back in your hometown after a year away, and your friend meets you at the station. 「{{ookii|stem|大[おお]きく}}{{naru-become|ta|なった}}ね」isn't the sentence you reach for — what you actually notice is *change still happening*, something that was one way and is sliding toward another. Japanese has a pair of endings built exactly for that: **ていく** and **てくる**. They turn any verb into a story about direction — away from now, or toward now.

```jp
{{tenki||天[てん]気[き]}}が{{dandan||だんだん}}{{atatakai|stem|暖[あたた]かく}}{{naru-become|te|なって}}くる。
```

*The weather is gradually getting warmer (and it's happening right now, moving toward us).*

## How it works

Both endings attach to the **te-form** of a verb, then add {{iku-v||行[い]く}} (いく, to go) or {{kuru-v||来[く]る}} (くる, to come). That's the whole structure: te-form + いく, or te-form + くる. The "go / come" meaning is mostly bleached out — what's left is a sense of *direction*, either away from the present moment (**ていく**) or toward it (**てくる**).

Think of it on a timeline with "now" as a fixed point. **てくる** describes something arriving at now, coming closer, building up to this point. **ていく** describes something leaving now, heading off, continuing on from here.

```jp
{{kodomo-v||子[こ]供[ども]}}は{{dandan||だんだん}}{{ookii|stem|大[おお]きく}}{{naru-become|te|なって}}いく。
```

*The child keeps growing bigger and bigger (moving forward from now).*

```jp
{{kare||彼[かれ]}}は{{maiban||毎[まい]晩[ばん]}}{{osoi|stem|遅[おそ]く}}{{kaeru-v|te|帰[かえ]って}}くる。
```

*He comes home late every night (repeatedly arriving back, toward here).*

This works with plain motion verbs too, and there the "go/come" sense is much more literal — it just adds the direction relative to the speaker.

```jp
{{tomodachi||友[とも]達[だち]}}が{{kochira||こちら}}へ{{aruku|te|歩[ある]いて}}くる。
```

*My friend is walking this way (toward me).*

```jp
{{watashi||私[わたし]}}は{{eki||駅[えき]}}まで{{aruku|te|歩[ある]いて}}いく。
```

*I'll walk to the station (away from here).*

The same logic covers actions that aren't physical movement at all — a habit, a change, a process that keeps going. {{shigoto||仕[し]事[ごと]}}を{{tsuzukeru-v||続[つづ]ける}} (to continue work) plus ていく says the continuing is aimed at the future.

```jp
{{kanojo||彼[かの]女[じょ]}}は{{shigoto||仕[し]事[ごと]}}を{{tsuzukeru-v|te|続[つづ]けて}}いく。
```

*She's going to keep going with her work (carrying it forward from here).*

## Rules and exceptions

Both endings need the verb's te-form first — there's no shortcut version that skips it. `大きいてくる` is not a real word; you need `大きくなってくる`, because it's {{naru-become||なる}} (to become) that's carrying the ていく/てくる, not the adjective itself.

> {{kuru-v||来[く]る}} itself can take てくる: {{kuru-v|te|来[き]て}}くる. It looks redundant — "come and come" — but it's genuinely rare and > mostly shows up with other movement verbs stacked on top, so don't reach for it as your default てくる example.

The direction reading (away vs. toward) is the default with change-of-state verbs like {{naru-become||なる}}, but with plain motion verbs like {{aruku||歩[ある]く}} or {{hashiru||走[はし]る}}, ていく/てくる simply mark which way the person is heading relative to whoever's talking. Context tells you which flavor you're getting — there's no separate grammar for it.

```jp
{{inu||犬[いぬ]}}が公[こう]園[えん]から{{hashiru|te|走[はし]って}}くる。
```

*The dog comes running out of the park (heading toward the speaker).*

## Casual speech

In relaxed conversation, ていく often shrinks to てく — the い drops out, the same way て{{iru-exist||いる}} shrinks to てる. てくる doesn't contract the same way; it usually stays whole even in casual speech.

- Neutral: {{watashi||私[わたし]}}は{{eki||駅[えき]}}まで{{aruku|te|歩[ある]いて}}いく。
- Casual: {{watashi||私[わたし]}}は{{eki||駅[えき]}}まで{{aruku|stem|歩[ある]い}}てく。

## Contrast

You already know て{{iru-exist||いる}} for an action in progress or a state that's settled in — it freezes a moment. ていく/てくる instead point at *movement between* moments: where something is coming from, or where it's headed. {{ookii|stem|大[おお]きく}}{{naru-become|te|なって}}{{iru-exist||いる}} says a child is currently in a bigger state; {{ookii|stem|大[おお]きく}}{{naru-become|te|なって}}いく says the growing is still going to keep happening from here on.

You also know てしまう for finishing something completely, often with a note of regret. てしまう closes a door; ていく/てくる describe someone walking through one, mid-step, either arriving or leaving.

Hold onto that "toward now / away from now" picture — it comes back once you meet ても and てはいけない, where the same te-form is doing a completely different job, but the habit of reading a te-form ending as a small grammatical hinge will already feel familiar.
caution_notes: Both endings require the te-form first — an adjective like 大きい cannot take てくる directly; you need the verb なる carrying the ending, as in 大きくなってくる.
てくる with 来る itself (来てくる) is grammatically valid but very rare — don't treat it as the standard pattern.
With plain motion verbs (歩く, 走る), ていく/てくる mark literal direction relative to the speaker, not a change over time — read the verb first to know which sense applies.
てくる rarely contracts in casual speech the way ていく shrinks to てく — don't force a casual shortening onto てくる.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're supposed to meet a friend at the park at six. At five-thirty it starts raining, hard. You text them anyway: {{ame-v||雨[あめ]}}が{{furu-rain|te|降[ふ]って}}も、公[こう]園[えん]を{{aruku||歩[ある]く}}。 Rain or no rain, you're going. That flip — "no matter what happens, the plan holds" — is what ても does. It bolts onto the te-form you already know and turns any verb or adjective into "even if / even though X."

## How it works

The base is the same te-form you've been using for て{{iru-exist||いる}}, て{{aru||ある}}, ておく, and the rest — you're just handing it to a new job. Take the te-form, add も (the word that works like *even / also*), and you get "even if / even though."

```jp
{{isogashii|te|忙[いそが]しくて}}も、{{mainichi||毎[まい]日[にち]}}{{benkyou-suru||勉[べん]強[きょう]する}}。
```

*Even if I'm busy, I study every day.*

With verbs, the te-form does all the work — も just rides on the end. With い-adjectives, drop the い, add くて, then も:

```jp
{{isogashii||忙[いそが]しい}} → {{isogashii|te|忙[いそが]しくて}} → {{isogashii|te|忙[いそが]しくて}}も
```

For な-adjectives and nouns, the connector is で, and ても becomes でも (the same shape as the word for "but" — more on that below):

```jp
{{genki||元[げん]気[き]}}でも、{{kyou||今日[きょう]}}は{{yasumu||休[やす]む}}。
```

*Even though I'm fine, I'm resting today.*

```jp
{{genki||元[げん]気[き]}} → {{genki||元[げん]気[き]}}で → {{genki||元[げん]気[き]}}でも
```

One more shape worth knowing early: pair ても with a question word like 何[なん]回[かい] (how many times) and you get "no matter how many times."

```jp
何[なん]回[かい]{{kiku-v|te|聞[き]いて}}も、{{wakaru|nai|分[わ]からない}}。
```

*No matter how many times I ask, I don't understand.*

That's the whole mechanic. One connector, four flavors depending on what it's attached to — verb, い-adjective, な-adjective/noun, or a question word.

## Rules and exceptions

ても doesn't care whether the outcome is good or bad, expected or not — it just says "this condition doesn't change the result." Compare that to から (for reasons) or ので (softer reasons), which you'll meet elsewhere: those explain *why* something happens. ても explains why something *doesn't stop* happening.

```jp
{{takai-adj|te|高[たか]くて}}も、{{ano||あの}}{{tokei||時計[とけい]}}を{{kau-v||買[か]う}}。
```

*Even if it's expensive, I'll buy that watch.*

Nobody's giving a reason here — {{takai-adj||高[たか]い}} isn't the cause of buying the watch, it's the obstacle that fails to change the decision. That's the whole flavor of ても: expect it wherever a sentence in English has "even if," "no matter," or "however X is."

> A common first-week slip is dropping the も and just leaving the te-form alone: `忙しくて、毎日勉強する` reads as "I'm busy, and so I study every day" — a plain reason, the opposite of what you meant. The も is not optional decoration; it's the whole concession.

でも after a noun or な-adjective looks exactly like でも the conjunction meaning "but" (the one sitting in your vocabulary list already). They really are the same word wearing two hats: sentence-initial でも contrasts two whole sentences, while attached でも at the end of a noun or な-adjective contrasts a single condition against its result. Context tells them apart fast — one starts a sentence, the other ends a clause.

## Contrast

You already know a handful of jobs the te-form can do: て{{iru-exist||いる}} marks something in progress, てしまう marks something finished (often with a little regret), ていく and てくる track a change moving away from or toward you. ても is another one of those jobs, and it's worth keeping straight from the others precisely because the *shape* is so similar — te-form plus one more piece.

The difference is what that piece asks. て{{iru-exist||いる}}, てしまう, ていく, and てくる all describe what's happening *to the action itself* — is it ongoing, complete, moving. ても doesn't touch the action's own status at all; it's entirely about the relationship between a condition and a result that refuses to budge. {{isogashii|te|忙[いそが]しくて}}も{{benkyou-suru||勉[べん]強[きょう]する}} isn't telling you anything about the studying being finished or ongoing — it's telling you the studying happens *regardless* of the business.

## Closing thought

Every time you reach for ても, you're saying "here's the obstacle, and here's the outcome that ignores it." Hold onto that shape — you'll want it again soon, when ても{{ii||いい}} turns the same connector into asking permission instead of describing defiance.
caution_notes: Dropping the も and leaving only the te-form turns a concession into a plain reason, so 忙しくて means 'because I'm busy,' not 'even though I'm busy.'
でも attached to a noun or な-adjective is the same word as the conjunction でも (but) — only its position in the sentence tells you which job it's doing.

items.explanation_markdown:
Your friend leans over during lunch and asks what you're doing this weekend. You already know the answer — you're not guessing, you're not hoping, you've already decided. What you need is the phrase for *I'm planning to*, and that's exactly what つもり gives you. It takes a plain verb and turns it into a stated intention, something you're announcing as your own decision rather than a fact about the world.

```jp
{{shuumatsu||週[しゅう]末[まつ]}}、{{eiga||映[えい]画[が]}}を{{miru-v||見[み]る}}つもりです。
```

*This weekend, I'm planning to watch a movie.*

## How It Works

つもり attaches straight onto the dictionary form of a verb — the plain, unconjugated form you'd find listed in a dictionary. There's no te-form, no stem change, nothing to memorize beyond the shape you already know. You say the verb exactly the way you'd think it to yourself, and つもり rides along right after it.

```jp
{{ashita||明日[あした]}}、{{toshokan||図[と]書[しょ]館[かん]}}で{{benkyou-suru||勉[べん]強[きょう]する}}つもりだ。
```

*Tomorrow, I'm planning to study at the library.*

Notice the だ sitting at the end there. That's the plain copula (the word that works like *is/am/are*), and its job is to turn つもり from a bare noun-like word — closer to "intention" on its own — into a complete sentence: "it's my intention." Drop だ entirely and bare つもり still reads as a finished statement in speech; swap だ for です and the sentence gets politer without the meaning shifting even slightly.

```jp
{{rainen||来[らい]年[ねん]}}、{{nihongo||日本[にほん]語[ご]}}を{{benkyou-suru||勉[べん]強[きょう]する}}つもりです。
```

*Next year, I'm planning to study Japanese.*

So つもり, つもりだ, and つもりです are all accepted, and choosing between them is purely a question of how formal the room is — a plain つもり with friends, つもりです with your teacher or a stranger. The dictionary form doing the heavy lifting in front of it is really the whole grammar lesson here.

```jp
{{miru-v||見[み]る}} → {{miru-v||見[み]る}}つもり
```

*see → planning to see*

Whatever the plain form looks like — {{miru-v||見[み]る}}, {{benkyou-suru||勉[べん]強[きょう]する}}, {{kaeru-v||帰[かえ]る}}, {{hikkosu||引[ひ]っ越[こ]す}} — that's exactly what goes in front of つもり. No exceptions, no irregular attachments to track.

## Rules and Exceptions

Here's the part that's easy to miss at first: つもり describes what's inside your head *right now*, not a fact about how the future will actually go. That's a real difference from a fixed schedule — つもり can describe an intention that quietly falls apart later, and saying it doesn't promise anything actually happens. It just reports your current resolve, honestly, at the moment you say it.

That subjective feel matters even more when you're talking about someone else's plans instead of your own.

> Using つもり to describe someone else's intention can sound like you're speaking for them with total certainty. Among close friends who talk about everything, that's completely normal — toward someone you barely know, it can come across as oddly presumptuous, like you're announcing their decision before they have.

```jp
{{kare||彼[かれ]}}は{{mou||もう}}{{kaeru-v||帰[かえ]る}}つもりだ。
```

*He's already planning to go home.*

A common wrong guess, especially early on, is trying to attach つもり directly to a noun or a plain adjective, the way `静かつもり` gets typed by someone reaching for "I intend to be quiet." That doesn't work — つもり only follows the dictionary form of a verb, full stop, never a bare noun or adjective standing on its own.

## Casual Speech

In relaxed conversation, だ often gets swapped for だよ, which softens a flat, declarative statement into something warmer and more conversational — roughly the effect "you know" has tacked onto the end of an English sentence.

```jp
{{kyou||今日[きょう]}}は{{hayai-early|stem|早[はや]く}}{{neru||寝[ね]る}}つもりだよ。
```

*I'm planning to go to bed early today, you know.*

That だよ isn't required and it isn't more "correct" than だ — it's just the sound of someone talking to a friend instead of reading off a form.

## Contrast: つもり vs なければ{{naru-become|nai|ならない}}

You already know なければ{{naru-become|nai|ならない}} for the things you have no real choice about — homework due tomorrow, a deadline nobody's moving for you. つもり lives in completely different territory: it's the plan *you* chose, not the obligation life handed you. Swap one pattern for the other in an otherwise identical sentence and the entire feel of it flips.

```jp
{{ashita||明日[あした]}}、宿[しゅく]題[だい]を{{suru|stem|し}}なければ{{naru-become|nai|ならない}}。
```

*I have to do my homework tomorrow.*

```jp
{{ashita||明日[あした]}}、宿[しゅく]題[だい]を{{suru||する}}つもりだ。
```

*I'm planning to do my homework tomorrow.*

Same homework, same day, same person saying it — but the first sentence carries the weight of a burden, and the second sounds like someone quietly proud of a decision they've already made. That contrast is worth sitting with, because English "I'm going to do my homework" flattens a distinction Japanese keeps sharply separate.

```jp
{{watashi||私[わたし]}}は{{raigetsu||来[らい]月[げつ]}}{{hikkosu||引[ひ]っ越[こ]す}}つもりです。
```

*I'm planning to move next month.*

つもり is how you tell someone what's already settled in your own head, whether or not the day itself ever cooperates. Hold onto that self-directed, decision-first feel — it's exactly the muscle ように{{suru||する}} leans on later, once the intention needs ongoing upkeep instead of a single statement.
caution_notes: つもり states your current intention, not a guarantee — the plan itself can still fall through.
Stating someone else's つもり as fact can sound presumptuous unless you know them well.
つもり attaches only to the dictionary form of a verb, never directly to a noun or a plain adjective.
Ending with だ, です, or nothing at all after つもり only changes politeness, not the meaning.

items.explanation_markdown:
Your doctor takes one look at your blood sugar numbers and tells you plainly: cut back on sweets. You don't need a magic diet, you need a habit — a small deliberate effort, repeated. That's exactly the shape ようにする was built for.

```jp
{{maiasa||毎[まい]朝[あさ]}}、{{yasai||野[や]菜[さい]}}を{{taberu||食[た]べる}}ようにしている。
```
*I make a point of eating vegetables every morning.*

That sentence isn't reporting what you did once. It's reporting a standing effort — something you've set up as a rule for yourself and keep chasing, even on the days you fall short.

## How it works

ようにする attaches straight onto the dictionary form of a verb for a habit you're aiming for, or the ない form for one you're trying to avoid. Nothing else changes — no te-form, no stem-shaving, just the plain form plus ようにする.

```jp
{{taberu||食[た]べる}} → {{taberu||食[た]べる}}ようにする
```
*to eat → to make it a habit to eat*

```jp
{{taberu|nai|食[た]べない}} → {{taberu|nai|食[た]べない}}ようにする
```
*to not eat → to make it a habit not to eat*

{{suru||する}} here is doing its ordinary job — the word for "to do" — so it conjugates exactly like every other {{suru||する}} verb you already know: past ように{{suru|ta|した}}, negative ように{{suru|nai|しない}}, and so on.

The form you'll meet constantly is ようにしている — the て-form of {{suru||する}} plus {{iru-exist||いる}}, the same "ongoing state" marker you already use for continuous actions. ようにする by itself is closer to a decision you're making right now; ようにしている is the report that the effort has been running for a while.

```jp
{{amai||甘[あま]い}}{{mono||物[もの]}}を{{taberu|nai|食[た]べない}}ようにしている。
```
*I try not to eat sweets.*

```jp
{{maiban||毎[まい]晩[ばん]}}{{hayai-early|stem|早[はや]く}}{{neru||寝[ね]る}}ようにする。
```
*I'm going to make a habit of going to bed early.*

Notice the difference: the sweets sentence is a lifestyle you've already built ({{suru|te|して}}{{iru-exist|masu|います}}), while the early-bedtime one is you announcing the plan today, before the habit exists yet.

## Rules and exceptions

ようにする is for effort toward a repeated behavior, not for a single one-off action. "I made sure to lock the door this one time" isn't this pattern — that's just a plain past-tense sentence. ようにする wants something you're trying to keep doing, day after day, whether or not you always succeed.

> The "try" is doing real work here. ようにする never promises the outcome — it promises the attempt. Someone can say {{yasai||野[や]菜[さい]}}を{{taberu||食[た]べる}}ようにしている and still skip vegetables some days; the sentence is honest about that built-in slack.

A common wrong guess is treating ようにする like a flat statement of fact, the way you'd use {{suru||する}} alone. `野菜を食べるにする` drops the necessary よう and just sounds broken — the よう isn't optional decoration, it's the part that turns "do" into "orient yourself toward doing."

## Contrast: ようにする vs つもり

You already have つもり for stating a plan — {{yasai||野[や]菜[さい]}}を{{taberu||食[た]べる}}つもりだ, "I intend to eat vegetables." That's a single decision, and it says nothing about follow-through or repetition; you could mean tonight, once.

```jp
{{yasai||野[や]菜[さい]}}を{{taberu||食[た]べる}}つもりだ。
```
*I intend to eat vegetables.*

```jp
{{yasai||野[や]菜[さい]}}を{{motto||もっと}}{{taberu||食[た]べる}}ようにしている。
```
*I make a point of eating more vegetables.*

Swap the two and the sentence changes shape, not just tone: つもり is a plan you're holding in your head; ようにしている is a habit you can already point to evidence for, because you've been doing the work.

```jp
{{mainichi||毎[まい]日[にち]}}{{sanpo-suru||散[さん]歩[ぽ]する}}ようにしている。
```
*I make a point of taking a walk every day.*

## Closing thought

ようにする is the grammar of trying on purpose, day after day, not the grammar of a single decision — hold onto that distinction, because ことに{{suru||する}}, when you meet it, looks deceptively similar but marks a one-time choice instead of a standing effort.
caution_notes: ようにする describes a repeated effort, not a single one-off action — don't use it for something you only did once.
The よう is required — dropping it (as in `食べるにする`) isn't a shortcut, it's a mistake.
ようにしている reports an effort already underway; ようにする by itself is closer to announcing the plan today.
Don't confuse this with つもり — つもり is a plan you're holding, ようにする is an effort you're actively building.

items.explanation_markdown:
Your doctor just told you your blood pressure is a little high, and you're sitting in the waiting room deciding what to actually do about it. Not "I should probably think about maybe cutting back" — an actual decision, made right now, that you're committing to. That's the job ことにする does: it turns a choice you've just made into a sentence.

```jp
{{ashita||明日[あした]}}から{{maiasa||毎[まい]朝[あさ]}}{{hayai-early|stem|早[はや]く}}{{okiru||起[お]きる}}ことにする。
```
*I've decided to start getting up early every morning from tomorrow.*

The moment you say that sentence, the decision exists. Nobody made it for you, nothing forced it — you weighed it and chose it, and ことにする is the grammar that records the choice.

## How it works

こと is a **nominalizer** — a little word that turns a whole verb phrase into a thing you can talk about, the way "going" turns "go" into something you can point at. ことにする then works with に + {{suru||する}} (to do) — literally something like "make it the thing of going," which is a clunky translation but explains why the whole phrase reads as *deciding on* an action.

The attachment point is the plain dictionary form of the verb, exactly as it appears in a dictionary, right before こと.

```jp
{{kotoshi||今年[ことし]}}は{{nihongo||日本[にほん]語[ご]}}を{{naru||習[なら]う}}ことにしました。
```
*I've decided to learn Japanese this year.*

When the choice is to stop or avoid something instead, the ない form goes in that same slot.

```jp
{{amai||甘[あま]い}}{{mono||物[もの]}}を{{taberu|nai|食[た]べない}}ことにする。
```
*I've decided not to eat sweets.*

{{suru||する}} verbs behave exactly the same way — the {{suru||する}} in {{shokuji||食[しょく]事[じ]}}を{{suru||する}} is just doing its normal job as "to do," and the whole phrase still slots in front of ことにする like any other dictionary form.

```jp
{{shuumatsu||週[しゅう]末[まつ]}}は{{resutoran||レストラン}}で{{shokuji||食[しょく]事[じ]}}を{{suru||する}}ことにしました。
```
*I've decided to have a meal at a restaurant this weekend.*

Both tenses matter here, and they carry a real difference. ことにする, left in the present, sounds like the decision is happening as you speak — you're announcing it. ことにしました, in the past, reports a decision you already made and are now living by. Most of the time you'll reach for ことにしました, because you're usually telling someone about a choice you settled on earlier, not narrating it live.

## Rules and exceptions

> ことにする is strictly about **your own** decision. If the outcome was decided by someone else, by circumstances, or by a rule, this pattern is the wrong tool — that job belongs to ことに{{naru-become||なる}}, which you'll meet soon.

A common wrong guess is reaching for the て-form or the ます-stem before こと. Neither works. It has to be the plain dictionary form for "I will do this" or the plain ない form for "I won't do this" — nothing in between.

```jp
{{nomu-v||飲[の]む}} → {{nomu-v|nai|飲[の]まない}}ことにする
```

That arrow is the whole rule in miniature: take the dictionary form, negate it if the decision is to stop doing something, then attach ことにする. Nothing else changes.

## Contrast

You already have つもり for stating an intention — "I plan to." つもり can be looser than ことにする; it can describe something you're leaning toward without having fully committed.

```jp
{{raigetsu||来[らい]月[げつ]}}{{ryokou-suru||旅[りょ]行[こう]する}}つもりです。
```
*I plan to travel next month.*

Swap that つもり for ことにする and the sentence tightens: it stops sounding like a plan you're still holding loosely and starts sounding like a decision you've closed the door on.

よう に{{suru||する}} lives in a nearby but different space too — it's about the ongoing effort to make something a habit, not the single moment of deciding.

```jp
{{mainichi||毎[まい]日[にち]}}{{yasai||野[や]菜[さい]}}を{{taberu||食[た]べる}}ように{{suru||する}}。
```
*I'm making it a habit to eat vegetables every day.*

ことにする is the decision itself, made once. ように{{suru||する}} is the standing effort you keep applying afterward — you might say ことにする the day you decide to change your diet, then describe the follow-through with ように{{suru||する}} for months after.

```jp
{{osake||お酒[さけ]}}を{{nomu-v|nai|飲[の]まない}}ことにしました。
```
*I've decided not to drink alcohol.*

That's the shape you'll use constantly once you start noticing it — someone announcing a resolution, big or small, about their own behavior.

Hold onto this one: ことに{{naru-become||なる}} looks almost identical on the page but flips who's behind the wheel — it shows up next, for decisions and outcomes that land on you rather than ones you make.
caution_notes: ことにする reports a decision the speaker themselves made — use ことになる instead when the outcome was decided by someone else or by circumstances.
The slot before ことにする takes only the plain dictionary form or the plain ない form, never the て-form or the ます-stem.
ことにしました describes a decision already made and being kept, while ことにする can sound like the decision is happening at the moment of speaking.
Don't confuse this with つもり — つもり is a loose intention you might still change, while ことにする is the closed decision itself.

Sure!</reading>": nobody asked, he <grammar>decided to</grammar> go <grammar>all by himself</grammar>. {{kasa||傘}}を{{kau-v||買う}}<reading>ことにしました</reading>。

items.explanation_markdown:
Your company just told you you're being transferred. Nobody asked what you wanted — the decision landed on your desk already finished, and now you're the one explaining it to your family. In Japanese, you wouldn't say {{watashi||私[わたし]}}は{{atarashii-adj||新[あたら]しい}}{{kaisha||会[かい]社[しゃ]}}で{{hataraku|masu|働[はたら]きます}}, as if the whole thing were your idea. You'd reach for the phrase that makes the decision sound like it arrived from somewhere else, because it did.

```jp
{{raigetsu||来[らい]月[げつ]}}、{{atarashii-adj||新[あたら]しい}}{{kaisha||会[かい]社[しゃ]}}で{{hataraku||働[はたら]く}}ことになりました。
```
*Next month, it's been decided that I'll work at a new company.*

ことになる is built from こと — a nominalizer, a little grammatical word that takes a whole verb phrase ({{atarashii-adj||新[あたら]しい}}{{kaisha||会[かい]社[しゃ]}}で{{hataraku||働[はたら]く}}, "to work at a new company") and turns it into a thing you can talk about, almost like wrapping it in quotation marks — plus {{naru-become||なる}}, "to become." Put together, the verb phrase itself becomes the outcome: it isn't that you decided to work there, it's that working there became the state of affairs. You're reporting a fact that formed around you, not a plan you made. That's the whole logic of the pattern in miniature, and once it clicks, you'll start noticing ことになる everywhere — memos, announcements, casual updates about anyone's life.

## How it works

The base attachment point is the plain dictionary form of a verb — no て-form, no ます, nothing conjugated first:

```jp
{{rainen||来[らい]年[ねん]}}から宿[しゅく]題[だい]が{{fueru-v||増[ふ]える}}ことになる。
```
*Starting next year, it turns out homework increases.*

Nobody sat down and personally decided that homework should increase — but ことになる still fits, because the pattern covers two overlapping ideas at once: an outcome someone else arranged, and an outcome that simply turns out to be true given how things are. Both share the same emotional shape — this wasn't your call, and honestly it wasn't really anyone's individual call either.

When the outcome is that something *won't* happen, the negative sits on the verb, not on {{naru-become||なる}}. Turn the verb into its ない form first, then attach ことになる as usual:

```jp
{{ashita||明日[あした]}}は{{kaisha||会[かい]社[しゃ]}}に{{iku-v|nai|行[い]かない}}ことになりました。
```
*It's been decided that I won't go to the company tomorrow.*

{{iku-v||行[い]く}} becomes {{iku-v|nai|行[い]かない}}, and ことになりました rides on top of that — never `行くないことになりました`, which puts the negative in the wrong place entirely. Past tense, ことになりました, is the form you'll meet constantly, because you're almost always reporting a decision after it's already settled, not narrating one as it happens.

There's a third shape worth learning early: swap ました for て{{iru-exist||いる}}, and the sentence stops describing one piece of news and starts describing a standing arrangement — the kind of thing that's simply how the schedule works, not something anyone announced today.

```jp
{{maishuu||毎[まい]週[しゅう]}}{{getsuyoubi||月[げつ]曜[よう]日[び]}}に{{kaigi||会[かい]議[ぎ]}}が{{aru||ある}}ことになっている。
```
*There's a standing arrangement that there's a meeting every Monday.*

Nobody sent a memo about this particular Monday. It's just the rule, repeating quietly in the background. That's the real difference between ことになりました (one decision, reported once, usually past) and ことになっている (an ongoing arrangement, always true, no matter when you check).

## Rules and exceptions

ことになる needs an outside cause standing behind it — a company, a school, a group, circumstance in general. It doesn't stretch to cover plain wants or feelings, because wanting something isn't a fact that gets decided for you. You wouldn't say `お茶が欲しいことになりました` for "I ended up wanting tea" — nobody arranges a craving.

> Japanese speakers reach for ことになりました even when the news is obviously their own doing — a couple announcing their wedding, someone accepting a job they applied for themselves. Framing the outcome as something that "came to be decided," rather than "I decided," reads as modest instead of self-congratulatory, and it shows up constantly in exactly these personal-announcement moments.

```jp
{{watashitachi||私[わたし]たち}}、{{kekkon-suru||結[けっ]婚[こん]する}}ことになりました。
```
*We're getting married.*

Nobody forced this couple together — but ことになりました is still the natural way to share it. Saying ことに{{suru|masu|しました}} instead ("we decided to get married") would sound almost transactional, businesslike where the moment calls for warmth.

This is worth sitting with, because a beginner's instinct is to reach for whichever verb feels literally true — "I decided" means ことに{{suru||する}}, right? Not always. Politeness culture often outranks literal accuracy here, and ことになる wins even when everyone in the room knows exactly whose decision it was.

The same softening shows up when you're the one turning something down. Baldly saying {{hanasu-v|masu|話[はな]しません}} ("I won't speak") reads as a personal refusal and can land harder than intended; wrapping the same fact in ことになりました makes it sound like circumstances settled the matter, not you.

```jp
{{sono||その}}{{kaigi||会[かい]議[ぎ]}}で{{hanasu-v|nai|話[はな]さない}}ことになりました。
```
*It's been decided that I won't speak at that meeting.*

## Contrast

The pattern's closest relative is ことに{{suru||する}}, and mixing them up is easy — same skeleton, dictionary or ない form plus こと plus a verb. The difference is entirely about who's driving. {{suru||する}} is something you actively do; {{naru-become||なる}} is something that happens to you. ことに{{suru||する}} is a resolution you made yourself; ことになる is one that reached you from outside, whether that outside force is a person, an institution, or plain circumstance.

```jp
{{watashi||私[わたし]}}は{{nihongo||日本[にほん]語[ご]}}を{{benkyou-suru||勉[べん]強[きょう]する}}ことに{{suru|masu|しました}}。
```
*I decided to study Japanese.*

That's a personal resolution — nobody assigned this, the speaker chose it. Keep the exact same activity but let a university set the requirement instead, and the sentence's whole feel shifts even though barely a word changed:

```jp
{{daigaku||大[だい]学[がく]}}で{{nihongo||日本[にほん]語[ご]}}を{{benkyou-suru||勉[べん]強[きょう]する}}ことになりました。
```
*It was decided that I'd study Japanese at university.*

Same subject, same verb, completely different source behind the decision. Whenever you're unsure which one to reach for, ask yourself whose choice it actually was — the honest answer picks the verb for you every time.

Hold onto ことに{{naru-become|ta|なった}}: pair it with 〜ばかり later and you'll be able to say something was decided *just now*, freshly, before you've even had the chance to tell anyone — ことに{{naru-become|ta|なった}}ばかり。
caution_notes: Reserve ことになる for outcomes decided by someone or something else — for your own choice, use ことにする instead.
The negative goes on the verb (行かないことになる), never on なる itself.
Japanese speakers often announce even personal news — a marriage, a job offer they applied for — with ことになりました rather than ことにしました, because it sounds modest rather than self-congratulatory.
ことになっている describes a standing rule or arrangement, not a one-time decision — use ことになりました for news you're reporting once.

items.explanation_markdown:
Your host family's little brother has a bowl of {{okashi||お菓[か]子[し]}} in front of him every single time you walk into the kitchen — breakfast, lunch, it doesn't matter. Vegetables sit on the plate untouched, day after day, and eventually you want to say it out loud, the way you'd say "he only eats sweets" in English. That's the job ばかり does: it plants itself right after a noun and announces "nothing else, just this — and it's been going on."

```jp
{{otouto||弟[おとうと]}}は{{okashi||お菓[か]子[し]}}ばかり{{taberu|te|食[た]べて}}{{iru-exist||いる}}。
```

*My younger brother eats nothing but sweets.*

Notice what's missing from that sentence: no negative verb, no extra word bolted on to spell out the exclusion. ばかり does the whole job by itself, and it leans a little judgmental while it does it — you're not neutrally reporting a diet, you're complaining about one, and native listeners will hear that complaint whether you meant to put it there or not.

That single word is doing two jobs at once, and it's worth separating them before you go any further, because mixing them up is the single most common mistake with this pattern. One job is about *what*: out of everything that could be true, only this one thing is. The other job, which you'll meet a little further down, is about *when*: something happened, and it happened so recently that it still feels like news. Both jobs share the same name and the same little word, but they attach to different pieces of grammar, and only context tells you which one a given sentence means.

## How it works

ばかり attaches directly to a noun, no particle needed in between most of the time — though a topic marker like は often rides along outside it, the way it did in that first sentence, marking who the whole comment is about. The meaning underneath is always "nothing but X": whatever else could reasonably be happening instead is conspicuously absent, and that absence is the point.

Your own week can look the same some months. Think back to a stretch where every evening after class disappeared into one activity and nothing else got touched — that's exactly the shape ばかり is built for.

```jp
{{watashi||私[わたし]}}は宿[しゅく]題[だい]ばかり{{suru|te|して}}{{iru-exist||いる}}。
```

*I'm doing nothing but homework.*

That sentence works because ばかり sits directly on 宿[しゅく]題[だい], the thing being done exclusively. It doesn't matter whether that's actually true down to the minute — you slept, you ate, you did other things too — ばかり is about what stands out when you look back on the stretch as a whole. That's the flavor: not a literal 100%, but "this is what defined the period."

ばかり has a second job that looks completely different on the surface: bolt it onto the Ta-form — the plain past form you already know from -た, like {{okiru|ta|起[お]きた}} for "woke up" — and it stops meaning "nothing but" and starts meaning "just did." The trigger switches from exclusivity to timing: this thing finished so recently that it's still fresh, close enough that mentioning it feels current rather than historical.

```jp
{{okiru||起[お]きる}} → {{okiru|ta|起[お]きた}} → {{okiru|ta|起[お]きた}}ばかり
```

*wake up → woke up → just woke up*

Same verb, three stages: dictionary form, plain past, and plain past plus ばかり for "moments ago." Once ばかり lands on the Ta-form, it almost always shows up with です or だ closing the sentence out, because the whole point is usually a comment about right now — someone asking what's going on, and you answering with what just happened.

```jp
{{ima||今[いま]}}、{{okiru|ta|起[お]きた}}ばかりです。
```

*I just woke up.*

The same shape works for anything that recently wrapped up, not just waking up. Picture texting a friend who's clearly stressed and finding out why: it turns out they only clocked in for the first time yesterday, so of course everything still feels overwhelming.

```jp
{{tomodachi||友[とも]達[だち]}}は{{shigoto||仕[し]事[ごと]}}を{{hajimeru|ta|始[はじ]めた}}ばかりだ。
```

*My friend just started the job.*

## Rules and exceptions

The Ta-form requirement for the "just did" reading is not optional, and this is where the two jobs of ばかり can genuinely trip you up. Attach ばかり to a dictionary-form verb hoping for "just do" and you don't get that meaning at all — you get something that doesn't parse the way you intended, because ばかり on its own carries no sense of completion. The completion has to already be sitting in the Ta-form before ばかり arrives to comment on how recent it was.

> Don't reach for `起きるばかり` when you mean "just woke up" — the Ta-form ({{okiru|ta|起[お]きた}}) is what carries the "this already happened" meaning; ばかり only adds "and it happened recently." Drop the Ta-form and there's nothing left for ばかり to attach its timing to.

There's also a nuance trap on the noun side, and it trips up learners in the opposite direction — not a grammar mistake, but a tone one. Noun + ばかり is technically neutral; it just states an exclusive fact about what's happening. But in real conversation it almost always carries a complaint, the same way English "all he does is..." sounds annoyed even though it's, strictly speaking, just a true statement. There's no way to keep the same word and strip the attitude back out — the raised eyebrow comes bundled in, every time.

The "just did" reading has one more sharp edge worth naming: "recently" is a feeling, not a stopwatch. Whether たばかり sounds natural depends on how the speaker sees the gap, not on an actual number of minutes. Someone who moved cities a month ago might still say {{hikkosu|ta|引[ひ]っ越[こ]した}}ばかりだ if the boxes are still unpacked and the new routine hasn't settled in — the sentence is really about how fresh the change still feels to the person saying it, not a strict cutoff you can look up.

## Casual speech

In relaxed conversation, ばかり often stretches into ばっかり — same meaning, heavier emphasis, the kind of sound you'd expect from someone who's genuinely fed up rather than just reporting a fact. {{otouto||弟[おとうと]}}は{{okashi||お菓[か]子[し]}}ばっかり{{taberu|stem|食[た]べ}}てるよ carries the exact same complaint as the very first example in this lesson, just with the volume turned up: ばかり lengthens into ばっかり, and て{{iru-exist||いる}} contracts down to てる the way it usually does when people are talking quickly. Save ばっかり for friends and family. Written Japanese, and anything even slightly formal, wants the fuller ばかり.

## Contrast

You already have ことが{{aru||ある}} for talking about experience — something you've done at some undefined point in your life, with no particular claim about when. Ta-form plus ばかり looks almost identical on the page, since both sit on the exact same Ta-form starting point, but the two constructions are answering completely different questions: not "has this ever happened to you," but "did this happen just moments ago."

```jp
{{nihon||日本[にほん]}}に{{iku-v|ta|行[い]った}}ことが{{aru||ある}}。
```

*I have been to Japan before.*

```jp
{{watashi||私[わたし]}}は{{nihon||日本[にほん]}}に{{iku-v|ta|行[い]った}}ばかりだ。
```

*I just went to Japan.*

Same verb, same destination, same Ta-form beginning — and the two endings send the sentence to opposite ends of a timeline. ことが{{aru||ある}} points backward with no particular date attached, a fact filed away in your personal history. たばかり points at right now, looking back over its shoulder at something that only just wrapped up. Swap one ending for the other and you've swapped "at some point in my life" for "as of a few minutes ago," which is exactly why this pair is worth slowing down on the first few times you meet it.

Hold onto that "just wrapped up" feeling — you're about to meet ところ, a cousin construction that covers the same general territory from a few different angles at once: about to happen, happening right now, or just finished, all wrapped into one word. ばかり only ever handles that last piece, the "just finished" edge, but it's good preparation for seeing how much more ground ところ ends up covering.
caution_notes: ばかり only gives the 'just did' meaning when it follows the Ta-form — attaching it to a dictionary-form verb doesn't work.
Noun + ばかり almost always sounds like a complaint in real conversation, even though it's grammatically just a neutral statement of exclusivity.
ばっかり is a casual stretch of ばかり — save it for friends, not for anything formal or written.
Don't confuse たばかり (something just happened) with ことがある (something has happened at some point) — they share the same Ta-form but answer different questions.

items.explanation_markdown:
Your phone buzzes. A friend texts: {{dekakeru||出[で]かける}}？ You already have your {{kaban||かばん}} in one hand and your {{kutsu||靴[くつ]}} on your feet, standing right by the {{doa||ドア}}, keys warm from your palm. There's only one honest answer, and it isn't a statement of general intent — it's a report on exactly where you are, right this second.

```jp
{{ima||今[いま]}}、{{deru-v||出[で]る}}ところです。
```

*I'm just about to leave.*

Not {{deru-v|masu|出[で]ます}}, which only states a plan with no sense of *when*. ところ does something narrower and more useful: it freezes the clock and names the exact instant you're standing in — a beat before an action starts, right in the thick of it, or a beat after it's already ended. You've probably met ところ before as a plain noun meaning "place" — {{toshokan||図[と]書[しょ]館[かん]}}の{{chikaku||近[ちか]く}}のところ, roughly "the area near the library." This grammar use borrows that same idea and narrows it, from physical space down to a single point in time: not where you're standing, but where you're standing *inside the action*.

## How it works

### The moment before: dictionary form + ところ

Attach ところ straight onto a verb's plain dictionary form and you get the instant right before the action starts. Everything is lined up for it — you've decided, your body is already halfway into motion — but nothing has actually happened yet. That's the shape in the opening line above, {{ima||今[いま]}}、{{deru-v||出[で]る}}ところです. Here's the same shape with a different verb.

```jp
{{ima||今[いま]}}、{{denwa-suru||電[でん]話[わ]する}}ところです。
```

*I'm just about to make a phone call.*

You can feel why {{deru-v|masu|出[で]ます}} and {{deru-v||出[で]る}}ところです land so differently now. {{deru-v|masu|出[で]ます}} could be true at any point today. {{deru-v||出[で]る}}ところです is only true for the few seconds you're actually saying it.

### The middle: ~ているところ

Swap in て{{iru-exist||いる}}, the ongoing-action form you already know from describing habits and states, and ところ moves right along with it. Now you're not standing before the action — you're inside it, mid-motion, and someone asking you a question would be interrupting.

```jp
{{ima||今[いま]}}、{{benkyou||勉[べん]強[きょう]}}しているところです。
```

*I'm right in the middle of studying.*

```jp
{{ima||今[いま]}}、掃[そう]除[じ]{{suru|te|して}}いるところです。
```

*I'm right in the middle of cleaning.*

This is the version you'll reach for most in daily conversation, because "I'm doing X right now" is a far more common thing to report than "I'm about to" or "I just did." Notice that て{{iru-exist||いる}} alone would already mean roughly the same thing — ところ just sharpens the focus onto this precise moment, the way pointing at a spot on a map is sharper than gesturing at a whole city.

### The moment after: た-form + ところ

Use the plain past た-form you already know from ことが{{aru||ある}}, and ところ steps to the other side of the action — the instant right after it ended, close enough that there's no real gap between finishing and speaking.

```jp
{{ima||今[いま]}}、{{asagohan||朝[あさ]ご飯[はん]}}を{{taberu|ta|食[た]べた}}ところです。
```

*I just finished eating breakfast.*

```jp
{{ima||今[いま]}}、宿[しゅく]題[だい]を{{suru|ta|した}}ところです。
```

*I just finished my homework.*

Say either of these an hour late and something feels off, the way it feels off to say "I just woke up" at three in the afternoon. たところ is honest about the clock — it only works when the gap really is close to zero.

The shape never changes once you know which side of the action you're describing: keep whichever verb form fits the moment, then set ところ right after it.

```jp
{{deru-v||出[で]る}} → {{deru-v||出[で]る}}ところ
```

*leave → about to leave*

## Rules and exceptions

ところ describes one instant, not a stretch of time, and it doesn't get along with words that imply repetition, like {{mainichi||毎[まい]日[にち]}} (every day). Something that happens over and over isn't a single moment you can point at — `毎日勉強しているところです` reads like a contradiction, because "every day" pulls toward a habit while ところ insists on right now, once, and nowhere else.

> ところ only ever follows a conjugated verb — never a plain adjective sitting on its own. `暑いところです` isn't a way to say "it's hot right now"; for that you just need the adjective and です by themselves ({{ima||今[いま]}}、{{atsui-hot||暑[あつ]い}}です).

In casual speech, the です at the end can drop the way it does after most plain-form sentences, so a friend might just say {{ima||今[いま]}}、{{deru-v||出[で]る}}ところ with the sentence trailing off. But ところ itself never contracts or shortens — it's the polite ending around it that relaxes, not the word doing the actual work.

## Contrast

You already know ばかり for "just did" — Ta-form + ばかり. It sits close enough to たところ that it's easy to reach for the wrong one without noticing. たところ insists on zero gap: you're speaking in almost the same breath as the action ending. ばかり is looser — the action could have wrapped up a few minutes ago, even longer, and you'd still reach for it as long as it still feels recent to you.

```jp
宿[しゅく]題[だい]を{{suru|ta|した}}ばかりです。
```

*I only just finished my homework (and it still feels recent).*

Say it the instant the last page closes, and 宿[しゅく]題[だい]を{{suru|ta|した}}ところです is exact. Say it an hour later, still a little pleased with yourself, and 宿[しゅく]題[だい]を{{suru|ta|した}}ばかりです is the one that's honest — たところ at that point would be quietly lying about the clock, claiming a freshness that's already worn off.

ところ is a stopwatch, not a calendar — it only ever names the instant you're standing in, whether that's a beat before an action, right inside it, or a beat after it lets go of you. Hold onto that instinct for freezing a single moment; you'll want it again soon, when {{aida||間[あいだ]}} asks you to describe not one instant but the whole stretch of time something else was happening around it.
caution_notes: ところ marks a single instant, not a stretch of time, so it clashes with repeated or habitual phrasing like 毎日勉強しているところです.
ところ only attaches after a conjugated verb, never directly after a plain adjective, so 暑いところです is not a way to talk about right now.
たところ and ばかり look similar but aren't interchangeable — たところ claims zero gap between the action and the moment of speaking, while ばかり tolerates a small gap.
ところです can drop its です in casual speech, but ところ itself never changes shape or contracts.
