items.explanation_markdown:
You're at your desk with headphones on, working through kanji flashcards while your family is out running errands. By the time they get back, you've gone through half the deck — for the entire stretch they were gone, you were studying. In Japanese, saying "for this whole period, this other thing was also true" is exactly the job of 間[あいだ]・間[あいだ]に (あいだ・あいだに), a phrase that turns a stretch of time into a container you can put another action inside.

```jp
{{watashi||私[わたし]}}が{{benkyou||勉[べん]強[きょう]}}して{{iru-exist||いる}}間[あいだ]、{{neko||猫[ねこ]}}は{{neru|te|寝[ね]て}}{{iru-exist|ta|いた}}。
```

*While I was studying, the cat was sleeping.*

Both halves of that sentence cover the same stretch — my studying and the cat's napping ran side by side, start to finish. That's plain 間[あいだ] doing its job: it says "for this whole period," and both clauses are describing something that lasted the entire time.

This pattern shows up constantly once you start listening for it, because so much of ordinary conversation is about two things happening around the same stretch of time — someone cooking while someone else sets the table, rain falling while you wait at a station, a phone staying silent while you're in a meeting. English usually reaches for "while" or "during" without thinking twice about which one; Japanese wants you to decide something more specific first.

## How it works

間[あいだ] (あいだ) is the ordinary word for "interval" or "the space between two things" — you'll also meet it on its own, meaning "between," in phrases like {{ie||家[いえ]}}と{{eki||駅[えき]}}の間[あいだ] (between the house and the station). As a grammar pattern, it attaches after a verb in its て{{iru-exist||いる}} form, or after a plain noun with の, and either way it names a block of time that the rest of the sentence gets placed against.

```jp
{{benkyou-suru||勉[べん]強[きょう]する}} → {{benkyou||勉[べん]強[きょう]}}して{{iru-exist||いる}}間[あいだ]
```

*to study → while studying*

Dictionary form → て-form + {{iru-exist||いる}} → add 間[あいだ]. The て{{iru-exist||いる}} step matters: 間[あいだ] wants an ongoing state, not a single completed action, because it's marking off a *span*, and a span needs something continuous running across it — a state you could freeze at any point in the middle and still be true.

Add に right after 間[あいだ] and the meaning shifts in a small but important way. 間[あいだ] alone says "this whole stretch"; 間[あいだ]に says "at some point within this stretch, one thing happened."

```jp
{{watashi||私[わたし]}}が{{benkyou||勉[べん]強[きょう]}}して{{iru-exist||いる}}間[あいだ]に、{{neko||猫[ねこ]}}が{{mado||窓[まど]}}から{{deru-v|ta|出[で]た}}。
```

*While I was studying, the cat went out through the window.*

The cat didn't spend the whole study session climbing out — it happened once, at some moment inside that stretch. に is doing the work of pinning a single event somewhere inside the block of time, instead of spreading it across the whole thing the way 間[あいだ] alone would.

The same split shows up with nouns, no verb required. Attach の間[あいだ](に) straight onto a noun that names a period, and you get the same two flavors again — the whole stretch, or one moment somewhere inside it.

```jp
{{kaigi||会[かい]議[ぎ]}}の間[あいだ]、{{denwa||電[でん]話[わ]}}を{{kesu|ta|消[け]した}}。
```

*During the meeting, I turned off my phone.*

```jp
{{kaigi||会[かい]議[ぎ]}}の間[あいだ]に、{{ame-v||雨[あめ]}}が{{furu-rain|ta|降[ふ]った}}。
```

*It started raining sometime during the meeting.*

My phone stayed off for the entire meeting, start to finish — that's plain 間[あいだ]. The rain wasn't a condition that lasted the whole meeting; it started at some unspecified point inside it, so 間[あいだ]に is the one that fits. Notice that neither sentence needed a verb before 間[あいだ] at all — の間[あいだ] sits directly on the noun, the same way ことが{{aru||ある}} sits on a verb but もの can sit on a plain adjective; each pattern has its own attachment rule, and this one is a noun's.

That noun version is worth pausing on, because it's the one you'll reach for most in casual talk about your day. Any word that names a period with a clear start and end — {{kaigi||会[かい]議[ぎ]}}, {{jugyou||授[じゅ]業[ぎょう]}}, {{shuumatsu||週[しゅう]末[まつ]}} — can slot straight into の間[あいだ](に) without any conjugation at all. You don't need to know how to turn {{kaigi||会[かい]議[ぎ]}} into a verb, because you don't; the noun already names the block of time you need.

## Rules and exceptions

The whole system comes down to one question: is the main-clause event a *stretched-out state*, or a *single occurrence*? 間[あいだ] wants the first. 間[あいだ]に wants the second. It sounds abstract until you test it against a sentence where the main clause is neither a verb nor an obvious action.

```jp
{{jugyou||授[じゅ]業[ぎょう]}}の間[あいだ]、{{kyoushitsu||教[きょう]室[しつ]}}は{{totemo||とても}}{{shizuka||静[しず]か}}だった。
```

*During class, the classroom was very quiet.*

"Very quiet" isn't a one-off event — it's a condition that held for the entire class period, so plain 間[あいだ] is correct, matching the same logic as the て{{iru-exist||いる}} examples even though there's no verb in sight. As long as the described state covers the whole span, plain 間[あいだ] belongs there.

> Mixing these two up is the single most common mistake with this pattern. Writing `勉強している間、猫が窓から出た。` sounds like the cat was somehow going out through the window continuously for the entire study session, which doesn't make sense — going out is something that happens once, not something you can stretch across an hour. The fix is just adding に:

```jp
{{benkyou||勉[べん]強[きょう]}}して{{iru-exist||いる}}間[あいだ]に、{{neko||猫[ねこ]}}が{{mado||窓[まど]}}から{{deru-v|ta|出[で]た}}。
```

*While I was studying, the cat went out.*

One more edge worth knowing: because 間[あいだ] needs an ongoing predicate, you generally can't drop it straight onto a verb that names a sudden, single change — something like {{deru-v||出[で]る}} (to go out) — without て{{iru-exist||いる}} first. て{{iru-exist||いる}} is what turns a one-shot action into a state you can stretch a block of time around; without it, there's nothing for 間[あいだ] to measure.

There's also a smaller trap hiding in sentences like the meeting example. Nothing stops you from writing a sentence where *both* halves are stretched-out states, which is exactly the shape 間[あいだ] wants — but it's easy to reach for に out of habit anyway, because English "during" doesn't force you to think about duration versus a single moment the way Japanese does. Whenever you catch yourself about to add に, stop and ask what the main-clause verb or adjective is actually describing: a state that fills the whole block, or an event you could point to on a clock. In casual conversation this pattern doesn't contract or drop politeness the way です/だ pairs do — 間[あいだ] and 間[あいだ]に sound exactly the same whether you're texting a friend or writing a report, which is one less thing to track while you're getting the duration-versus-moment choice right.

## Contrast

You already know ところ for catching an action mid-process — {{dekakeru||出[で]かける}}ところ, "just about to head out," or {{dekakeru|te|出[で]かけて}}{{iru-exist||いる}}ところ, "in the middle of heading out." ところ zooms in on one specific point along that process, almost like pausing a video. 間[あいだ] does the opposite: it steps back and treats the whole process, start to finish, as a single block of time you can talk about. {{dekakeru||出[で]かける}}ところ is a freeze-frame; {{dekakeru|te|出[で]かけて}}{{iru-exist||いる}}間[あいだ] is the whole clip playing start to end.

That difference matters because the two aren't interchangeable just because they can follow the same verbs. If your friend calls you exactly as you're stepping out the door, that's a ところ moment — one instant, caught mid-action. If your friend calls at some unspecified point while you're out for an hour, that's an 間[あいだ]に moment — the interval itself is doing the work, not one exact instant inside a single motion.

Take the meeting sentences from earlier and imagine swapping in ところ instead: `会議のところ` doesn't really work the way {{kaigi||会[かい]議[ぎ]}}の間[あいだ] does, because ところ needs something with a clear "middle" to catch you in — a verb in progress, not a noun that just names a block of time. That's the giveaway when you're unsure which one to reach for: if you can point to a single instant and say "right there, that's the point," ところ is available; if you're describing a whole stretch, or something landing anywhere inside that stretch, 間[あいだ] or 間[あいだ]に is what you want. 間[あいだ] and 間[あいだ]に don't compete with ところ so much as sit on a different scale of time — ところ is a point, 間[あいだ] is a stretch, and 間[あいだ]に is a point that happens to land somewhere inside a stretch.

Keep that distinction in mind, because a close cousin of 間[あいだ] comes later, at N3: {{uchi||うち}}に, which also frames a stretch of time but adds a sense of urgency — "while it's still true, before it stops being true." For now, 間[あいだ]・間[あいだ]に stays neutral: no ticking clock, just two things that happened to share the same stretch of time.
caution_notes: Use plain 間 only when the main clause describes a state or action that fills the entire stretch of time, not something that happens once.
Use 間に when the main-clause event is a single occurrence landing somewhere inside the background stretch, not something continuous.
間 needs an ongoing predicate before it — a verb in ている form or a plain noun with の — never a bare single-shot action.
ところ marks one specific point in a process, while 間 marks the whole span around it, so the two are not interchangeable even after similar verbs.

items.explanation_markdown:
Picture this: you're texting a friend about tomorrow's hike, but the forecast is shaky. You don't want to promise it'll rain — you just want to cover what happens if it does. That's the shape 場[ば]合[あい] is built for. It doesn't predict anything. It labels a possible scenario and lets you say what you'll do if that one turns out to be the one that happens.

Japanese has plenty of ways to talk about conditions, and you'll meet more of them soon. 場[ば]合[あい] is the one for laying out a specific case — this situation, as opposed to some other one — and then responding to it directly.

## How it works

場[ば]合[あい] (ばあい) is itself a noun meaning "case" or "instance." You build the scenario in front of it, then treat the whole thing as a launching point for what comes next. With a verb, the clause in front just stays in plain form — the same shape you'd use to end a sentence on its own.

```jp
{{densha||電[でん]車[しゃ]}}が{{okureru||遅[おく]れる}}場[ば]合[あい]は、連[れん]絡[らく]{{suru|te|して}}ください。
```

*If the train is late, please contact me.*

Notice {{okureru||遅[おく]れる}} sits there completely unchanged, present-tense and plain, the way it would if you were just saying "the train is late" to a friend. 場[ば]合[あい]は then turns that into "in the case where that happens."

With a noun in front, you can't jump straight to 場[ば]合[あい] — you need の bridging the two nouns first, the same の that links {{tomodachi||友[とも]達[だち]}}の{{ie||家[いえ]}} or {{watashi||私[わたし]}}の{{kasa||傘[かさ]}}.

```jp
{{ame-v||雨[あめ]}} → {{ame-v||雨[あめ]}}の場[ば]合[あい]
```

*rain → in the case of rain*

```jp
{{ame-v||雨[あめ]}}の場[ば]合[あい]、{{kasa||傘[かさ]}}を{{motsu|te|持[も]って}}{{iku-v|masu|行[い]きます}}。
```

*In case of rain, I'll bring an umbrella.*

Past and negative clauses slot in exactly the same way, because they're still plain forms — 場[ば]合[あい] doesn't care about timing, only about the shape of what's in front of it.

```jp
{{wakaru|nai|分[わ]からない}}場[ば]合[あい]は、{{sensei||先[せん]生[せい]}}に{{kiku-v|te|聞[き]いて}}ください。
```

*If you don't understand, please ask the teacher.*

```jp
財[さい]布[ふ]を{{nakusu|ta|無[な]くした}}場[ば]合[あい]、警[けい]官[かん]に{{iu-v|masu|言[い]います}}。
```

*If I lose my wallet, I'll tell a police officer.*

That second one is worth sitting with — {{nakusu|ta|無[な]くした}} is past tense, describing a scenario that hasn't happened yet. That feels backwards in English, but in Japanese the past form there just marks the loss as a completed event *within* the hypothetical, the way "if I've lost my wallet" reads more naturally than "if I lose my wallet" once you notice it.

## Rules and exceptions

The の between a noun and 場[ば]合[あい] isn't optional style — it's structural.

> `病気場合` isn't a sentence a Japanese speaker would produce. It has to be `病気の場合` — の is doing real grammatical work, not sitting there for decoration.

は after 場[ば]合[あい] is common but not required. Reach for it when you're contrasting this case against some other one you're aware of; skip it when you're simply laying out one scenario on its own.

```jp
{{byouki||病[びょう]気[き]}}の場[ば]合[あい]、{{gakkou-v||学[がっ]校[こう]}}を{{yasumu|masu|休[やす]みます}}。
```

*If I'm sick, I take the day off school.*

```jp
{{isogashii||忙[いそが]しい}}場[ば]合[あい]は、{{tetsudau|te|手伝[てつだ]って}}ください。
```

*If you're busy, please help me.*

One more trap worth naming early: even when the scenario you're describing is about something that might happen later, the clause in front of 場[ば]合[あい] stays plain present or plain past — never a guessing form like `遅れるだろう場合`. 場[ば]合[あい] wants a fact-shaped clause sitting in front of it; the hedging about whether it'll actually happen lives outside the grammar, in your tone and context, not baked into the sentence itself.

## 場[ば]合[あい] vs たら

You've already met たら for "if / when X happens, then Y." On the page, たら and 場[ば]合[あい] can cover the same ground: {{ame-v||雨[あめ]}}が{{furu-rain|stem|降[ふ]っ}}たら and {{ame-v||雨[あめ]}}の場[ば]合[あい] can both open a plan for a rainy day. But they're answering different questions. たら also works for things that will certainly happen — it just marks the point after which the next thing follows. 場[ば]合[あい] says *if this particular thing comes up, here's my plan* — with no claim at all about whether it actually will.

```jp
{{ie||家[いえ]}}に{{kaeru-v|stem|帰[かえ]っ}}たら、{{denwa||電[でん]話[わ]}}します。
```

*When I get home, I'll call you.*

You are definitely going home; たら only says the call comes after. Swap in 場[ば]合[あい] — `家に帰った場合、電話します` — and getting home turns into an uncertain outcome you're planning around, as if you might not make it. Reach for 場[ば]合[あい] when you're laying out a contingency, the kind of line you see in instructions and notices; reach for たら for everyday "when / if" sentences.

Hold onto that distinction — 場[ば]合[あい] sets up a scenario without committing to it coming true, and that's exactly the territory と will move into soon, for situations where one thing leads to another automatically, no maybe about it.
caution_notes: Between a noun and 場合 you always need の — `病気場合` is wrong; it must be `病気の場合`.
場合 lays out a possible scenario without claiming it will happen, so don't dress the clause in front of it with a guessing form like だろう.
場合 and たら aren't interchangeable — たら also covers things that will certainly happen (家に帰ったら), while 場合 only names a scenario that may or may not come up.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're staying at a friend's place, and their phone starts buzzing on the table. Before anyone reaches for it, their cat leaps a foot in the air and knocks a cup off the shelf. Every single time, without fail, that's how it goes — the phone rings, the cat panics. There's no discussion involved, no choice, no "maybe" about it. That's exactly the shape of と: it connects two things where the first one triggers the second automatically, the way a light switch is wired straight to a bulb.

```jp
{{denwa||電[でん]話[わ]}}が{{naru-ring||鳴[な]る}}と、{{neko||猫[ねこ]}}が驚[おどろ]く。
```

*The phone rings, and the cat gets startled.*

That's と doing its real job — not describing a one-off event, but describing how things just go, every time, without anyone stepping in to decide anything. English blurs "if" and "when" together in a dozen different ways, but と narrows the range on purpose: reach for it only when the second half isn't up for debate.

Think of と as a wire, not a suggestion. Once you connect the two ends, current flows whether anyone's watching or not. A friend's cat isn't consulted before it flinches, and neither is the weather, the season, or your own face after a drink — those are exactly the situations と was built for, and the rest of this lesson is mostly about learning to spot them.

## How it works

と attaches directly to the plain, present-tense form of whatever leads into it — the same casual form you'd use to end a sentence on its own. と itself never conjugates, and it doesn't care about politeness levels; whatever comes before it just needs to already be in plain present shape, and everything else builds off that one clause.

```jp
{{mado||窓[まど]}}を{{akeru||開[あ]ける}}と、{{kaze-wind||風[かぜ]}}が{{hairu-v||入[はい]る}}。
```

*Open the window, and wind comes in.*

{{mado||窓[まど]}}を{{akeru||開[あ]ける}} is already plain present ("open"), so と simply hooks onto the end of it. Whatever follows と has to be something that occurs as a direct, mechanical consequence of the first half — never something you're planning, arranging, or deciding to do. Open the window, wind arrives; there's no gap in between for anyone to weigh in.

い-adjectives slot in the same way — the plain present form of an い-adjective is just the adjective itself, no extra piece needed before と:

```jp
{{osake||お酒[さけ]}}を{{nomu-v||飲[の]む}}と、{{kao||顔[かお]}}が{{akai|stem|赤[あか]く}}{{naru-become||なる}}。
```

*Drink this, and your face turns red.*

{{akai|stem|赤[あか]く}}{{naru-become||なる}} is {{akai||赤[あか]い}} (red) reshaped into {{akai|stem|赤[あか]く}} and paired with {{naru-become||なる}} ("to become") — a bodily reaction nobody has to choose, it just happens. This く{{naru-become||なる}}/に{{naru-become||なる}} + と combination shows up constantly with seasons and general changes in the world, because seasons and bodies don't ask permission either:

```jp
{{fuyu||冬[ふゆ]}}に{{naru-become||なる}}と、{{yuki||雪[ゆき]}}が{{furu-rain||降[ふ]る}}。
```

*When winter comes, snow falls.*

```jp
{{haru||春[はる]}}に{{naru-become||なる}}と、{{atatakai|stem|暖[あたた]かく}}{{naru-become||なる}}。
```

*When spring comes, it turns warm.*

Both sentences use に{{naru-become||なる}} or く{{naru-become||なる}} as the "turns into" hinge, then chain the result on with と. Seasons arriving, temperatures shifting, routines kicking in — と is the natural home for all of it, because none of it is a decision anyone makes. Worth pausing on one small trap here: {{naru-ring||鳴[な]る}} (to ring, from the phone example) and {{naru-become||なる}} (to become) sound identical but are completely different words written with different kanji. Context sorts them out fast once you've seen a few of each, but the first week they can blur together.

と has a second job worth knowing: reporting something you found out the moment the first action wrapped up.

```jp
{{ie||家[いえ]}}に{{kaeru-v||帰[かえ]る}}と、{{ame-v||雨[あめ]}}だった。
```

*I got home, and it was raining.*

Here the second half sits in the past ({{ame-v||雨[あめ]}}だった), because you're reporting a discovery, not stating a standing rule — you walked in the door and, huh, it turns out it's raining. The half in front of と still has to stay present plain regardless of when the whole sentence is set — {{kaeru-v||帰[かえ]る}}, never {{kaeru-v|ta|帰[かえ]った}}, even though the story itself already happened.

## Rules and exceptions

Here's where と gets strict: the second half has to be something that just happens on its own — never something anyone requests, invites, orders, or plans. Requests, invitations, suggestions, and stated intentions are all off-limits after と, no matter how naturally they'd translate into English with "when" or "if."

> Something like `忙しいと、手伝ってください` doesn't work. Being busy doesn't automatically produce a request for help the way a phone ringing automatically startles a cat — a request is a choice someone makes, not a reflex, so と can't carry it.

For that kind of sentence, 場[ば]合[あい] does the job instead — it was built to hold plans, requests, and advice, which is exactly what と refuses to hold:

```jp
{{isogashii||忙[いそが]しい}}場[ば]合[あい]、{{tetsudau|te|手伝[てつだ]って}}ください。
```

*If you're busy, please help.*

場[ば]合[あい] marks a particular situation and leaves plenty of room for a decision, a request, or a plan tied to it. と refuses that room on purpose — it's reserved for the automatic and the inevitable, the sentences where nobody is actually choosing anything.

## Contrast: と vs 場[ば]合[あい]

You already know 場[ば]合[あい] for flagging "in the case of X" before advice or a plan. と looks similar on the surface — both sit after a plain clause and set up a second half — but they carry very different weight. 場[ば]合[あい] describes a scenario someone is reasoning about ahead of time; と describes something that simply keeps happening, rain or shine, decision or no decision.

```jp
{{ame-v||雨[あめ]}}の場[ば]合[あい]、公[こう]園[えん]に{{iku-v|nai|行[い]かない}}。
```

*If it rains, we won't go to the park.*

```jp
{{ame-v||雨[あめ]}}が{{furu-rain||降[ふ]る}}と、公[こう]園[えん]に{{iku-v|nai|行[い]かない}}。
```

*When it rains, we don't go to the park.*

Both sentences land on the same outcome, but they sound different. The 場[ば]合[あい] version reads like a plan somebody worked out in advance — "in the case that it rains, here's what we've decided." The と version reads like a fact about how things go — rain shows up, the park trip just doesn't happen, every time, no planning involved, almost like a rule of the household rather than a choice anyone is making today. Swap them and you swap the flavor: と turns a decision into a law of nature, 場[ば]合[あい] turns a law of nature back into a choice.

This is also why と sentences tend to sound more confident, almost blunt, next to their 場[ば]合[あい] counterparts. Saying {{ame-v||雨[あめ]}}の場[ば]合[あい]、公[こう]園[えん]に{{iku-v|nai|行[い]かない}} leaves a little space — maybe circumstances change, maybe someone reconsiders. Saying {{ame-v||雨[あめ]}}が{{furu-rain||降[ふ]る}}と、公[こう]園[えん]に{{iku-v|nai|行[い]かない}} closes that space entirely. If you've ever wondered why a textbook example with と can sound oddly matter-of-fact in translation, this is usually why: the grammar itself is doing the work of removing doubt, not just describing a sequence of events.

One more small thing worth knowing: unlike some connectors you've seen, と doesn't shrink or shift in casual speech. Friends talking quickly still say と exactly as written — there's no shortened version to learn here, so once the plain-present-plus-と shape is solid, you already have the whole pattern in every register.

Reach for と when you're stating something automatic, habitual, or freshly discovered. Reach for 場[ば]合[あい] the moment a request, a suggestion, or a real decision needs to sit in the second half. Keeping that line clear is most of what と actually asks of you — and it's the same instinct you'll lean on again once から shows up for reasons that are simply true, rather than reasons someone is asking you to accept.

One last thing worth carrying forward: と rewards paying attention to what kind of sentence you're actually building before you reach for it. If you catch yourself about to type a request, an invitation, or a plan right after と, that's the signal to stop and swap in 場[ば]合[あい] instead — not a sign that と is broken, just a sign it's the wrong tool for that particular sentence. Get comfortable with that swap and the rest of the pattern mostly takes care of itself.
caution_notes: Never put a request, invitation, order, or suggestion in the clause after と — for those, use 場合 instead.
The clause right before と must stay in plain present form even when the second half describes something in the past, like a discovery.
と states something automatic or habitual; if the outcome is really a plan or decision someone made, 場合 is the better fit.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're texting a friend to bail on plans tonight. "{{isogashii||忙[いそが]しい}}から、{{ikeru|nai|行[い]けない}}" — busy, so no. Blunt, quick, done. Now picture writing your teacher the reason you missed class. Same idea, "because," but that same から would land like you're arguing with them. You reach for something softer instead: ので.

That's the whole tension in this lesson. から and ので both mean "because," they attach to sentences in nearly the same way, and one of them is going to sound rude in a room where the other sounds completely normal. Time to learn which is which.

## How it works

Both patterns follow the plain form of whatever caused the situation, with the reason first and the result second.

```jp
{{isogashii||忙[いそが]しい}}から、{{ikeru|nai|行[い]けない}}。
```
*Busy, so [I] can't go.*

Verbs and い-adjectives don't need anything extra — the plain, dictionary-style form attaches straight to both patterns, no changes required.

```jp
{{isogashii||忙[いそが]しい}} → {{isogashii||忙[いそが]しい}}から
```
*busy → because [I'm] busy*

Nouns and な-adjectives are where the two patterns split from each other. から wants the plain copula だ in front of it, exactly like any other plain-form sentence. ので wants な instead — the だ disappears completely.

```jp
{{shizuka||静[しず]か}} → {{shizuka||静[しず]か}}なので
```
*quiet → since [it's] quiet*

```jp
{{shizuka||静[しず]か}}{{dakara||だから}}、{{koko||ここ}}が{{suki||好[す]き}}です。
```
*Because it's quiet, [I] like this place.*

```jp
{{shizuka||静[しず]か}}なので、{{koko||ここ}}が{{suki||好[す]き}}です。
```
*Since it's quiet, [I] like this place.*

Read those last two sentences side by side. The meaning barely moves — that's the whole point of this lesson. What actually changes is the room you can say each one in.

## Rules and exceptions

The real difference between から and ので isn't grammar, it's stance. から presents the reason as *yours* — an opinion, a decision, something you're standing behind and ready to defend if someone pushes back. ので presents the reason as a plain fact of the situation, something anyone in the room would agree with, which is exactly why it lands as more polite: you're not arguing your case, you're just reporting what's true.

That's also why ので shows up constantly in notes to teachers, apologies, and formal requests, while から shows up in casual talk and in sentences where you're explaining yourself or trying to persuade someone. Compare {{isogashii||忙[いそが]しい}}から、{{yasumu|masu|休[やす]みます}} (I'm taking the day off — busy, that's my call) against {{isogashii||忙[いそが]しい}}ので、{{yasumu|masu|休[やす]みます}} (I'm taking the day off; I'm busy, as you can see) — same words, same day off, a completely different feel.

```jp
{{atama||頭[あたま]}}が{{itai||痛[いた]い}}ので、{{yasumu|masu|休[やす]みます}}。
```
*My head hurts, so I'll rest today.*

> Commands, invitations, and "let's" sentences almost always want から, not ので. `危ないので、走らないで` reads like you're trying to sound polite while telling someone what to do, and it comes out strange. から is built for that job.

```jp
{{abunai||危[あぶ]ない}}から、{{hashiru|nai|走[はし]らないで}}。
```
*It's dangerous, so don't run.*

The だ/な split from the last section is the easiest place to slip — writing `静かだので` or `静かなから` will sound off to a Japanese ear immediately, even when every other piece of the sentence is right.

## Casual speech

In relaxed speech, ので often shrinks to んで. The meaning doesn't change at all — it's just faster to say.

```jp
{{isogashii||忙[いそが]しい}}んで、{{ikeru|nai|行[い]けない}}。
```
*Busy, so [I] can't go.* (casual)

から doesn't contract the same way. It stays から whether you're texting a friend or writing something formal — the word itself never softens; only the situation you choose to use it in does.

## Contrast

You've already met と for describing something that happens automatically once a condition is met. と can't carry a decision or an opinion the way から can — {{byouki||病[びょう]気[き]}}{{dakara||だから}}、{{yasumu||休[やす]む}} is you choosing to rest, while と would need the resting to just follow on its own, with no room for you deciding anything. から and ので are both about a reason someone is putting forward; と isn't really about a reason at all, it's about an automatic result.

So the real question with から and ので was never "which one is more correct" — it's "am I stating a fact, or standing behind an opinion." Keep that instinct close, because it comes back almost unchanged when というより shows up at N3: instead of restating a reason, it lets you correct one you already gave.
caution_notes: ので presents a reason as a plain fact you're reporting, not an opinion you're pushing — reach for it in notes, apologies, and requests instead of から.
Commands, invitations, and volitional sentences almost always take から; ので sounds strange right in front of them.
Nouns and な-adjectives take だ before から but な before ので — mixing the two, like 静かだので or 静かなから, is the single most common slip.
から never contracts, but casual ので often shortens to んで in relaxed speech.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're catching up with a friend who just got back from a trip, and you've got a dozen questions lined up — the food, the flight, whether it rained the whole time. In English you'd just say "tell me about the trip." Japanese has one small, extremely useful piece of grammar that does that exact job: について, glued directly onto whatever noun you want to ask, talk, or think about.

```jp
{{ryokou||旅[りょ]行[こう]}}について{{hanasu-v|stem|話[はな]し}}ましょう。
```

*Let's talk about the trip.*

That's the whole shape of it: **noun + について** = "about / regarding [noun]." No verb changes, no conjugation to learn — you just attach it and go. English "about" is a slippery little word that can mark a topic, an approximate amount, or a direction ("walking about the park"); について only ever does the first job, which actually makes it easier to use once you stop reaching for a one-to-one English match.

## How it works

について started life as に + ついて, from a verb that means something like "to touch on" or "to be attached to" — you don't need to memorize that, but it's why the pattern feels like it's "landing on" a topic rather than describing it from a distance. All you need in practice is the shape: it bolts straight onto a noun, with nothing in between — no の, no な, nothing.

```jp
{{ryokou||旅[りょ]行[こう]}} → {{ryokou||旅[りょ]行[こう]}}について
```

*trip → about the trip*

Once it's attached, the whole について phrase works like an adverbial add-on: it tells a verb like {{hanasu-v||話[はな]す}} (to speak), {{kangaeru||考[かんが]える}} (to think), {{shiru||知[し]る}} (to know), or 質[しつ]問[もん]{{suru||する}} (to ask a question) what it's aimed at.

```jp
{{kare||彼[かれ]}}は{{sono||その}}{{eiga||映[えい]画[が]}}について{{nani||何[なに]}}も{{shiru|nai|知[し]らない}}。
```

*He doesn't know anything about that movie.*

```jp
{{sensei||先[せん]生[せい]}}に{{nihon||日本[にほん]}}の歴[れき]史[し]について質[しつ]問[もん]{{suru|ta|した}}。
```

*I asked the teacher a question about Japanese history.*

Notice that に is still doing its normal job in that second sentence, marking who got asked — について doesn't replace any particle you already know. It just adds "on the subject of X" on top of whatever the sentence is already doing. You'll also want について for asking about a topic in the first place, with a question word standing in for the noun.

```jp
{{nani||何[なに]}}について{{hanasu-v|te|話[はな]して}}{{iru-exist|masu|います}}か。
```

*What are you talking about?*

That's the natural question that a について answer replies to — someone asks {{nani||何[なに]}}について, and you answer with {{ryokou||旅[りょ]行[こう]}}について, {{eiga||映[えい]画[が]}}について, whatever fits.

There's also a more formal cousin: につき. It means exactly the same thing, "regarding," but it belongs to written notices, memos, and business Japanese rather than conversation.

```jp
宿[しゅく]題[だい]の問[もん]題[だい]につき、{{setsumei||説[せつ]明[めい]}}します。
```

*Regarding the homework problem, I'll explain it.*

You'll meet につき on posted signs and formal documents far more often than in speech — keep について for talking to people, and recognize につき when you're reading something official.

One more shape worth knowing: について can also sit in front of の and modify a noun, turning "about X" into "the [thing] about X." Compare a plain topic sentence with a noun phrase built the same way.

```jp
{{ryokou||旅[りょ]行[こう]}}についての{{hanashi||話[はなし]}}は{{omoshiroi|ta|面白[おもしろ]かった}}。
```

*The story about the trip was interesting.*

Here について isn't attached to a verb at all — it's attached to {{hanashi||話[はなし]}} (story) through の, describing what kind of story it was. The underlying idea never changes; only the job the whole phrase is doing in the sentence does.

## Rules and exceptions

について is not a topic marker the way は is. は tells the whole sentence "here's what we're discussing from now on"; について tells one specific verb "here's what you're aimed at." Because they're doing different jobs, you can actually stack them — について + は gives you an "as for the topic of X..." feel, useful when you're pivoting to a new subject partway through a conversation.

```jp
{{sono||その}}問[もん]題[だい]については{{ashita||明日[あした]}}{{kangaeru|masu|考[かんが]えます}}。
```

*As for that problem, I'll think about it tomorrow.*

> について needs a plain noun sitting in front of it — never a verb directly. Something like `会うについて` (trying to say "about meeting") doesn't work; you'd first need to turn the verb into a noun-shaped phrase, which is further down the road. For now, keep について glued to things, not actions.

The other trap is picking a verb that can't take a "subject matter" in the first place. について pairs naturally with verbs of talking, thinking, knowing, asking, and writing — the kind of verb that can be "about" something. It doesn't pair with verbs of motion or plain existence; "about the store" doesn't combine with {{iku-v||行[い]く}} or {{aru||ある}} the way it combines with {{hanasu-v||話[はな]す}} or {{kangaeru||考[かんが]える}}. If the verb can't logically have a topic, について has nothing to attach its meaning to, and native speakers will just find the sentence confusing rather than politely correcting the grammar.

It's also worth being honest that について can feel a little formal or writerly even in its plain form — in very casual chatting, people sometimes just drop the topic in with は or leave it implied by context rather than reaching for について at all. That's not a rule you need to apply yourself yet; just don't be surprised if a native speaker's casual speech has fewer について phrases than a textbook dialogue does.

Learners often reach for について when they actually mean "because," and the two have nothing to do with each other. から marks a reason — the thing that caused something — while について marks a topic — the thing being discussed. "I'm worried about the exam" sounds like it should use について, but if what you mean is "because of the exam" (the exam is the cause of the worry), that's から territory, not について. Ask yourself whether the noun is the subject matter of a conversation or the reason something happened; that question sorts the two every time.

## Contrast: について vs を

You've known を since your first lessons, and with a verb like {{hanasu-v||話[はな]す}} it sits in exactly the slot について wants — right after the noun, nothing in between. But を makes the noun the thing the verb acts on; について makes it the topic the verb is about. Swap one for the other and the sentence's meaning changes, not just its tone.

```jp
{{kanojo||彼[かの]女[じょ]}}は{{nihongo||日本[にほん]語[ご]}}を{{hanasu-v|ta|話[はな]した}}。
```

*She spoke Japanese.*

```jp
{{kanojo||彼[かの]女[じょ]}}は{{nihongo||日本[にほん]語[ご]}}について{{hanasu-v|ta|話[はな]した}}。
```

*She talked about Japanese.*

Same words, same slot in the sentence, and the only difference — を versus について — decides whether Japanese was the language coming out of her mouth, or the subject she was discussing. This pair trips people up for a while because both patterns look so similar on the page; the only fix is slowing down and asking "is this noun the thing itself, or the topic?"

Worth remembering too: と、から and 場[ば]合[あい] all attach to very different structures — plain-form clauses, not bare nouns — so について doesn't compete with them the way it competes with を. を is the one particle close enough in shape to actually cause mix-ups, which is exactly why it's worth this much attention. If you can ask yourself "is this noun the thing itself, or is it what's being discussed?" before you pick a particle, the two stop colliding.

Whenever you catch yourself reaching for "about" in Japanese, check first whether you're pointing at a topic mid-sentence (について) or naming the thing itself (を) — they'll keep bumping into each other until that split becomes automatic. Once that split feels settled, について itself will start showing up everywhere: in questions, in answers, in the small talk that opens almost any conversation, because "what's this about" is one of the most useful questions there is.

Down the line you'll meet によると, which sounds related but marks something else entirely: not what you're discussing, but whose word you're taking it on.
caution_notes: について needs a plain noun in front of it — it can't attach directly to a verb.
につき is the formal, written-notice version of について; use について when you're speaking.
について only pairs with verbs that can take a subject matter, like 話す or 考える — not verbs of motion or existence like 行く or ある.
日本語を話す and 日本語について話す mean different things — with を the noun is the thing you speak, with について it is the topic — so swapping one for the other changes what the sentence means.

items.explanation_markdown:
You're deciding whether to bring an umbrella tomorrow, and you haven't looked at the sky yourself — you're going by what the newspaper said this morning. That's the whole job によると does: it hangs a claim off a source, so nobody mistakes the information for your own opinion or guess.

```jp
{{shinbun||新[しん]聞[ぶん]}}によると、{{ashita||明日[あした]}}は{{ame-v||雨[あめ]}}です。
```
*According to the newspaper, tomorrow it will rain.*

You didn't decide it would rain. The newspaper did. によると is the little tag that keeps that distinction visible every time you repeat something you heard, read, or were told, instead of quietly presenting it as your own conclusion.

This matters more in Japanese conversation than English speakers expect. Stating something flatly, with no source attached, can sound like you're claiming personal authority over it — "it will rain tomorrow," full stop, as if you checked yourself. によると lets you soften that into "here's what I was told," which is both more honest and, often, more polite.

It also protects you. If the newspaper turns out to be wrong, "the newspaper said so" is a very different claim from "I said so." Attaching a source up front means you're never stuck defending information you never generated in the first place — you were just the messenger, and によると makes sure everyone knows it.

## How it works

によると attaches straight onto a noun — the person, place, or medium the information came from. No の, no な, nothing wedged in between; it just glues on directly, the way a label sticks to a jar.

You already know と for a natural, automatic result: if X happens, Y follows as a matter of course. によると is built from that same と. により is a slightly formal way of saying "based on / by way of," and stacking と onto it gives you "if you go by [source], then [what follows] comes out like this." Read that way, the literal shape of the phrase and its English meaning line up almost exactly — you're not memorizing an arbitrary chunk, you're recognizing a pattern you already know wearing a more formal outfit.

```jp
{{rajio||ラジオ}}によると、{{kyou||今日[きょう]}}は{{yuki||雪[ゆき]}}です。
```
*According to the radio, today it's snowing.*

The source doesn't have to be a single word. Any noun phrase can sit in front of によると, as long as it still names where the information came from rather than describing what happened.

```jp
{{tomodachi||友[とも]達[だち]}}の{{hanashi||話[はなし]}}によると、{{tesuto||テスト}}は{{raishuu||来[らい]週[しゅう]}}です。
```
*According to what my friend said, the test is next week.*

{{tomodachi||友[とも]達[だち]}}の{{hanashi||話[はなし]}} — "my friend's talk" — is one noun phrase, so によると attaches to the whole thing exactly the same way it attaches to {{shinbun||新[しん]聞[ぶん]}} or {{rajio||ラジオ}}. Swap in {{sensei||先[せん]生[せい]}}の{{hanashi||話[はなし]}} or {{isha||医[い]者[しゃ]}}の{{hanashi||話[はなし]}} and nothing else about the sentence changes. A bare person also works just as well as a media source: a teacher, a doctor, anyone whose word you're relaying rather than your own.

```jp
{{sensei||先[せん]生[せい]}}によると、宿[しゅく]題[だい]は{{ashita||明日[あした]}}までです。
```
*According to the teacher, the homework is due tomorrow.*

```jp
{{isha||医[い]者[しゃ]}}によると、{{byouki||病[びょう]気[き]}}は{{sugu||すぐ}}{{naoru|masu|治[なお]ります}}。
```
*According to the doctor, the illness will heal soon.*

Notice that what follows によると is always a plain, complete statement — {{ashita||明日[あした]}}は{{ame-v||雨[あめ]}}です, {{byouki||病[びょう]気[き]}}は{{sugu||すぐ}}{{naoru|masu|治[なお]ります}}. によると doesn't reach into that statement and change its tense or its politeness level; it just frames where the statement came from. You can put a past-tense claim, a present-tense claim, or a plain guess after it, and the source phrase in front never has to match that tense. {{isha||医[い]者[しゃ]}}によると is present tense, but the doctor could just as easily have been describing something that already happened — the tense of the source and the tense of the claim are independent of each other.

That independence is also why によると sits so comfortably at the very front of a sentence. It's setting up context — where this information is from — before you get to the actual news, the same way "according to the newspaper" leads an English sentence rather than trailing at the end.

## Rules and exceptions

によると only takes a noun. It can't hang off a full sentence the way から can — you can't say something like `雨が降るによると` and expect it to mean "according to the fact that it's raining." If the source you want to name is an event or a whole idea rather than a person, place, or piece of media, によると usually isn't the tool for the job; you'd need to turn that idea into a noun phrase first, the way {{tomodachi||友[とも]達[だち]}}の{{hanashi||話[はなし]}} turns "my friend talked" into something によると can attach to.

> Because によると always marks somebody else's information, `私によると` — literally "according to me" — sounds strange when it's meant as "in my opinion." The whole phrase assumes the claim is being relayed from an outside source, not generated on the spot by the speaker. For your own view, you'd reach for a completely different pattern, not によると.

によると also has a near-twin, によれば — same meaning, same attachment rule, fully interchangeable in most sentences. によれば leans a little more formal and shows up more often in writing, announcements, and news broadcasts than in casual chat, but nobody will blink if you use either one in either setting. Some learners assume the two must split some subtle difference in meaning, the way many near-synonym pairs do — here, that's mostly not the case. Pick whichever sounds smoother to your ear once you've been exposed to enough real sentences.

```jp
{{tomodachi||友[とも]達[だち]}}によれば、{{kare||彼[かれ]}}は{{genki||元[げん]気[き]}}です。
```
*According to my friend, he's doing well.*

That's the same structure as every other example so far — noun, then によれば, then the plain statement being relayed — just with the more formal-sounding half of the pair. Try reading it back with によると instead; nothing about the meaning shifts, only the register does, and only slightly.

## Contrast

から states your own reason for doing something; it's your logic, your conclusion. によると states someone else's information; you're not vouching for it, just passing it along. Swap one for the other and the sentence stops meaning what you intended, because they answer different questions — "why are you doing this?" versus "where did this claim come from?"

```jp
{{tenki||天[てん]気[き]}}が{{warui||悪[わる]い}}から、{{kasa||傘[かさ]}}を{{motsu|te|持[も]って}}{{iku-v|masu|行[い]きます}}。
```
*Because the weather is bad, I'm bringing an umbrella.*

{{tenki||天[てん]気[き]}}が{{warui||悪[わる]い}}から is something you concluded yourself, probably from looking outside or checking the sky. {{shinbun||新[しん]聞[ぶん]}}によると is a fact somebody else supplied. If you tried to say {{tenki||天[てん]気[き]}}が{{warui||悪[わる]い}}によると, it wouldn't parse as "because the weather is bad" — によると needs a noun sitting directly in front of it, not a whole clause, and から is doing a fundamentally different job in the first place: giving a reason, not naming a source.

について marks what's being talked about; によると marks where the talk came from. The two answer different questions and can even sit in the same conversation without stepping on each other.

```jp
{{tenki||天[てん]気[き]}}について{{hanasu-v|masu|話[はな]しました}}。
```
*I talked about the weather.*

{{tenki||天[てん]気[き]}}について{{hanasu-v||話[はな]す}} just names the topic — weather — and says nothing about who told you what. That's the exact gap によると fills. Imagine reporting both pieces at once: what the conversation was about, and where the claim inside it came from. について handles the first job, によると the second, and neither one can do the other's work.

Put all of that together and by the time you're a few weeks past this lesson, the choice between によると, から, and について should feel less like a grammar rule and more like a reflex: ask yourself whether you're naming a source, giving your own reason, or flagging a topic, and the right particle chain more or less picks itself.

によると is a small, specific job: crediting a source before you hand over a claim. It's not about being formal for its own sake — it's about being accurate regarding whose information you're actually repeating. Hold onto that instinct; it comes back at N3, once we reach 限[かぎ]り, another phrase built around "as far as," except that one marks the edge of what you personally know rather than where you heard it.
caution_notes: によると always attaches directly to a noun naming the source — never to a verb or full clause.
によると relays someone else's information; for your own opinion or reasoning, use a different pattern, not 私によると.
によれば is interchangeable with によると but leans a bit more formal and written.
Don't confuse によると (where the information came from) with について (what is being discussed).

items.explanation_markdown:
You're standing on the platform, bag in one hand, coffee in the other, when the overhead speaker crackles on: {{taifuu||台[たい]風[ふう]}}のため、{{densha||電[でん]車[しゃ]}}が{{okureru|te|遅[おく]れて}}{{iru-exist|masu|います}}。 You don't need much Japanese to catch the shape of it — a typhoon, then のため, then a delay. That のため is doing all the connective work in the sentence: it states the typhoon as the reason for the delay, and it does it in the flat, matter-of-fact voice you'd expect from a station announcement, not from a friend texting you an excuse for being late. Nobody on that platform is personally responsible for the storm, and the sentence is built to make that clear — the typhoon is simply named as the fact behind what happened.

```jp
{{taifuu||台[たい]風[ふう]}}のため、{{densha||電[でん]車[しゃ]}}が{{okureru|te|遅[おく]れて}}{{iru-exist|masu|います}}。
```

*Because of the typhoon, the trains are running late.*

That's ため in its cause sense — a formal "because of" or "due to" that turns up constantly in announcements, notices, and news, anywhere someone wants to state a reason as a plain fact rather than as their own personal excuse. It sounds formal in translation, but it isn't rare or bookish in daily life: it's the wording on the handwritten sign taped to a closed shop's door, the line in a note home from your child's school, or the sentence a doctor writes on a note excusing you from work. Anywhere someone needs to state a reason without arguing for it, ため is usually close by.

## How ため works

ため actually started life as an ordinary noun, something close to "sake" or "result" — you can almost feel the old sense of "for the sake of X" sitting underneath every sentence that uses it this way. Whatever's doing the causing sits right in front of it, and whatever happened as a result follows after the comma. The part that takes getting used to is what "right in front of it" looks like, because the shape changes depending on what kind of word is doing the causing — a noun needs different handling than an adjective, and an adjective needs different handling than a verb.

**Noun + の + ため.** This is exactly the pattern you just saw with {{taifuu||台[たい]風[ふう]}}のため. It's the same の that glues two nouns into one phrase, the way {{nihon||日本[にほん]}}の{{kuruma||車[くるま]}} means "the car of Japan" — {{taifuu||台[たい]風[ふう]}} and ため get joined the same way, with {{taifuu||台[たい]風[ふう]}} filling the role that {{nihon||日本[にほん]}} fills in that other phrase.

```jp
{{kaze-cold||風邪[かぜ]}}のため、{{gakkou-v||学[がっ]校[こう]}}を{{yasumu|masu|休[やす]みました}}。
```

*I took the day off school because of a cold.*

**な-adjective + な + ため.** An adjective like {{shizuka||静[しず]か}} (quiet) can't sit directly against ため any more than a noun can — it needs the same な bridge it would use in front of any noun it's describing, the way you'd say {{shizuka||静[しず]か}}な{{heya||部屋[へや]}} for "a quiet room."

```jp
{{kono||この}}公[こう]園[えん]は{{shizuka||静[しず]か}}なため、{{yoku||よく}}{{sanpo-suru|masu|散[さん]歩[ぽ]します}}。
```

*Because this park is quiet, I often take walks here.*

**い-adjective, plain form, no bridge needed.** い-adjectives already end in something that can attach straight onto whatever comes next, so {{isogashii||忙[いそが]しい}} (busy) just walks right up to ため with nothing in between — no な, no の, nothing.

```jp
{{konshuu||今[こん]週[しゅう]}}は{{isogashii||忙[いそが]しい}}ため、{{ryokou||旅[りょ]行[こう]}}に{{ikeru|masu|行[い]けません}}。
```

*Because this week is busy, I can't go on the trip.*

**Verb, plain form.** Same idea again: no だ, no です, just the plain form of the verb sitting directly in front of ため.

```jp
{{densha||電[でん]車[しゃ]}}が{{okureru|ta|遅[おく]れた}}ため、{{kaigi||会[かい]議[ぎ]}}に{{okureru|masu|遅[おく]れました}}。
```

*Because the train was late, I was late for the meeting.*

Notice that the verb there is in the past tense — {{okureru|ta|遅[おく]れた}}, not {{okureru||遅[おく]れる}}. That's not an accident, and it's exactly what the next section is about.

## Rules and exceptions

ため has a second life you'll bump into constantly, and it's worth naming early so it doesn't trip you up later: when it follows a verb of deliberate action in the plain non-past form, it means "in order to" instead of "because of." {{benkyou-suru||勉[べん]強[きょう]する}}ため means "in order to study" — something you're choosing to do on purpose, not a reason that's been forced on you from outside. The cause meaning you're learning here shows up instead with adjectives, nouns, and verbs describing a state, a result, or something nobody chose — which is exactly why {{okureru|ta|遅[おく]れた}}, already finished and nobody's fault, reads naturally as a cause, while {{benkyou-suru||勉[べん]強[きょう]する}}, something you're actively deciding to do, reads as a purpose instead. Once you notice this split, it stops being confusing and starts being useful: the tense and the verb type are quietly telling you which meaning you're looking at before you've even reached ため itself.

> If you're ever unsure which meaning you're looking at, ask whether the person could have chosen not to do it. A typhoon, a cold, a delayed train — nobody picks those. Studying, working — those are choices, and ため after a plain dictionary-form verb like that almost always means "in order to."

There's a second trap worth naming, and it's a purely mechanical one. Unlike から, which sits happily right after だ ({{gakusei||学[がく]生[せい]}}{{dakara||だから}}, {{shizuka||静[しず]か}}{{dakara||だから}}), ため never tolerates だ in front of it, no matter how natural that might feel by analogy. This one catches people who've already gotten comfortable with から, because the instinct is to reach for だ out of habit before the noun or な-adjective settles in.

> A noun takes の and an な-adjective takes な in front of ため — never だ. `病気だため` and `静かだため` are both wrong; it has to be {{byouki||病[びょう]気[き]}}のため and {{shizuka||静[しず]か}}なため.

One last note, this time on spelling rather than meaning: ため and ために mean exactly the same thing here and attach exactly the same way to everything above. ために is just the fuller of the two forms, and either one shows up in writing without any real shift in meaning or formality — pick whichever one sounds better to your own ear in the moment.

```jp
{{tenki||天[てん]気[き]}}が{{warui||悪[わる]い}}ために、洗[せん]濯[たく]が{{dekiru|masu|できません}}。
```

*Because the weather is bad, I can't do the laundry.*

## Contrast with から

You already have から for stating a reason, and から carries your own voice in it — it's the shape of an explanation you're personally standing behind, whether that's an excuse to a friend or a reason you're offering for something you did. ため does the same basic job on paper, but drops your voice out of the sentence entirely and just states the fact instead.

```jp
{{byouki||病[びょう]気[き]}}{{dakara||だから}}、{{kaisha||会[かい]社[しゃ]}}を{{yasumu|masu|休[やす]みます}}。
```

*Because I'm sick, I'm taking the day off work.*

```jp
{{byouki||病[びょう]気[き]}}のため、{{kaisha||会[かい]社[しゃ]}}を{{yasumu|masu|休[やす]みます}}。
```

*Owing to illness, I will be absent from work.*

Same illness, same absence, but a different register. The first line sounds like a text you'd send a friend — casual, personal, your own reasoning in your own words. The second sounds like the line inside the email you'd actually send your boss, or the notice pinned to a break-room board: the same facts, dressed in ため's stiffer, more distant voice. Reach for から when you're explaining yourself; reach for ため when you're just reporting the situation as a fact and letting the reader draw their own conclusions.

This is also where the noun-attachment rule from the last section earns its keep: から sits after だ ({{byouki||病[びょう]気[き]}}{{dakara||だから}}), while ため replaces that だ with の ({{byouki||病[びょう]気[き]}}のため). Once that swap is automatic, telling the two patterns apart in the wild gets a lot faster — you'll catch yourself recognizing the register a sentence is written in before you've even finished reading the reason itself.

It's worth being honest that the line between the two isn't always crisp. Spoken Japanese borrows ため for effect sometimes, and formal writing occasionally leans on から when the writer wants to sound a little more direct. Treat から versus ため as a strong tendency you can lean on, not an unbreakable law — the two patterns share the same job, and real speech shuffles the boundary around more than any textbook rule likes to admit.

So ため takes whatever's sitting in front of it — noun, な-adjective, い-adjective, or plain verb — bridges the gap with の or な wherever one's needed, and hands you a stated cause with your own voice left out of it, exactly where から would feel too casual. Hold onto that sense of something sitting outside anyone's control: it comes back at N3, when 限[かぎ]り starts marking just how far a fact like that holds true.
caution_notes: Nouns and な-adjectives never take だ before ため — it has to be 病気のため and 静かなため, never 病気だため or 静かだため.

When ため follows a plain non-past verb describing something someone chose to do, like 勉強するため, it usually means 'in order to' rather than 'because of' — the cause reading shows up with adjectives, nouns, and verbs describing states or already-finished events.
ため is a formal, written-feeling connector; in casual conversation about your own personal reasons, から still sounds far more natural.

items.explanation_markdown:
Your study partner didn't show up yesterday. No text, no warning, just an empty seat where they usually sit. Today they slide in next to you looking a little sheepish, and before "hey" is even out of your mouth you're already asking:

```jp
{{kinou||昨日[きのう]}}、{{dou||どう}}{{suru|ta|した}}んですか。
```

*What happened yesterday?*

Notice this isn't a cold, out-of-nowhere question — the empty seat already told you something was off, and your question is built to lean on that. んですか is the polite question form of the pattern you're learning today: んだ in its plain, unpolished form, のです when it's dressed up further. Both spellings do the same job — they frame whatever comes before them as *the explanation*, not just a fact floating in space. Ask a bare {{dou||どう}}{{suru|masu|しました}}か instead and you sound like you're asking a stranger for directions, no shared context assumed.

English doesn't really force you to choose here — "I was sick" works whether you're announcing it cold or answering a direct question. Japanese does force the choice, because a plain です/だ sentence reads as a freestanding fact, dropped into the room with no strings attached. んです exists specifically to tie a sentence back to something already sitting between you and the listener — a question, a weird situation, an obvious gap that needs filling. It isn't extra politeness and it isn't decoration; it's a signal that says "this is the reason for what we were just talking about."

Your friend answers:

```jp
{{byouki||病[びょう]気[き]}}だったんです。
```

*I was sick.*

That んです at the end isn't decoration. It's doing one specific job: framing {{byouki||病[びょう]気[き]}}だった (I was sick) as the answer to the question hanging in the air, not as a random fact your friend decided to volunteer. Drop it — a plain {{byouki||病[びょう]気[き]}}でした — and the sentence stops sounding like an answer and starts sounding like small talk about the weather.

## How it works

The mechanics are almost insultingly simple once you see them: take a sentence in its plain form — the form you'd use talking to yourself, or scribbling in a diary, not the polite form you'd use with your teacher — and tack んです (or the fuller のです) onto the end. Verbs are the simplest case of all: dictionary form and all, nothing shifts, nothing gets dropped.

```jp
{{tomodachi||友[とも]達[だち]}}が{{kuru-v||来[く]る}}んです。
```

*A friend is coming over.*

That's what you'd say if someone found you scrubbing the kitchen floor at nine at night and wanted to know why. {{kuru-v||来[く]る}} never bends to fit んです — んです just rides on top of whatever the plain form of the verb already was, past, present, or negative alike.

い-adjectives work exactly the same way.

```jp
{{isogashii||忙[いそが]しい}}んです。
```

*I'm busy.*

{{isogashii||忙[いそが]しい}} just sits there exactly as it always does, and んです rides on top of it. Compare that to the noun and な-adjective case, which is the one spot in this whole pattern that actually trips people up, because their plain form doesn't naturally end in something んです can attach to.

```jp
{{genki||元[げん]気[き]}} → {{genki||元[げん]気[き]}}なんです
```

*healthy/fine → It's that I'm doing fine*

{{genki||元[げん]気[き]}} on its own isn't a full sentence — you'd normally need だ or です to finish it off, and it's that だ that vanishes and gets replaced with な the moment んです shows up. Say `元気んです` and it just sounds broken, like a word with a piece missing, because there's no plain form ending in ん for んです to land on. You'll meet this same な wedge again outside of んです entirely, wherever a plain-form pattern attaches to a noun or な-adjective — this is just the first time it's forcing you to notice it.

```jp
{{kyou||今日[きょう]}}は{{genki||元[げん]気[き]}}なんです。
```

*I'm doing fine today.*

Picture someone checking in on you after yesterday, worried you might still be feeling rough, and this is your reply. {{genki||元[げん]気[き]}} alone would read as a flat status update; {{genki||元[げん]気[き]}}なんです answers the actual worry sitting behind their question.

## Rules and exceptions

Past tense skips the な problem entirely, because だった (the plain past of だ) already ends in a shape んです can attach to directly — exactly what you saw with {{byouki||病[びょう]気[き]}}だったんです a moment ago. The な wedge only shows up in the plain present affirmative, the one tense where だ itself would otherwise disappear without a trace.

> Writing `学生んです` for "I'm a student" is one of the most common slips at this stage. The correct form is {{gakusei||学[がく]生[せい]}}なんです — the な isn't optional decoration, it's standing in for the だ that would be there if んです weren't attaching to it.

んです also isn't something you sprinkle onto every sentence you happen to say. Announcing something like {{kyou||今日[きょう]}}は{{suiyoubi||水[すい]曜[よう]日[び]}}なんです out of absolutely nowhere, with nobody asking and nothing unusual going on, comes across as if you're bracing the listener for bad news that never shows up. Save it for the moments where something genuinely needs explaining, or where somebody just asked.

> Don't stack it on top of です the way you might guess from the spelling. です already is the polite copula doing its own job — んです replaces the plain だ underneath it, it doesn't sit next to it. `だんです` isn't a form anyone uses.

The question version carries its own particular flavor, too. んですか reads as "something's going on here — tell me about it," which is exactly why it fits your friend showing up sheepish after a missed day, but would feel oddly probing coming from someone who has no reason to suspect anything's up in the first place.

## Casual speech

Among friends, んです contracts down to んだ — same job, same framing, just with the politeness layer stripped off.

```jp
{{isogashii||忙[いそが]しい}}んです → {{isogashii||忙[いそが]しい}}んだ
```

*I'm busy (polite) → I'm busy (casual, to a friend)*

```jp
{{kyou||今日[きょう]}}は{{isogashii||忙[いそが]しい}}んだ。
```

*I'm busy today.*

That's the line you'd actually text a friend who's asking why you're bailing on plans — んです there would sound stiff, almost like you're reading from a script. Formal writing swings the opposite direction: instead of contracting anything, it usually keeps the fuller のです, which reads as more deliberate and considered than everyday んです ever does.

```jp
{{kore||これ}}は{{taihen||大[たい]変[へん]}}な問[もん]題[だい]なのです。
```

*This is a serious problem.*

You'll run into なのです like this in notices, articles, anything meant to sound like it was composed rather than said out loud on the spot. Same mechanics as everything above — just a more formal register wrapped around them.

## Contrast

You've already met ため for stating a formal cause — dry, explicit, "due to X." んです is doing something different: it isn't naming a cause so much as framing an entire fact as the explanation the listener needed. Put near-identical sentences side by side and the difference in tone becomes obvious.

```jp
{{byouki||病[びょう]気[き]}}のため、{{yasumu|masu|休[やす]みました}}。
```

*Due to illness, I took the day off.*

That's the sentence you'd write on a form or say to your boss — factual, a touch formal, cause stated up front and then dropped. Compare it to {{byouki||病[びょう]気[き]}}だったんです from the hook: same illness, same missed day, but one reads like a report and the other reads like you're actually talking to a friend who wants to know what happened to you.

It helps to keep ため next to んです whenever a sentence feels like it needs *something* extra at the end — ため tells you the cause is the point, and んです tells you the whole fact is standing in as the answer to something already in the air. Mixing them up doesn't produce broken Japanese so much as Japanese that answers the wrong question.

## Closing

んです turns a plain statement into the answer to a question that didn't necessarily need to be spoken aloud — that's the entire trick, once the な stops being scary. It's also one of those pieces of grammar that native speakers use constantly without ever thinking about it, which is exactly why it's worth this much attention now: you're building an instinct they never had to build consciously. Hold onto that framing instinct; you'll want it again soon, when でしょう starts letting you soften a guess the same way んです frames a fact.
caution_notes: な-adjectives and nouns need な inserted before んです or んだ in the plain present — skipping it is one of the most common early mistakes.
んです and its casual form んだ can sound dramatic or accusatory when used for a neutral fact nobody asked about, so save them for moments that actually need explaining.
んです never sits alongside です as an addition — it replaces the plain だ underneath the polite copula, it doesn't stack on top of it.
んですか implies something noticeable is going on, so using it as a cold opening question to someone with no context can come across as oddly probing.
items.mnemonic_text: Dai, the giant baby, wails an earthquake across town. Asked why, he points at the bump on his forehead, "<reading>No duh</reading>", because <grammar>the thing is</grammar>, he hit his head. {{atama||頭}}が{{itai||痛い}}<reading>んだ</reading>。

items.explanation_markdown:
You pick up a pen at the convenience store counter to sign something, and the ink barely shows — every stroke drags like the paper doesn't want it. In Japanese you don't complain that you're bad at writing; you say something about the pen itself.

```jp
{{kono||この}}{{pen||ペン}}は{{kaku|stem|書[か]き}}にくいです。
```
*This pen is hard to write with.*

That にくい stuck onto the stem of {{kaku||書[か]く}} ({{kaku|stem|書[か]き}}) turns "write" into a built-in review of the pen — what it's like to use, not how one specific attempt went. やすい does the opposite job: it says a thing is easy to deal with, no matter who's holding it.

## How it works

Both にくい and やすい attach to the same spot on a verb: the stem, the part left over when you drop ます from the polite form ({{kaku|masu|書[か]きます}} → {{kaku|stem|書[か]き}}). Drop the tense information entirely and you're left with the bare stem, then the pattern glues straight onto it.

```jp
{{kaku||書[か]く}} → {{kaku|stem|書[か]き}}にくい
```

There's no extra word needed to make that grammatical — にくい and やすい are already complete い-adjectives the instant they're built, with their own です, their own past tense, their own negative. Swap the ending and the meaning flips:

```jp
{{kono||この}}{{hon||本[ほん]}}は{{yomu|stem|読[よ]み}}やすいです。
```
*This book is easy to read.*

Think of it this way: the verb hands over its stem and steps aside, and from that point the adjective is in charge of describing the object, not the action. Because the whole word is now an い-adjective, it conjugates exactly like {{ookii||大[おお]きい}} or {{muzukashii||難[むずか]しい}} does — nothing about the underlying verb changes anymore. Put it in the past and only the にくい/やすい part moves:

```jp
{{kaku|stem|書[か]き}}にくかったです。
```
*It was hard to write with.*

## Rules and exceptions

The pattern works on almost any verb whose stem you can pull out, which covers everything from {{hanasu-v||話[はな]す}} to {{aruku||歩[ある]く}}, so you'll see it attached to a wide range of everyday actions:

```jp
{{kono||この}}{{kutsu||靴[くつ]}}は{{aruku|stem|歩[ある]き}}やすいです。
```
*These shoes are easy to walk in.*

The one mix-up that catches people early: にくい/やすい is not doing the same job as the potential form ({{yomeru||読[よ]める}}, {{hanaseru||話[はな]せる}}, {{dekiru||できる}} — the word that says someone *can* do something). The potential form asks "am I capable of doing this?" — a fact about the person. にくい/やすい asks "what is this thing like to deal with?" — a fact about the object, independent of who's doing it. {{yomu|stem|読[よ]み}}にくい{{hon||本[ほん]}} is a badly laid-out book that would frustrate anyone; {{yomeru|nai|読[よ]めない}}{{hon||本[ほん]}} is a book one particular person can't read, maybe because it's in a language they don't know.

> Once にくい/やすい is attached, treat the whole word as one adjective from then on. The negative is `書きにくくない`, built off にくい itself — never something like `書きませんにくい`, which tries to negate the verb underneath and just breaks.

One phrase built from this pattern is worth flagging on its own, because it shows up everywhere outside grammar explanations too:

```jp
{{kare||彼[かれ]}}の{{hanashi||話[はなし]}}は{{wakaru|stem|分[わ]かり}}やすいです。
```
*His talk is easy to understand.*

{{wakaru|stem|分[わ]かり}}やすい has basically become its own compliment — "clear," "easy to follow" — said about teachers, directions, books, anything that communicates well.

## Contrast

You already know かもしれない for "might happen" — a guess about one specific event, made with whatever information you have right now. にくい/やすい is a different kind of statement: it isn't a guess about whether something will happen this time, it's a claim about what the thing is generally like.

```jp
{{kono||この}}{{sara||皿[さら]}}は{{kowareru|stem|壊[こわ]れ}}やすいです。
```
*This dish breaks easily.*

```jp
{{kono||この}}{{sara||皿[さら]}}は{{kowareru||壊[こわ]れる}}かもしれません。
```
*This dish might break.*

The first sentence is a review of the dish itself — thin, fragile, badly made, whatever the reason, it tends to break. The second is a one-off worry: maybe today, maybe because someone's about to drop it, with no claim about the dish's overall build. Mix the two up and you'll either tell someone a solid dish is fragile, or make a fragile one sound like it's only at risk this once.

にくい/やすい shares its attachment point with another word you'll meet soon — すぎる, which turns {{taberu||食[た]べる}} into "ate too much." Same spot on the verb, same instinct: look at the stem, then decide what quality to bolt onto it.
caution_notes: にくい and やすい attach to the verb's stem (the ます-form minus ます), never to the dictionary form.
Once attached, the whole word behaves like a regular い-adjective, so negate and conjugate the ending itself, not the verb underneath.
Don't confuse にくい/やすい, an inherent tendency of the object, with the potential form, which describes a specific person's ability.
かもしれない marks uncertainty about one specific event, while にくい/やすい describes a general, ongoing tendency of the thing itself.

items.explanation_markdown:
You and a friend are grading each other's practice problems, one at a time. Problem two looks brutal on its own, but set next to problem one, it barely counts as hard. You don't want to say "problem two is easy" — that's not quite true either. You want to measure it against problem one specifically, and say it falls short of that particular mark.

That specific kind of comparison — not just "less," but "less than *this* particular thing" — is what ほど is built for.

```jp
{{kore||これ}}は{{sore||それ}}ほど{{muzukashii|nai|難[むずか]しくない}}
```

*This one isn't as difficult as that one.*

ほど attaches right after your yardstick — {{sore||それ}}, "that one" — and the sentence needs a negative predicate ({{muzukashii|nai|難[むずか]しくない}}, not {{muzukashii||難[むずか]しい}}) to land as a comparison. Read it as: "measured against that, this one doesn't reach the same level of hard."

## How it works

The shape is always noun (or noun-equivalent) + ほど + a negative predicate, and it works for anything you can hold up as a reference point — a book, a movie, a person, an earlier attempt.

```jp
{{ano||あの}}{{eiga||映[えい]画[が]}}は{{kono||この}}{{hon||本[ほん]}}ほど{{omoshiroi|nai|面白[おもしろ]くない}}
```

*That movie isn't as interesting as this book.*

Word order carries the meaning here: the thing being judged comes first ({{ano||あの}}{{eiga||映[えい]画[が]}}), the yardstick sits right before ほど ({{kono||この}}{{hon||本[ほん]}}), and the negative predicate closes the sentence out. Swap the two nouns and you've reversed who's being judged against whom, so it's worth reading sentences like this slowly until the order feels automatic.

ほど doesn't need a noun at all, though. Attach it straight to a verb or adjective in plain form (the dictionary-style shape, with no polite endings) and it stops comparing two separate things and starts measuring how far one single thing went.

```jp
{{atama||頭[あたま]}}が{{itai|stem|痛[いた]く}}{{naruhodo||なるほど}}{{benkyou||勉[べん]強[きょう]}}した
```

*I studied until my head started to hurt.*

The clause in front of ほど — {{atama||頭[あたま]}}が{{itai|stem|痛[いた]く}}{{naru-become||なる}}, "my head starts to hurt" — isn't really the point of the sentence. It's a stand-in for "a lot," made vivid by naming something concrete that actually happened. The real point, {{benkyou||勉[べん]強[きょう]}}した, comes after. This is exactly the kind of specific, physical detail that makes a sentence like this stick in memory instead of sliding past.

```jp
{{koe||声[こえ]}}が{{deru-v|nai|出[で]ない}}ほど{{warau|ta|笑[わら]った}}
```

*I laughed until my voice gave out.*

Notice that the clause before ほど can be an adjective turning into a verb ({{itai|stem|痛[いた]く}}{{naru-become||なる}}, "gets painful") or a plain negative verb ({{deru-v|nai|出[で]ない}}, "doesn't come out") — ほど doesn't care what shape the extent-clause takes, only that it's plain form and it paints a specific picture.

There's a third shape, built by doubling a verb: the same verb once in its ば-form (the "if" shape — {{renshuu-suru||練[れん]習[しゅう]する}} becomes {{renshuu-suru|stem|練[れん]習[しゅう]すれ}}ば) and once more in plain form, with ほど closing it off. This is how Japanese says "the more X, the more Y" — the two halves climb together, step for step.

```jp
{{renshuu-suru|stem|練[れん]習[しゅう]すれ}}ば{{suru||する}}ほど{{jouzu||上手[じょうず]}}に{{naru-become||なる}}
```

*The more you practice, the better you get.*

```jp
{{hanasu-v|stem|話[はな]せ}}ば{{hanasu-v||話[はな]す}}ほど{{tanoshii|stem|楽[たの]しく}}{{naru-become||なる}}
```

*The more we talk, the more fun it gets.*

ほど itself never changes for politeness — only the predicate in front of or after it does. {{kore||これ}}は{{sore||それ}}ほど{{muzukashii|nai|難[むずか]しくない}}です stays polite by conjugating the ending, not by touching ほど at all.

## Rules and exceptions

> Drop the negative and the comparison disappears. {{kore||これ}}は{{sore||それ}}ほど{{muzukashii||難[むずか]しい}}, without ない, doesn't mean "not as hard" — it just states plain degree on its own, and it will sound unfinished to a native ear. The negative isn't optional decoration here; it's the mechanism that makes the comparison work at all.

The doubled ば〜ほど form only works when both halves are the same verb. {{renshuu-suru|stem|練[れん]習[しゅう]すれ}}ば{{renshuu-suru||練[れん]習[しゅう]する}}ほど is fine in full (and often shortened to {{renshuu-suru|stem|練[れん]習[しゅう]すれ}}ば{{suru||する}}ほど, dropping the repeated verb stem); swapping in a different verb for the second half breaks the pattern entirely — there's no mixing {{renshuu-suru|stem|練[れん]習[しゅう]すれ}}ば with a different verb before ほど.

## Contrast: ほど vs すぎる vs {{kanari||かなり}}

You've already met two other ways to talk about degree, and ほど earns its keep by doing something neither of them does. すぎる flags excess — something crossed a line, and that's usually framed as a problem.

```jp
{{isogashii|stem|忙[いそが]し}}すぎて{{koe||声[こえ]}}が{{deru-v|nai|出[で]ない}}
```

*I'm so busy I can't even speak.*

{{kanari||かなり}}, on the other hand, just states a flat, fairly high degree, with no reference point and no complaint attached.

```jp
{{kyou||今日[きょう]}}は{{kanari||かなり}}{{isogashii||忙[いそが]しい}}
```

*Today is fairly busy.*

ほど sits between the two: it measures against something concrete, without すぎる's built-in complaint or {{kanari||かなり}}'s flatness. {{atama||頭[あたま]}}が{{itai|stem|痛[いた]く}}{{naruhodo||なるほど}}{{benkyou||勉[べん]強[きょう]}}した isn't a gripe about studying too much — it's a vivid way of showing exactly how much, by naming what it actually felt like.

Three jobs, one word: "not as much as" with a negative, "to the point that" with a plain form, and "the more, the more" doubled with ば. Watch for くらい soon — it covers some of the same ground, with its own twist on how the comparison lands.
caution_notes: Dropping the negative predicate after ほど turns a comparison into a plain degree statement, not 'not as much as.'
Word order matters: the thing being judged comes before the yardstick, then ほど, then the negative predicate — swapping the nouns reverses who's being judged.
In the doubled ば〜ほど form, both halves must be the same verb; you can't swap in a different verb for the second half.
ほど itself doesn't conjugate for politeness — only the predicate attached to it does.
