items.explanation_markdown:
Picture texting a friend about Saturday's get-together: "Is everyone coming?" Almost everyone — one person can't make it. You want to say "everyone except Ken," and Japanese has a clean, single word for that job: 以[い]外[がい] (igai), meaning "except" or "other than." It attaches directly onto whichever noun you're pulling out of the group, so you never have to build a whole clause around it.

```jp
{{watashi||私[わたし]}}以[い]外[がい]は{{minna||みんな}}{{kuru-v|masu|来[き]ます}}。
```
*Everyone except me is coming.*

Notice what happened there: 以[い]外[がい] sits right after {{watashi||私[わたし]}} (me) — no verb, no connector, just a person and then the word that says "not counting this one." That's the entire shape of the pattern: **Noun + 以[い]外[がい]**.

## How it works

以[い]外[がい] always follows a noun — whatever you're carving out of a larger group. Once it's attached, everything else in the sentence is understood to apply to the rest of that group, not to the noun sitting in front of 以[い]外[がい].

If what you want to exclude is an action rather than a thing, you can't hand 以[い]外[がい] a bare verb — it needs a noun first, so you build one with こと (a little word that turns a whole verb phrase into a thing you can talk about):

```jp
{{oyogu||泳[およ]ぐ}} → {{oyogu||泳[およ]ぐ}}こと
```
*to swim → swimming (the thing itself)*

```jp
{{oyogu||泳[およ]ぐ}}こと以[い]外[がい]、{{supootsu||スポーツ}}が{{nigate||苦[にが]手[て]}}です。
```
*Other than swimming, I'm bad at sports.*

Two shapes show up constantly, and they're really just 以[い]外[がい] riding on a particle you already know:

- **以[い]外[がい]に** — leans toward "besides / in addition to." Common with a positive verb ("besides X, also Y") and just as common with a negative one ("nothing besides X").
- **以[い]外[がい]は** — leans toward "as for everything except X," setting X up as the one exception to whatever comes next.

```jp
{{ongaku||音[おん]楽[がく]}}以[い]外[がい]に{{shumi||趣[しゅ]味[み]}}が{{aru|masu|ありません}}。
```
*I don't have a hobby besides music.*

```jp
{{nihongo||日本[にほん]語[ご]}}以[い]外[がい]に{{eigo||英[えい]語[ご]}}も{{hanaseru|masu|話[はな]せます}}。
```
*Besides Japanese, I can also speak English.*

```jp
{{doyoubi||土[ど]曜[よう]日[び]}}以[い]外[がい]は{{mainichi||毎[まい]日[にち]}}{{benkyou||勉[べん]強[きょう]}}します。
```
*I study every day except Saturday.*

に and は aren't doing anything new here — they're the same particles you've used since week one. に leans toward "additionally," は leans toward "as for the rest of the group." Neither one changes what 以[い]外[がい] itself means; they just tint the sentence around it.

## Rules and exceptions

The one rule that trips people up: 以[い]外[がい] wants a noun immediately in front of it. In English, "except" can follow almost any kind of phrase, but Japanese draws a harder line. A bare plain-form verb can't feed straight into 以[い]外[がい].

> Don't write `泳ぐ以外` on its own to mean "other than swimming." A verb needs to be turned into a noun first — usually with こと — before 以[い]外[がい] can attach: {{oyogu||泳[およ]ぐ}}こと以[い]外[がい].

以[い]外[がい] pairs naturally with a negative predicate to mean "only this one." That's not really a separate rule — it's just what "not X except Y" collapses to once you say it out loud:

```jp
{{kare||彼[かれ]}}以[い]外[がい]は{{dare-mo||誰[だれ]も}}{{shiru|masu|知[し]りません}}。
```
*No one knows except him.*

Read literally, that's "as for other than him, nobody knows" — which lands as "only he knows." Once you notice that shape, 以[い]外[がい] plus a negative keeps showing up wherever the real meaning is "only."

> 以[い]外[がい] marks what's outside the group — it says nothing about how big the group itself is.

```jp
{{sakana||魚[さかな]}}以[い]外[がい]は{{suki||好[す]き}}です。
```
*I like everything except fish.*

That sentence tells you fish is out. It doesn't tell you whether "everything" means two dishes or twenty — 以[い]外[がい] draws the boundary, not the headcount.

以[い]外[がい] doesn't care about politeness level either. It sits comfortably in plain speech and in です・ます sentences without changing shape, so you don't need a separate casual version to learn — the word itself never bends. In a quick spoken answer, people will sometimes drop the は or に and let bare 以[い]外[がい] carry the whole thought as a fragment — someone asks what you don't eat, and {{sakana||魚[さかな]}}以[い]外[がい]。 is a complete answer on its own.

## Contrast

Everything else you've learned so far — {{sorede||それで}}も, {{soko||そこ}}で, {{sono||その}}ため, {{suru||する}}と — links two full sentences together. 以[い]外[がい] works differently: it's a small word riding directly on a noun, not a bridge between clauses. You can't swap it in for one of those connectors and expect the sentence to hold together; they're built for different jobs.

Where they do overlap is in mood, and {{sorede||それで}}も is the closest one to check yourself against. {{sorede||それで}}も says "even given that, X still happened" — it concedes something and pushes past it:

```jp
{{atama||頭[あたま]}}が{{itai|ta|痛[いた]かった}}。
{{sorede||それで}}も{{shigoto||仕[し]事[ごと]}}に{{iku-v|ta|行[い]った}}。
```
*I had a headache.*
*Even so, I went to work.*

以[い]外[がい] doesn't concede anything; it just draws a line around one item and says "not this one." If you ever reach for {{sorede||それで}}も to mean "except for this," that's the moment to reach for 以[い]外[がい] instead — {{sorede||それで}}も answers "what happened anyway?" while 以[い]外[がい] answers "what's left out?"

以[い]外[がい] also isn't the same word as {{hoka||他[ほか]}} (ほか), even though both get translated as "other." {{hoka||他[ほか]}} is a plain noun — "another one" — that can stand on its own and take its own particles, like a subject or an object. 以[い]外[がい] never stands alone; it only exists attached to the noun it's excluding.

This is worth holding onto beyond today: 以[い]外[がい] belongs to a small family of patterns that bolt straight onto a noun instead of linking two sentences. You'll meet another member of that family at N3 in 以[い]来[らい], which uses the same "Noun +" shape to mean "ever since."
caution_notes: 以外 needs a noun right in front of it — a bare plain-form verb has to become a noun with こと first, as in 泳ぐこと以外.
以外 only marks what's left out of the group; it says nothing about how large the rest of the group is.
以外 plus a negative predicate usually means 'only this one,' not a double exclusion, so read 彼以外は誰も知りません as 'only he knows.'

items.explanation_markdown:
It's late, you're at the desk with your textbook open, and your eyelids have that heavy pull that means you're one blink away from losing the fight. You're not asleep yet — you catch yourself right on the edge of it. Japanese has one small pattern built exactly for that edge, the instant before something happens: そうになる.

```jp
{{neru||寝[ね]る}} → {{neru|stem|寝[ね]}}そうになる
```

*to sleep → to be right on the edge of falling asleep*

## How it works

そうになる attaches to the stem of a verb — the same stem you already strip off before adding other endings. For an ichidan verb like {{neru||寝[ね]る}}, drop the る to get {{neru|stem|寝[ね]}}そうになる. For a godan verb, swap the final u-sound for its i-row partner first: {{wasureru||忘[わす]れる}} is actually ichidan too ({{wasureru|stem|忘[わす]れ}}そうになる, not {{wasureru||忘[わす]れる}}そうになる), but a true godan verb like {{naku||泣[な]く}} becomes {{naku|stem|泣[な]き}}そうになる instead of {{naku||泣[な]く}}そうになる. Whatever the verb, the meaning is the same shape: the subject was right at the threshold of that action or state, close enough to feel it, before it either happened or was caught in time.

```jp
{{jugyou||授[じゅ]業[ぎょう]}}で{{neru|stem|寝[ね]}}そうになりました。
```

*In class, I nearly fell asleep.*

Most of the time you'll meet this pattern in the past tense, そうに{{naru-become|ta|なった}}, because you're reporting a close call after the fact — the moment has already passed by the time you're telling someone about it.

```jp
約[やく]束[そく]を{{wasureru|stem|忘[わす]れ}}そうになりました。
```

*I nearly forgot the appointment.*

## Rules and exceptions

そうになる almost always describes something the subject didn't actually want — falling, crying, forgetting, being late. Nothing in the grammar forces that, but in real use it's overwhelmingly the pattern for near misses you're glad didn't fully land.

> Don't confuse そうになる with the appearance pattern そうだ ("it looks like it's about to rain," {{ame-v||雨[あめ]}}が{{furu-rain|stem|降[ふ]り}}そうだ). そうだ is a guess about something you're watching from outside; そうになる is the subject itself standing right at the edge of an event. The stem attachment looks similar, but the meaning is not interchangeable.

The other trap is attaching it to the wrong form. The stem loses its dictionary-form る or u-ending before そうになる goes on — `食べるそうになる` is wrong; it has to be {{taberu|stem|食[た]べ}}そうになる. If you can say the plain stem on its own and it sounds incomplete, that's the piece そうになる wants.

```jp
{{densha||電[でん]車[しゃ]}}に{{okureru|stem|遅[おく]れ}}そうになりました。
```

*I nearly missed the train.*

```jp
{{kaidan||階[かい]段[だん]}}で{{ochiru|stem|落[お]ち}}そうになりました。
```

*I nearly fell on the stairs.*

```jp
{{kanashii||悲[かな]しい}}{{eiga||映[えい]画[が]}}を{{miru-v|te|見[み]て}}、{{naku|stem|泣[な]き}}そうになりました。
```

*I watched a sad movie and nearly cried.*

## Contrast: そうになる vs ていく・てくる

You already know ていく and てくる for change that unfolds over a stretch of time — something drifting steadily in one direction. そうになる is the opposite shape: not a stretch, a single moment right at the tipping point. Put them side by side and the difference is obvious.

```jp
{{nimotsu||荷[に]物[もつ]}}が{{dandan||だんだん}}{{omoi|stem|重[おも]く}}{{naru-become|te|なって}}いく。
```

*The luggage keeps getting heavier and heavier.*

```jp
{{demo||でも}}、{{kyou||今日[きょう]}}は{{omoi|te|重[おも]くて}}、{{michi-v||道[みち]}}で{{ochiru|stem|落[お]ち}}そうに{{naru-become|ta|なった}}。
```

*But today it was so heavy that I nearly dropped it in the street.*

The first sentence describes a slow slide that's still going; the second is one sharp instant inside that slide, the point where it almost got away from you.

## Closing thought

そうになる is for the instant something almost happens to you — the near miss, caught right before it lands. Later on you'll meet ように{{suru||する}}, which is the deliberate opposite: not something that almost happens to you, but something you push yourself to make happen on purpose.
caution_notes: そうになる attaches to the verb stem, not the dictionary form — 食べるそうになる is wrong; it must be 食べそうになる.
Don't confuse そうになる (the subject is right at the edge of an event) with そうだ (a guess about something you're observing).
そうになる almost always describes an unwanted near miss, even though nothing in the grammar itself requires that.
items.mnemonic_text: Chuu the mouse claws up the mountain trail to one step below the vending machine, then slides to the bottom. He squeaks "<reading>So near</reading>!": he <grammar>almost</grammar> made it. 落ち<reading>そうになる</reading>。

items.explanation_markdown:
You're sitting in the yard with your family after dinner, looking up, and it slips out: {{maiban||毎[まい]晩[ばん]}}{{hoshi||星[ほし]}}を{{miru-v|ta|見[み]た}}ものだ。You don't mean "I watched stars every night" the way you'd read a fact off a form. You mean it with a little sigh — back then, this was just what you did, over and over, and some part of you misses it. That sigh is もの. Drop it and the sentence goes flat; keep it and the listener hears exactly how you're holding that memory.

もの is a small word that, on its own, just means "thing." Tacked onto the end of a sentence like this, though, it stops naming an object and starts coloring the whole sentence — it tells the listener *how* to feel about what you just said, not *what* you said. English does something similar with a tag like "...those were the days," except もの is built into the grammar instead of added as an afterthought, and it does double duty: sometimes it's nostalgia, sometimes it's a half-defensive reason.

You'll hear もの most often from people looking backward — a parent talking about raising their kids, a friend catching up after years apart, someone explaining why they did something the way they did. It's less about the facts of the memory and more about the feeling that's still attached to it. Learn to recognize that feeling first; the grammar rules underneath it are actually short.

## How it works

The nostalgic use is the one you'll reach for most often. Take a verb in its plain past form — the casual た-form you already use for "I did X" — and add ものだ.

```jp
{{maiban||毎[まい]晩[ばん]}}{{hoshi||星[ほし]}}を{{miru-v|ta|見[み]た}}ものだ。
```

*I used to watch the stars every night.*

{{miru-v|ta|見[み]た}} is just the plain past of {{miru-v||見[み]る}}, nothing new there. ものだ is what turns "I watched" into "I used to watch, and it meant something." The pattern works the same way with any verb once it's sitting in that plain past shape:

```jp
{{otouto||弟[おとうと]}}と{{yoku||よく}}公[こう]園[えん]で{{asobu|ta|遊[あそ]んだ}}ものだ。
```

*My little brother and I used to play in the park a lot.*

```jp
{{haha||母[はは]}}は{{yoku||よく}}{{uta||歌[うた]}}を{{utau|ta|歌[うた]った}}ものだ。
```

*My mother used to sing songs often.*

Notice both of those lean on {{yoku||よく}} ("often"). もの itself doesn't mean "repeatedly" — but it almost always shows up describing something that happened over and over, because a single one-off memory rarely gets the wistful treatment. If your sentence is about something that happened exactly once, もの usually isn't the tool you want; save it for the kind of thing you did so many times it became part of who you were.

There's also a quiet assumption baked into every one of these sentences: you don't do this anymore, or at least not the way you used to. {{otouto||弟[おとうと]}}と{{yoku||よく}}公[こう]園[えん]で{{asobu|ta|遊[あそ]んだ}}ものだ carries the sense that those park afternoons belong to a chapter that's closed now — you and your brother grew up, moved on, stopped going. Swap in a habit you still keep up today and もの starts to feel wrong, because there's no distance yet for the nostalgia to sit in.

The second job もの does is give a reason, and the flavor is emotional rather than logical — closer to "well, I was busy, okay?" than to a calm から explanation. This もの closes the sentence, often after だって ("but, well"). Here the plain form comes straight from an い-adjective, and もの attaches with nothing in between:

```jp
だって、{{isogashii|ta|忙[いそが]しかった}}もの。
```

*Well, I was busy, okay?*

{{isogashii|ta|忙[いそが]しかった}} is already a complete plain-form adjective, so もの just clips onto the end. You're not reporting your schedule to a stranger; you're defending yourself a little, the way you would to someone who already half-knows the excuse.

The two uses share more than they look like they do. In both cases もの is pointing at something the listener can't argue with directly — a memory that already happened, or a feeling that's already true. から would let someone push back on your logic; もの just states the fact of the feeling and leaves it there.

## Rules and exceptions

For nouns and な-adjectives, you can't attach もの straight onto the plain form the way you can with an い-adjective — you need だ in between, giving you だもの:

```jp
{{mada||まだ}}{{wakaru|nai|分[わ]からない}}よ。{{kodomo-v||子[こ]供[ども]}}だもの。
```

*They still don't understand. They're a kid, after all.*

{{kodomo-v||子[こ]供[ども]}} is a noun, so it needs だ before もの can land. Think of だもの as one fused unit for nouns and な-adjectives, the same way ものだ is one fused unit closing off a nostalgic verb sentence — the だ moves to whichever side keeps the whole thing sounding complete.

> もの carries real feeling, so it resists cold, purely informational sentences. Saying {{mainichi||毎[まい]日[にち]}}{{kaisha||会[かい]社[しゃ]}}に{{iku-v||行[い]く}}ものだ to mean nothing more than "I go to the office every day" sounds strange — there's no wistfulness and nothing to defend in that statement, so もの has no feeling to attach to.

A guess that trips people up: because もの looks like an ordinary noun, learners sometimes try to conjugate it as if it followed the polite ます-form, writing something like `見ますもの`. もの only ever follows the *plain* form — the ます-form never sits in front of it. Another trap: もの doesn't work well in questions or orders, since you're stating a memory or defending a feeling rather than asking or commanding anyone.

So the checklist, once you strip away the categories, is short: verbs and い-adjectives take もの with nothing between them; nouns and な-adjectives insert だ first. The だ isn't decoration — without it, `子供もの` sounds broken, the same way "kid thing" sounds broken in English where "it's a kid thing" doesn't.

## Casual speech

In relaxed conversation, もの often shrinks to もん. The meaning doesn't change at all, only the register does — the same way わからない can shrink to わかんない among friends.

```jp
だって、{{isogashii|ta|忙[いそが]しかった}}もの。
だって、{{isogashii|ta|忙[いそが]しかった}}もん。
```

*Well, I was busy, okay?*
*Well, I was busy, okay?*

Say the first one to your teacher and the second one to your little brother. Same excuse, same grammar underneath, different company.

You'll hear もん a lot from kids and from adults talking to people they're close to — it has a slightly pouty, self-justifying ring to it even in writing. The nostalgic ものだ almost never contracts this way; もん belongs to the reason-giving side of the pattern, where the emotional register is already higher.

## Contrast

You've already met ことが{{aru||ある}} for talking about the past — "I've done X, at least once." Compare it against the park sentence from earlier:

```jp
公[こう]園[えん]で{{asobu|ta|遊[あそ]んだ}}ことが{{aru||ある}}。
```

*I've played in the park before.*

That sentence is a checkbox: this happened, at some point, full stop. There's no feeling attached, and it doesn't matter whether it happened once or fifty times. {{otouto||弟[おとうと]}}と{{yoku||よく}}公[こう]園[えん]で{{asobu|ta|遊[あそ]んだ}}ものだ, on the other hand, insists on the repetition and the mood behind it — it's a memory you're replaying, not an item you're confirming. If someone asks whether you've ever done something, reach for ことが{{aru||ある}}; if you're the one bringing up the memory unprompted, with a little weight behind it, that's もの's job.

Try the swap test when you're not sure which one fits: if the sentence would still make sense as an answer to "have you ever...?", ことが{{aru||ある}} is doing the work. If the sentence only makes sense as something you'd say unprompted, half to yourself, もの is the one you want.

もの won't come up again for a while, but keep an ear out for the same reflective, slightly self-justifying tone once you meet ところ later — except ところ freezes a single instant in the middle of an action, while もの looks back on a whole stretch of time that's already over.
caution_notes: もの needs genuine wistfulness or self-justification behind it — using it on a flat, purely factual statement sounds off.
もの follows the plain form only; it never attaches after the polite ます-form.
Nouns and な-adjectives need だ before もの (だもの); い-adjectives and verbs take もの directly.
もの doesn't fit questions or commands — it states a memory or a feeling, not a request.

items.explanation_markdown:
Your friend just poured you tea, and it's exactly the kind you love — hot enough to fog the cup, poured straight from the kettle. You get pulled into conversation, thirty seconds pass, and now it's lukewarm and a little sad. The move isn't "drink your tea" — it's drink it *now*, because this particular window is closing whether you notice or not.

```jp
{{ocha||お茶[ちゃ]}}が{{atsui-obj||熱[あつ]い}}うちに{{nomu-v|ta|飲[の]んだ}}{{hou||方[ほう]}}が{{ii||いい}}ですよ。
```
*You should drink the tea while it's still hot.*

That's うちに — a pattern for describing a state that's true right now but won't stay true, paired with something you need to squeeze in before it changes. The textbook gloss is "while" or "during," but that undersells it. The real feeling is closer to: there's a clock running, and everyone in the sentence knows it.

## How it works

うちに attaches to a plain-form clause — the same shape you already use in front of ことに{{suru||する}} or ところ (the plain form is just the casual, unconjugated shape of a verb or adjective: {{taberu||食[た]べる}}, not {{taberu|masu|食[た]べます}}). い-adjectives take it directly:

```jp
{{atsui-obj||熱[あつ]い}} → {{atsui-obj||熱[あつ]い}}うちに
```

The window here is "however long the tea stays hot." Once that's over, so is your chance.

Verbs usually show up in their て{{iru-exist||いる}} shape in front of うちに, because the window this pattern points at is almost always an ongoing state, not a single finished action:

```jp
{{kodomo-v||子[こ]供[ども]}}が{{neru|te|寝[ね]て}}{{iru-exist||いる}}うちに掃[そう]除[じ]{{suru|stem|し}}ましょう。
```
*Let's clean while the child is sleeping.*

The child being asleep is the window. It's open right now, it's temporary, and the sentence tells you exactly what to do with it before it shuts.

The other shape you'll meet constantly is negative: ない form + うちに, meaning "before [something that hasn't happened yet happens]." This one might actually be more common in daily speech than the plain affirmative version, because "do this before that" is a shape people reach for all the time.

```jp
{{wasureru|nai|忘[わす]れない}}うちに{{namae||名[な]前[まえ]}}を{{kaku|ta|書[か]いた}}。
```
*I wrote down the name before I could forget it.*

```jp
{{wasureru||忘[わす]れる}} → {{wasureru|nai|忘[わす]れない}}うちに
```

The logic flips slightly here: the window is "the stretch where you still remember," and it slams shut the instant you forget. {{wasureru|nai|忘[わす]れない}}うちに is close to a set phrase in Japanese — people reach for it constantly, well beyond any one grammar lesson.

うちに also attaches to na-adjectives with な ({{genki||元[げん]気[き]}}なうちに, "while you're still healthy") and to nouns with の, which turns a whole stretch of time into the window itself:

```jp
{{wakai||若[わか]い}}うちに{{takusan||たくさん}}{{ryokou||旅[りょ]行[こう]}}した{{hou||方[ほう]}}が{{ii||いい}}。
```
*You should travel a lot while you're young.*

"Young" isn't one instant — it's a stretch of years quietly running out the whole time you have it, which is exactly the shape of thing うちに was built for.

## Rules and exceptions

The state inside the うちに clause has to still be open. That means the nonpast plain form, or て{{iru-exist||いる}} for something ongoing — never the た-form. `寝たうちに` isn't something a native speaker would say: た marks something already finished, and うちに needs a window that hasn't shut yet. Once the state is over, うちに has nothing left to point at.

> うちに usually assumes the window is closing on its own — daylight fading, tea cooling, someone falling asleep — not because of anything the main-clause action does. If the action you're describing is what actually ends the state (you wake the child up by cleaning loudly, say), the sentence starts working against itself. Pick a different action, or a different pattern.

It also doesn't fit a state with no end in sight. You wouldn't use it for something permanent, because there's no clock to race — and racing a clock is the entire reason this pattern exists.

## Contrast

You already know {{aida||間[あいだ]}}・{{aida||間[あいだ]}}に for "during" — noun+の or verb+て{{iru-exist||いる}}{{aida||間[あいだ]}}(に). Run the same scenario through both, and the difference becomes obvious:

```jp
{{shuumatsu||週[しゅう]末[まつ]}}の{{aida||間[あいだ]}}に宿[しゅく]題[だい]を{{suru|ta|した}}。
```
*I did my homework during the weekend.*

```jp
{{shuumatsu||週[しゅう]末[まつ]}}のうちに宿[しゅく]題[だい]を{{suru|ta|した}}。
```
*I got my homework done while it was still the weekend.*

Same two nouns, same event, very different feeling. {{aida||間[あいだ]}}に is just reporting a timeframe — no urgency, no sense that anything was about to slip away. うちに frames the weekend as a window with an expiration date, and the sentence carries a quiet "I made it in time." Whenever the scenario has that flavor of racing a deadline — real or implied — うちに is the one doing the work; {{aida||間[あいだ]}}に would flatten the sentence into a plain fact.

Next time something around you is fading — the tea, the daylight, someone's patience — you've got the phrase for racing it. That same instinct, "this window won't stay open forever," is exactly what you'll need for たびに later, except たびに handles windows that reopen again and again instead of closing for good.
caution_notes: うちに needs the state in its clause to still be open, so pair it with the nonpast plain form or ている — never the た-form, since a finished state has no window left to race.
Reach for the negative shape (ない form + うちに) when you mean 'before X happens' — it's the version you'll hear far more often than the plain affirmative.
Don't let the main-clause action be what closes the うちに window itself (like waking someone up by cleaning near them) — that turns the sentence into a contradiction.
うちに carries a sense of racing a closing window, while 間・間に is neutral about timing — swap in 間に when there's no urgency to the timeframe.

items.explanation_markdown:
Your little sister visits for an hour, and by the time she leaves, the cat has vanished under the bed again. Not because of today's visit specifically — this happens every single time she comes over. You want a sentence that captures the whole pattern, not just today's incident, and Japanese has a tidy tool built exactly for that job.

```jp
{{imouto||妹[いもうと]}}が{{kuru-v||来[く]る}}たびに、{{neko||猫[ねこ]}}が{{nigeru||逃[に]げる}}。
```

*Every time my little sister comes over, the cat runs away.*

たびに is doing the heavy lifting in that sentence. It takes what sounds like a one-time news report — she came, the cat ran — and turns it into a standing fact about how these two things relate: every single time A happens, B follows, no exceptions worth mentioning.

## How it works

たびに attaches straight onto the dictionary form (the plain, unconjugated form you would look up in a dictionary) of a verb. No extra conjugation, no special stem, nothing to remember beyond taking the verb as it already is and adding たびに.

```jp
{{kuru-v||来[く]る}} → {{kuru-v||来[く]る}}たびに
```

*to come → every time (someone) comes*

That's the entire mechanic for verbs. Whatever the dictionary form already looks like — {{kau-v||買[か]う}}, {{miru-v||見[み]る}}, {{hanasu-v||話[はな]す}} — that's exactly the shape that sits in front of たびに.

Nouns work differently, because a bare noun can't glue onto たびに on its own. You need の in between — the same connecting の that links any two nouns together, the way it does in {{watashi||私[わたし]}}の{{hon||本[ほん]}}, meaning my book. Think of の as the piece that turns a noun into something たびに can attach to.

```jp
{{ryokou||旅[りょ]行[こう]}}のたびに、{{atarashii-adj||新[あたら]しい}}{{kutsu||靴[くつ]}}を{{kau-v||買[か]う}}。
```

*Every trip, I buy new shoes.*

The same shape covers events you attend, not just trips you take:

```jp
{{kaigi||会[かい]議[ぎ]}}のたびに、{{kare||彼[かれ]}}は{{okureru||遅[おく]れる}}。
```

*Every meeting, he's late.*

If you already know {{do-degree||度[ど]}} as the counter for counting how many times something happened, たびに is written with that same kanji, just read differently. That's not a coincidence — both readings point at the same idea: counting occasions one by one, and saying something holds true of every single one you'd count.

Notice what the two halves of these sentences are doing. {{kuru-v||来[く]る}}たびに and {{ryokou||旅[りょ]行[こう]}}のたびに just name the recurring trigger — the thing that keeps happening. The rest of the sentence is whatever reliably tags along whenever that trigger fires. The subject of each half doesn't even have to match: in {{kaigi||会[かい]議[ぎ]}}のたびに、{{kare||彼[かれ]}}は{{okureru||遅[おく]れる}}, the meeting itself doesn't have a particular doer, but {{kare||彼[かれ]}} is the one arriving late every time it rolls around.

## Rules and exceptions

The clause right before たびに — the trigger — stays in dictionary form no matter what tense the rest of the sentence lands on. Even when you're describing a pattern that played out entirely in the past, resist pulling that first verb into the past tense along with it.

```jp
{{kare||彼[かれ]}}が{{kuru-v||来[く]る}}たびに、{{neko||猫[ねこ]}}が{{nigeru|ta|逃[に]げた}}。
```

*Every time he came, the cat ran away.*

> The sentence is unmistakably about the past — {{nigeru|ta|逃[に]げた}} closes it out — but {{kuru-v||来[く]る}} stays in dictionary form. Writing `来たたびに` feels like it should match, and that instinct is exactly what trips people up; たびに simply never follows a past-tense verb.

The mirror-image mistake shows up with nouns: dropping の because the sentence already feels long enough. `旅行たびに` looks like a shortcut, but it isn't one — a noun always needs の to lead into たびに, the same way it needs の in front of any other noun phrase.

たびに also only earns its keep when something genuinely keeps happening. It's for the pattern you'd notice after the third or fourth time, not a single moment where this happened and then that happened. If you're only reporting one specific occasion, this word is off the table.

One thing you don't need to worry about: たびに doesn't shrink or contract in casual speech the way です or the negative forms do. You'll hear it exactly like this whether you're talking to a friend or writing something formal.

## Contrast: たびに vs {{aida||間[あいだ]}}に

You've already met {{aida||間[あいだ]}}に for while, during the interval — one particular stretch of time, with something happening once inside it. たびに is built for the opposite shape: not one window, but every window, each one counted on its own.

```jp
{{kare||彼[かれ]}}が{{hanasu-v|te|話[はな]して}}{{iru-exist||いる}}{{aida||間[あいだ]}}に、{{watashi||私[わたし]}}は宿[しゅく]題[だい]を{{suru|ta|した}}。
```

*While he was talking, I did my homework.*

```jp
{{kare||彼[かれ]}}が{{hanasu-v||話[はな]す}}たびに、{{watashi||私[わたし]}}は{{warau||笑[わら]う}}。
```

*Every time he talks, I laugh.*

The first sentence is about one occasion: he talked, and sometime during that stretch, the homework got done. Swap in たびに there and you'd suddenly be claiming this happens every time he talks — a far bigger claim than just this once. The second sentence is the opposite: a standing rule about every occasion. Swap in {{aida||間[あいだ]}}に there and the sentence collapses into describing a single conversation, which misses the entire point — the reason it's worth saying is that it happens over and over.

That distinction — one window versus every window — is worth sitting with, because it's easy to reach for whichever pattern you learned first out of habit. Ask yourself whether you're describing something that happened once during a stretch of time, or something that happens reliably, every single time. That question alone tells you which of the two you need.

Hold onto that repeating-pattern feeling. You'll meet it again from a different angle once と comes up for automatic, general results — when X happens, Y always follows, built into the grammar of a single clause rather than named from the outside. たびに says here's a pattern I've noticed; と will let you build that same inevitability directly into one sentence. For now, whenever you catch yourself thinking this always happens when, that's your cue to reach for たびに.
caution_notes: Keep the verb right before たびに in dictionary form even when the whole sentence is about the past — たびに itself never follows a past-tense verb.
Don't drop の when a noun leads into たびに; 旅行のたびに needs that の the same way any noun phrase does.
Save たびに for something that genuinely repeats — a pattern you'd notice after several occasions, not a single one-off event.
間に describes one window of time where something happens once; swapping it for たびに turns a single occasion into a standing, repeating rule.

items.explanation_markdown:
Your mother always makes dinner, but tonight she got stuck at the office. Someone still has to cook, and right now that someone is you — not because you're taking over her job for good, just for tonight, standing in her usual spot at the stove.

```jp
{{haha||母[はは]}}の代[か]わりに、{{watashi||私[わたし]}}が{{bangohan||晩[ばん]ご飯[はん]}}を{{tsukuru|masu|作[つく]ります}}。
```

*Instead of my mother, I'll make dinner.*

That little phrase, 代[か]わりに, is doing something specific in that sentence. It isn't a reason — you're not cooking *because* your mother is busy; that's a separate fact you could mention on its own, with a totally different word. And it isn't just "and also," stacking one fact on top of another. It marks a swap: one person, or one action, is taking the seat that was meant for another. Once you can hear that swap, 代[か]わりに starts showing up everywhere — someone covering a shift, someone answering a question that wasn't addressed to them, someone paying a bill that wasn't theirs to begin with.

## How it works

The most common shape is **Noun + の + 代[か]わりに**. You name whoever, or whatever, is being stood in for, attach の — the same の that links two nouns, like {{watashi||私[わたし]}}の{{hon||本[ほん]}} — and then 代[か]わりに. The person actually doing the substitute action shows up separately in the sentence, usually as its subject. It helps to think of 代[か]わりに as a kind of place-marker: の代[か]わりに is literally "in the spot of," and everything after it describes who or what is currently occupying that spot.

```jp
{{ani||兄[あに]}}が{{isogashii||忙[いそが]しい}}から、{{ani||兄[あに]}}の代[か]わりに{{otouto||弟[おとうと]}}が{{hataraku|masu|働[はたら]きます}}。
{{sensei||先[せん]生[せい]}}が{{isogashii||忙[いそが]しい}}から、{{sensei||先[せん]生[せい]}}の代[か]わりに{{seito||生[せい]徒[と]}}が{{kotae||答[こた]え}}ました。
```

*Because my older brother is busy, my younger brother works in his place.*
*Because the teacher is busy, the student answered in the teacher's place.*

Notice the の never drops, no matter how short the sentence gets. 代[か]わりに always needs something to hang off — a noun it's replacing, or, in the next pattern, a whole action it's replacing. That's a useful thing to hold onto, because in casual speech a lot of particles get dropped or slurred together, but this の is load-bearing. Drop it, and the sentence stops parsing as a substitution at all.

That second pattern is **dictionary form + 代[か]わりに** — the dictionary form being the plain, unconjugated shape you'd look a verb up under, like {{iku-v||行[い]く}} or {{taberu||食[た]べる}}. Here 代[か]わりに isn't swapping one person for another; it's swapping one action for another, inside the same person's own choices. You do B instead of doing A, and both A and B belong to you.

```jp
{{denwa-suru||電[でん]話[わ]する}}代[か]わりに、{{tegami||手[て]紙[がみ]}}を{{kaku|masu|書[か]きました}}。
{{isha||医[い]者[しゃ]}}に{{iku-v||行[い]く}}代[か]わりに、{{kusuri||薬[くすり]}}を{{nomu-v|masu|飲[の]みました}}。
```

*Instead of calling, I wrote a letter.*
*Instead of going to the doctor, I took medicine.*

Both halves of each sentence belong to the same person. Nobody else enters the picture — it's a private substitution, this action instead of that one, and the dictionary form is what marks the road not taken. You'll notice that the verb before 代[か]わりに doesn't care about tense at all; even if the letter got written yesterday, {{denwa-suru||電[でん]話[わ]する}} stays in the dictionary form, and only the final verb — {{kaku|masu|書[か]きました}} — carries the past tense for the whole sentence.

代[か]わりに has a second life beyond straight substitution: it can mark a trade, something given back in return for something else. The shape is identical — dictionary form + 代[か]わりに — but the feel shifts from "instead of" to "in return for."

```jp
{{kasa||傘[かさ]}}を{{kasu||貸[か]す}}代[か]わりに、{{sukoshi||少[すこ]し}}{{okane||お金[かね]}}を{{morau|masu|もらいます}}。
```

*In exchange for lending the umbrella, I get a little money.*

Nothing in the grammar itself tells you which reading is meant; the situation does. Lending an umbrella and getting money back is obviously a trade, not a replacement — nobody assumes you lent the umbrella *instead of* doing something else. Context carries the weight here, the same way it does with a lot of everyday Japanese: the words hand you a shape, and the scene fills in what that shape means.

## Rules and exceptions

> The の is not optional with nouns. `父代わりに行きます` is wrong — 代[か]わりに cannot bolt straight onto a noun. It has to be {{chichi||父[ちち]}}の代[か]わりに{{iku-v|masu|行[い]きます}}.

With verbs, the attachment point is just as fixed: always the dictionary form, never the て-form and never the plain stem. `食べて代わりに` isn't a sentence anyone would say — it has to be {{taberu||食[た]べる}}代[か]わりに. If you catch yourself reaching for a て-form right before 代[か]わりに, treat that as a signal to swap back to the dictionary form; the て-form belongs to a different family of patterns entirely, and 代[か]わりに just doesn't take it, no matter how natural it feels to chain て-forms together elsewhere.

代[か]わりに also doesn't need a noun or a verb attached to it at all — it can open a brand-new sentence on its own, pointing back at something you already said.

```jp
{{kyou||今日[きょう]}}は{{isogashii||忙[いそが]しい}}です。
代[か]わりに、{{ashita||明日[あした]}}{{au|stem|会[あ]い}}ましょう。
```

*Today I'm busy.*
*Instead, let's meet tomorrow.*

Used this way, it works almost like a spoken aside — "instead," full stop — leaning entirely on the sentence before it for its meaning. That's worth knowing, because this is the form you'll actually hear most in casual conversation: tucked at the front of a reply, not buried in the middle of one long sentence. You don't need to reconstruct a noun or a verb after it in your head; the previous sentence already did that work for you.

## Contrast: 代[か]わりに vs から

You already know から for stating a reason — *because* X, Y happens. It's tempting to think 代[か]わりに is doing the same job, since both often turn up in sentences about someone stepping in for someone else. They don't overlap, though. から explains *why* something is happening; 代[か]わりに tells you *who or what got swapped in*. You can have either one without the other, and plenty of real sentences only need one of them.

```jp
{{ane||姉[あね]}}が{{isogashii||忙[いそが]しい}}から、{{imouto||妹[いもうと]}}が{{bangohan||晩[ばん]ご飯[はん]}}を{{tsukuru|masu|作[つく]ります}}。
{{ane||姉[あね]}}が{{isogashii||忙[いそが]しい}}から、{{ane||姉[あね]}}の代[か]わりに{{imouto||妹[いもうと]}}が{{bangohan||晩[ばん]ご飯[はん]}}を{{tsukuru|masu|作[つく]ります}}。
```

*Because my older sister is busy, my younger sister makes dinner.*
*Because my older sister is busy, my younger sister makes dinner in her place.*

The first sentence only tells you why the younger sister is cooking — maybe she always cooks anyway, busy sister or not. The second makes a stronger claim: she's specifically doing a job that would otherwise have fallen to her sister. Same reason clause, different claim about whose turn it really was. That gap between the two sentences is the whole point of learning 代[か]わりに separately from から — without it, you can explain why something happened, but you can't say whose role got taken over to make it happen.

That distinction — swapping an actor versus just stating a reason — is exactly the kind of thing that stays blurry the first few times you meet it, so don't worry if your early 代[か]わりに sentences feel like they could've stopped at から instead. There's a rough test: if you can ask "instead of whom, or instead of what?" and get a real answer out of the sentence, 代[か]わりに belongs there. If there's no real answer to that question, you're probably just looking at a reason, and から is doing all the work on its own.

代[か]わりに earns its keep because Japanese cares a lot about naming exactly whose role got taken, and から alone can't do that job — it only ever tells you why, never who was supposed to be there first.

Hold onto that "stand-in" feeling. Later on you'll meet というより, which swaps not people or actions but *descriptions* — for when you want to correct how something was framed, rather than settle who actually did it.
caution_notes: 代わりに never attaches directly to a noun — always insert の first (兄の代わりに, not 兄代わりに).
With verbs, 代わりに attaches only to the dictionary form, never to the て-form or the stem.
The same 代わりに sentence can read as substitution or as a trade — only the situation tells you which, not the grammar.
から explains why something happens; 代わりに names who or what was swapped in — they answer different questions even in the same sentence.

items.explanation_markdown:
You are telling a friend about today's Japanese exam. {{muzukashii||難[むずか]しい}}, you start to say — difficult. Except that's not quite right. Every question was written in oddly indirect language, the time limit was tight, and by the end your hand hurt from writing — none of that is really what {{muzukashii||難[むずか]しい}} points at. What you actually mean is closer to annoying, and you want to say so without pretending you never said {{muzukashii||難[むずか]しい}} at all.

That is the exact job というより does. It does not erase the first word — it upgrades it. You put the first guess down, mark it as a rough draft with というより, and follow it with the sharper word.

```jp
{{kono||この}}試[し]験[けん]は{{muzukashii||難[むずか]しい}}というより{{mendokusai||面[めん]倒[どう]くさい}}。
```

*This exam isn't so much difficult as it is annoying.*

You could of course just say {{mendokusai||面[めん]倒[どう]くさい}} and stop there, dropping {{muzukashii||難[むずか]しい}} entirely. But that loses something real: the listener never finds out that {{muzukashii||難[むずか]しい}} was your first, natural reaction, and that you're now sharpening it on purpose. というより keeps both words in play and shows the correction happening in real time, which is exactly why it shows up so often in casual conversation — it's how people actually think out loud.

This is a small but useful trick for a learner, too. You don't always need the perfect word on the first try. Say the word you already know, then reach for というより and a second, closer word — the sentence still lands, and it sounds more natural than pausing mid-thought to hunt for the ideal adjective before you say anything at all.

## How it works

というより attaches to the plain form — the same shape you already use in front of から and と. If the word in front of it is an i-adjective or a verb, you don't touch it at all; you just tack というより straight onto the end.

It helps to see where the pattern comes from. という is built from と (a quoting particle — the little word that marks what someone said or thought) plus いう (to say), so というより literally reads something like more than saying that. より is the same より you'd use in a plain comparison. Put them together and you get exactly what the pattern does: more than saying the first thing, this is closer to the truth.

Nouns and na-adjectives work slightly differently, because their plain form usually carries だ ({{sensei||先[せん]生[せい]}}だ, {{shizuka||静[しず]か}}だ) — and というより doesn't want that だ sitting in front of it. Drop it, and put the bare noun or na-adjective directly before the pattern instead.

```jp
{{kare||彼[かれ]}}は{{sensei||先[せん]生[せい]}}というより{{tomodachi||友[とも]達[だち]}}だ。
```

*He's more a friend than a teacher.*

```jp
{{kono||この}}{{heya||部屋[へや]}}は{{shizuka||静[しず]か}}というより{{kurai||暗[くら]い}}。
```

*This room isn't so much quiet as it is dark.*

Notice the two halves don't have to match in part of speech. {{shizuka||静[しず]か}} is a na-adjective, {{kurai||暗[くら]い}} is an i-adjective, and というより sits between them without any trouble, because it isn't comparing grammar categories — it's comparing two descriptions of the same room.

The same freedom applies to verbs. Anything that ends in the plain dictionary form can sit in front of というより exactly as it is, with no extra piece bolted on. If you've been bracing for a special connecting form the way some patterns demand, you can relax here — the plain form you already default to is the whole story.

というより itself never changes shape. No past tense, no negative, no polite ます version living inside it. Whatever tense or politeness the sentence needs goes on the words sitting on either side of it, never on というより itself. That's one less thing to memorize than most of what you've met so far — the conjugation work all happens before というより, never to it.

## Rules and exceptions

というより always needs two descriptions of the same thing sitting in one sentence — a first guess and a better one. It has no life as a stand-alone reason the way から does; there's no reading of というより that works like because, even though both patterns attach to the same plain form.

That's also why というより never opens a conversation out of nowhere. There always has to be a first attempt sitting somewhere nearby for it to improve on — sometimes your own last sentence, sometimes something the other person just said.

This is also why というより tends to cluster with words that sit close together in meaning — {{muzukashii||難[むずか]しい}} and {{mendokusai||面[めん]倒[どう]くさい}}, {{isogashii||忙[いそが]しい}} and {{taihen||大[たい]変[へん]}}, {{tsumaranai||つまらない}} and {{kanashii||悲[かな]しい}}. Pick two words that have nothing to do with each other and the sentence stops making sense, because there's no shared thing left for the second word to describe more accurately than the first.

> The word *after* というより is the one that wins. Reverse the order and you reverse which description the speaker actually stands behind — {{isogashii||忙[いそが]しい}}というより{{taihen||大[たい]変[へん]}}だ and {{taihen||大[たい]変[へん]}}というより{{isogashii||忙[いそが]しい}} are not the same claim.

```jp
{{kyou||今日[きょう]}}は{{isogashii||忙[いそが]しい}}というより{{taihen||大[たい]変[へん]}}だ。
```

*Today isn't so much busy as it is rough.*

```jp
{{kono||この}}{{eiga||映[えい]画[が]}}は{{tsumaranai||つまらない}}というより{{kanashii||悲[かな]しい}}。
```

*This movie isn't so much boring as it is sad.*

It's also easy to reach for というより when what you actually mean is instead of. English rather than can carry both jobs — a corrected description, or a chosen action instead of a different one — but というより only does the first. It never swaps one action for another; that job belongs to 代[か]わりに, which shows up again below.

A related trap: というより doesn't mean more than in the sense of quantity, the way you might compare heights or prices. It's not measuring which word is bigger; it's judging which word is truer. {{isogashii||忙[いそが]しい}}というより{{taihen||大[たい]変[へん]}}だ isn't claiming {{taihen||大[たい]変[へん]}} outranks {{isogashii||忙[いそが]しい}} on some scale — it's saying {{taihen||大[たい]変[へん]}} is simply the more accurate word for today.

## Casual speech

In relaxed speech, と regularly contracts to って — というのは becomes っていうのは, and というより follows the same pattern: っていうより. You'll hear native speakers drop it mid-sentence, correcting themselves or someone else out loud, the same way you might in English with or, actually.

The full というより never disappears from writing or from careful, polite speech — a work email or a formal apology keeps it intact. っていうより belongs to texting, chatting with friends, and the kind of spoken Japanese where you're thinking as you talk. Treat the choice between them the same way you'd treat any other casual contraction you've already met: register, not meaning, is what changes.

If you're ever unsure which one to reach for, default to the full というより. It's never wrong, even in a casual conversation — it just sounds a shade more careful. っていうより only sounds wrong the other way around, dropped into a formal email where it reads as too loose for the occasion.

```jp
っていうより、{{mendokusai||面[めん]倒[どう]くさい}}だけだよ。
```

*More accurately, it's just annoying, that's all.*

## Contrast

から states a reason — a fact the speaker is pointing to as the cause of something. というより doesn't state a reason at all; it revises a description. {{muzukashii||難[むずか]しい}}から{{yasumu||休[やす]む}} means because it's hard, I'm resting — no correction is happening there, just a plain cause and effect.

```jp
{{muzukashii||難[むずか]しい}}から、{{kyou||今日[きょう]}}は{{yasumu||休[やす]む}}。
```

*Because it's difficult, I'll rest today.*

代[か]わりに is the pattern actually built for swapping — one action standing in for another, not one word standing in for another. Reach for というより when you're fixing how you described something, and 代[か]わりに when you're fixing what actually happened.

```jp
{{yasumu||休[やす]む}}代[か]わりに、{{heya||部屋[へや]}}を掃[そう]除[じ]{{suru|ta|した}}。
```

*Instead of resting, I cleaned the room.*

Put side by side, the difference is easy to feel: {{yasumu||休[やす]む}}代[か]わりに means resting got replaced by something else entirely — cleaning happened, not resting. If you swapped in というより there instead, you would need two descriptions of the same single event, which resting and cleaning simply are not. The pattern you pick tells the listener what kind of correction they're getting — a fact about the world, or a better choice of words.

というより never argues that the first word was wrong — only that the second one is closer. Later, と{{suru|te|して}} will pick up a different job entirely, handing a noun a role to stand in rather than correcting anything about it. Keep them separate in your head from the start, and you won't be tempted to reach for というより out of habit on a sentence where nothing actually needs revising.
caution_notes: というより corrects or refines a description you already put into words — it doesn't mean instead of the way 代わりに does, so don't swap the two.
Before a noun or na-adjective, drop だ — say 先生というより, never `先生だというより`.
というより can't stand alone as a reason for something; that's what から is for.
っていうより is the everyday casual contraction and fits speech, not formal writing.

items.explanation_markdown:
Picture this: your friend's family runs a small noodle shop, and today you're standing behind the counter helping out because they're short-handed. A regular customer glances over, assumes you work there, and asks a question about the menu. You want to be clear you're not staff — you're just here for the afternoon, because he's your friend, and nothing more official than that. Japanese has one small word built exactly for that clarification, and once you notice it, you'll start seeing it everywhere: on job applications, in weather reports, in the fine print under a photo caption.

```jp
{{watashi||私[わたし]}}は{{tomodachi||友[とも]達[だち]}}として{{tetsudau|te|手伝[てつだ]って}}{{iru-exist|masu|います}}。
```

*I'm helping as a friend.*

That として is doing all the work in that sentence. It's not saying who you are in general — it's saying what role you're filling right now, in this exact situation, for this exact stretch of time. Doctor, guest, teacher, a cardboard box pressed into service as a chair: として names the hat someone or something is wearing for the moment, without making any bigger claim about them beyond that.

## How it works

Structurally, として could not be simpler: it attaches directly to a noun, with nothing in between. Noun plus として means "in the capacity of [noun]," or, in more natural English, "as [noun]." There's no conjugation to learn and no politeness level to track — として itself never changes shape no matter what comes before or after it. That's the whole conjugation story for this pattern: there isn't one.

```jp
{{watashi||私[わたし]}}は{{isha||医[い]者[しゃ]}}として{{byouin||病[びょう]院[いん]}}で{{hataraku|te|働[はたら]いて}}{{iru-exist|masu|います}}。
```

*I work at the hospital as a doctor.*

Swap out the noun and the entire situation shifts with it. Put {{kyaku||客[きゃく]}} in that slot instead of {{isha||医[い]者[しゃ]}}, and suddenly you're not the one treating people at the hospital — you're the one being served somewhere else entirely.

```jp
{{kyou||今日[きょう]}}は{{kyaku||客[きゃく]}}として{{kuru-v|masu|来[き]ました}}。
```

*Today I came as a guest.*

としてisn't reserved for jobs and social roles, either. Any noun can slot into it, including an ordinary object being pressed into a purpose it wasn't originally built for. This is one of the more useful everyday uses of として, and it's easy to miss if you only ever practice it with professions.

```jp
{{hako||箱[はこ]}}を{{isu||椅[い]子[す]}}として{{tsukau|masu|使[つか]いました}}。
```

*I used the box as a chair.*

The box never stops being a box in any real sense — として just tells you what function it's serving in that particular moment. The same logic covers people wearing more than one hat over the course of a single day: a teacher explaining something to a class of students, or a family sharing one roof.

```jp
{{sensei||先[せん]生[せい]}}として{{gakusei||学[がく]生[せい]}}に{{setsumei||説[せつ]明[めい]}}しました。
```

*As the teacher, I explained it to the students.*

```jp
{{kazoku||家[か]族[ぞく]}}として{{issho-ni||一[いっ]緒[しょ]に}}{{sumu|te|住[す]んで}}{{iru-exist|masu|います}}。
```

*We live together as a family.*

By now you've seen として ride along with several very different nouns, and the shape never budges:

- {{isha||医[い]者[しゃ]}}として — as a doctor
- {{kyaku||客[きゃく]}}として — as a guest
- {{sensei||先[せん]生[せい]}}として — as a teacher
- {{kazoku||家[か]族[ぞく]}}として — as a family

Notice that in every one of these sentences, the noun in front of として is doing double duty. It names what the person or thing is, and として immediately narrows that down to say in what capacity that fact matters for the sentence you're building. Take away として and you're left with a bare noun sitting there with no job to do — the sentence stops making sense on its own.

## Rules and exceptions

としてonly ever follows a bare noun. Not an i-adjective, not a na-adjective, not a verb, and not a whole clause sitting there on its own — a noun, full stop. If you catch yourself reaching for something like `忙しいとして`, that's a sign you need an entirely different construction; adjectives and verbs simply don't slot into this pattern the way nouns do, and there's no version of として that patches around that gap.

> Resist the urge to add の in front of として out of habit. Some of the patterns you already know want Noun plus の sitting in front of them — として never does. `友達のとして` is not natural Japanese; it's simply {{tomodachi||友[とも]達[だち]}}として, noun straight into the particle with nothing between them.

Here's the part that trips people up once they've had として for a while: it doesn't claim the role is permanent. {{watashi||私[わたし]}}は{{isha||医[い]者[しゃ]}}として{{byouin||病[びょう]院[いん]}}で{{hataraku|te|働[はたら]いて}}{{iru-exist|masu|います}} tells you that, in this context — at the hospital, doing this specific job — the person is functioning as a doctor. It says nothing about whether medicine is their whole identity, whether they'll always be one, or what they do on the weekend. は would make a claim about identity in general, the kind of thing you'd put on a business card. として only ever talks about the capacity someone occupies for the purpose of the sentence sitting in front of you, and that capacity can change completely from one sentence to the next, even within the same conversation.

## Contrast: として vs 代[か]わりに

You've already met 代[か]わりに for "instead of" — one thing or person standing in for another. It's easy to blur the two together because both follow a noun and both, in a loose sense, involve someone occupying a position that isn't automatically theirs. But they answer different questions. として tells you what role someone is genuinely filling; 代[か]わりに tells you who or what they're replacing while that person is absent.

```jp
{{isha||医[い]者[しゃ]}}として{{hataraku|masu|働[はたら]きました}}。
```

*I worked as a doctor.*

```jp
{{isha||医[い]者[しゃ]}}の代[か]わりに{{hataraku|masu|働[はたら]きました}}。
```

*I worked in place of the doctor.*

Read those two side by side and the gap opens right up. The first sentence describes a doctor doing a doctor's job — nothing unusual about it at all. The second describes someone who is not the doctor stepping in because the doctor couldn't be there — maybe a nurse, maybe an intern, maybe you, on a very different kind of day. Same profession named, same verb, two completely different scenes, and として versus 代[か]わりに is the only thing telling them apart.

This is worth sitting with for a second, because the mix-up runs in a predictable direction: learners reach for として when they actually mean "filling in for," since both patterns get translated into English with some flavor of "as" or "in place of." If the sentence is about substituting for someone who's absent, you want 代[か]わりに. If it's about a role someone genuinely, presently occupies, として is the word you want, and no amount of translation-matching will save you from checking which situation you're actually describing.

For now, として is your word for naming which hat you're wearing in a given sentence — friend, doctor, guest, chair. Later on, when you want to talk about something instead of functioning as it — discussing your trip rather than acting as its guide through it — that job belongs to について, which is coming up soon.
caution_notes: として only ever follows a bare noun — never an i-adjective, a na-adjective, or a verb on its own.
Don't insert の before として; unlike some patterns you've learned, として attaches straight to the noun.
として names the role someone or something occupies for this sentence, not a permanent identity, so don't treat it like は.
として and 代わりに both follow a noun but answer different questions — として names the role occupied, 代わりに names who is being replaced — so swapping them flips the meaning.

items.explanation_markdown:
Your friend is trying to decide whether to swing by tonight, and texts you: is she actually going to be home? You haven't called to double-check, and the last thing you want is to promise something and be wrong about it. What you can say, honestly, is what you currently know:

```jp
{{watashi||私[わたし]}}の{{shiru||知[し]る}}限[かぎ]り、{{kanojo||彼[かの]女[じょ]}}は{{kyou||今日[きょう]}}、{{ie||家[いえ]}}に{{iru-exist||いる}}。
```

*As far as I know, she's home today.*

You've just hedged your answer instead of stating it as fact, and that difference matters — if it turns out she left an hour ago, you didn't lie, you just reported the edge of what you knew at the time. 限[かぎ]り comes from the verb `限る`, "to limit, to restrict" — as a noun it means "the extent, the boundary." Put a clause in front of it and you're saying "to the extent that this clause is true, here's my answer."

Depending on what's inside that clause, the same word reads as either "as far as ~" (the edge of what you personally can confirm — your knowledge, your eyes, your information) or "as long as ~" (the edge of how long some condition keeps holding true). It's the same underlying idea both times: 限[かぎ]り marks a boundary, and everything after it is only guaranteed to hold within that boundary. Whether the boundary is "what I happen to know" or "how long this situation lasts" just depends on the verb sitting in front of it.

## How it works

限[かぎ]り attaches to the end of a clause in its plain form — the same dictionary-form, plain-negative, or plain-adjective shape you already use in front of ため. Verbs work exactly as they are, no changes needed:

```jp
{{miru-v||見[み]る}}限[かぎ]り、{{kyou||今日[きょう]}}の{{tenki||天[てん]気[き]}}は{{ii||いい}}。
```

*As far as I can see, today's weather is good.*

Past tense works exactly the same way, and honestly reads a little more naturally for a lot of "as far as I've seen/heard" statements, since you're reporting something you already checked rather than something you're checking right now — {{miru-v|ta|見[み]た}}限[かぎ]り, "as far as I've looked and seen," instead of {{miru-v||見[み]る}}限[かぎ]り. Both show up constantly; pick whichever matches whether you're describing an ongoing habit of noticing something or one specific look you already took.

I-adjectives work as-is too — nothing gets inserted before 限[かぎ]り:

```jp
{{isogashii||忙[いそが]しい}}限[かぎ]り、{{kare||彼[かれ]}}は{{yasumu|nai|休[やす]まない}}。
```

*As long as he's busy, he doesn't rest.*

Na-adjectives need their な first, the same な you already use in front of a noun:

```jp
{{genki||元[げん]気[き]}}な限[かぎ]り、{{kare||彼[かれ]}}は{{maiasa||毎[まい]朝[あさ]}}{{hashiru||走[はし]る}}。
```

*As long as he's healthy, he runs every morning.*

One shape shows up on its own constantly: {{dekiru||できる}}限[かぎ]り, literally "to the extent that it's possible." In practice it's just "as much as I can":

```jp
{{dekiru||できる}}限[かぎ]り、{{watashi||私[わたし]}}は{{tetsudau||手伝[てつだ]う}}。
```

*I'll help as much as I possibly can.*

限[かぎ]り isn't stiff or bookish the way some "extent" vocabulary can feel — you'll hear {{watashi||私[わたし]}}の{{shiru||知[し]る}}限[かぎ]り and {{dekiru||できる}}限[かぎ]り in ordinary spoken conversation just as often as in writing. It carries a slightly careful, considered tone, the sound of someone being precise about what they can and can't back up, but it never sounds overly formal or out of place between friends.

Now look back at that very first example: {{watashi||私[わたし]}}の{{shiru||知[し]る}}限[かぎ]り, not {{watashi||私[わたし]}}が{{shiru||知[し]る}}限[かぎ]り. Inside the little clause that describes 限[かぎ]り — 「{{watashi||私[わたし]}}の{{shiru||知[し]る}}」, "the extent that I know" — the subject can take の instead of が. That's a small quirk of clauses that describe or modify something (this one is modifying 限[かぎ]り, the same way a clause can modify a noun): が still works fine too, and you'll hear both.

```jp
{{watashi||私[わたし]}}が{{shiru|te|知[し]って}}{{iru-exist||いる}}限[かぎ]り、{{kare||彼[かれ]}}は{{yakusoku||約[やく]束[そく]}}を{{wasureru|nai|忘[わす]れない}}。
```

*As far as I know, he doesn't forget his promises.*

Same meaning as the opening example, just built with {{shiru|te|知[し]って}}{{iru-exist||いる}} (the "currently in a state of knowing" form) and が instead of の. Neither is more correct than the other — の is simply the option that surfaces specifically inside clauses like this one, and 限[かぎ]り invites it constantly. You'll mostly see の with a short, single-word subject like {{watashi||私[わたし]}} right before the verb; once the clause gets longer or more complicated, が tends to take over, which is exactly why the {{shiru|te|知[し]って}}{{iru-exist||いる}} example above reaches for が instead.

## Rules and exceptions

限[かぎ]り only measures something the speaker can actually vouch for — their own knowledge, their own eyes, or a condition that's genuinely still true. That's why it reads as a hedge rather than a flat claim. Reach for it when you want to signal "this is the edge of what I can confirm," not when you're already certain — a plain sentence handles certainty just fine on its own.

The plain-form rule is strict about one thing: nothing gets inserted before 限[かぎ]り on a verb or an i-adjective. `忙しいだ限り` is wrong — the i-adjective already finishes the clause by itself, so that だ has nowhere to go. Only na-adjectives (and nouns) need something in that slot, and what they need is な, never だ: `元気だ限り` is wrong, {{genki||元[げん]気[き]}}な限[かぎ]り is right.

> {{dekiru||できる}}限[かぎ]り looks like it should build a fresh literal meaning every time — "the limit of what's possible" — but in practice it's frozen into a set phrase, the way "as far as possible" is frozen in English. Don't expect to take it apart and rebuild it; just learn it as a unit.

限[かぎ]り almost always describes something ongoing — a state of knowing, a state of health, a stretch of time — not a single finished event. That's part of why the "as long as" reading feels so natural with {{aru||ある}}限[かぎ]り or {{genki||元[げん]気[き]}}な限[かぎ]り: you're pointing at a condition that keeps being true, not something that happened once and ended. Try to build a sentence around a single completed action instead, and it stops making sense — there's no "edge" to measure, because the thing you'd be measuring already finished.

That's also why 限[かぎ]り doesn't do the job of a plain "if"-style hypothetical. Those ask what would follow from a possibility that might not hold at all. 限[かぎ]り instead leans on something the speaker is already treating as true right now — their current knowledge, a condition already in place — and measures how far that reaches. It's honest, mundane accounting of what you can vouch for, not speculation about what might happen.

## Contrast

限[かぎ]り and ため (cause) can end up sounding almost identical in English translation, which is exactly why they're worth setting side by side. Watch what happens when you swap one for the other:

```jp
{{jikan||時[じ]間[かん]}}が{{aru||ある}}限[かぎ]り、{{kare||彼[かれ]}}は{{hon||本[ほん]}}を{{yomu||読[よ]む}}。
```

*As long as he has time, he reads books.*

```jp
{{jikan||時[じ]間[かん]}}が{{aru||ある}}ため、{{kare||彼[かれ]}}は{{hon||本[ほん]}}を{{yomu||読[よ]む}}。
```

*Because he has time, he reads books.*

Same two facts, different logic underneath. The ため version claims that having time is the *reason* he reads — take away the time and the reasoning collapses. The 限[かぎ]り version makes no claim about cause at all; it just says his reading is tied to the whole *stretch* during which he has time, holding only as long as that condition does. A quick test: if you can swap your "because" for "for as long as" and the sentence still lands the same point, you're in 限[かぎ]り territory, not ため's.

This is where 限[かぎ]り's honesty about mess actually helps you: plenty of real situations sound fine described either way, because "he has time, and that's why/while he reads" is genuinely ambiguous between cause and duration in everyday thought. Japanese speakers don't agonize over which one to pick any more than you'd agonize over "because" versus "while" in English — they reach for whichever framing fits what they mean to emphasize, cause or extent, and move on.

The other patterns you've already met aren't close enough to cause real confusion here. について marks what you're talking *about*, によると marks where information *came from*, と{{suru|te|して}} marks a role someone is acting *in* — none of them measure an extent the way 限[かぎ]り does, so you won't find yourself reaching for the wrong one by accident. ため is the only real neighbor, precisely because cause and extent so often describe the very same situation from two different angles.

Hold onto that "edge of a condition" feeling — you'll want it again soon, when たとえ〜ても hands you the flip side: not the boundary of what's true, but what stays true even past it.
caution_notes: 限り reports the boundary of what you personally know, see, or feel — treat it as a hedge, not a claim of certainty.
Don't insert だ before 限り on a verb or an i-adjective — the plain form already ends the clause on its own.
A na-adjective needs its な before 限り (元気な限り, not 元気だ限り), the same な you'd use in front of a noun.
できる限り is a frozen set phrase meaning 'as much as possible' — don't expect to build a fresh literal reading out of it each time.

items.explanation_markdown:
You've been planning a Saturday hike with two friends for weeks. Thursday night the forecast flips: rain, all day, start to finish. Your phone buzzes. 'So we're canceling, right?' You are absolutely not canceling. What you need is a sentence that admits the rain is possible — and then walks straight past it without breaking stride.

Japanese builds that sentence with たとえ〜ても. Textbooks hand it to you at exactly this level for a reason: it is the first pattern whose whole job is to say, out loud, I have imagined the worst — and it changes nothing.

```jp
たとえ{{ame-v||雨[あめ]}}が{{furu-rain|te|降[ふ]って}}も、{{watashitachi||私[わたし]たち}}は{{yama-v||山[やま]}}に{{noboru|masu|登[のぼ]ります}}。
```

*Even if it rains, we will climb the mountain.*

Read it as two moving parts. たとえ, up front, means 'supposing' — a small flag that announces *what comes next is a what-if, not a report*. The 〜ても half is the 'even,' the part that does the actual conceding. Neither piece does the job alone; together they land as 'even if.'

## How it works

The structure is たとえ + te-form + も. You already own the te-form, so this is one more place it pays rent. And the も is the same も you use for 'me too.' Under the hood, {{ame-v||雨[あめ]}}が{{furu-rain|te|降[ふ]って}}も is almost 'it rains *too*' — the rain shows up, joins the day, and the plan carries on regardless. That little 'also' is doing all the heavy lifting, which is why the pattern feels so calm: nothing is being fought, just absorbed and stepped over.

Verbs are the easy case. Take the te-form and add も:

```jp
{{taberu||食[た]べる}} → {{taberu|te|食[た]べて}}も
```

*to eat → even if you eat*

So {{furu-rain||降[ふ]る}} becomes {{furu-rain|te|降[ふ]って}}も, {{iku-v||行[い]く}} becomes {{iku-v|te|行[い]って}}も, {{suru||する}} becomes {{suru|te|して}}も. If you can build the te-form, you can build this pattern — there are no new endings to memorize, only a new job for an old one.

I-adjectives trade their final い for くても:

```jp
{{takai-adj||高[たか]い}} → {{takai-adj|te|高[たか]くて}}も
```

*expensive → even if it is expensive*

```jp
たとえ{{kono||この}}{{hon||本[ほん]}}が{{takai-adj|te|高[たか]くて}}も、{{kau-v|masu|買[か]います}}。
```

*Even if this book is expensive, I will buy it.*

Picture yourself in the bookshop, holding the one dictionary you actually came for, and the price tag is genuinely rude. {{takai-adj|te|高[たか]くて}}も — fine. You are buying it anyway. Notice that たとえ does not touch the price itself; it touches your attitude toward the price.

Na-adjectives and nouns have no te-form, so they take {{demo||でも}} directly — one shape for both word types, a rare free lunch:

```jp
{{ame-v||雨[あめ]}} → {{ame-v||雨[あめ]}}{{demo||でも}}
```

*rain → even if it rains*

```jp
たとえ{{ashita||明日[あした]}}{{yuki||雪[ゆき]}}{{demo||でも}}、{{gakkou-v||学[がっ]校[こう]}}は{{aru|masu|あります}}。
```

*Even if it snows tomorrow, there will still be school.*

{{shizuka||静[しず]か}}{{demo||でも}}, {{genki||元[げん]気[き]}}{{demo||でも}}, {{yuki||雪[ゆき]}}{{demo||でも}} — the same move every time, no exceptions hiding in the corners.

Negatives behave too. {{iru-exist||いる}} becomes {{iru-exist|nai|いなくて}}も, and {{iku-v|nai|行[い]かない}} becomes {{iku-v|nai|行[い]かなくて}}も. たとえ{{sensei||先[せん]生[せい]}}が{{iru-exist|nai|いなくて}}も — even if the teacher is not there — and you can already finish that thought yourself.

You might wonder whether you can drop たとえ and just say {{ame-v||雨[あめ]}}が{{furu-rain|te|降[ふ]って}}も on its own. You can, and people do, all the time. But without the flag up front, ても can also concede plain facts, so the sentence loses some of its what-if flavor. たとえ is you announcing, before anything else, that you are about to bend reality on purpose. Keep it in while you are learning — it makes your intention unmistakable.

One thing to feel in your bones: this is a **strong concession**. The second half of the sentence is not a wish or a maybe. It states what stands *no matter what* — a decision, a fact, a refusal to budge. The worse the condition in the first half, the more stubborn the second half sounds. That stubbornness is the whole personality of the pattern.

## Rules and exceptions

たとえ is a supposition flag, so it only flies over what-ifs. If the thing actually happened, たとえ is the wrong tool. About last Saturday's very real rain, `たとえ昨日雨が降っても、家にいました` sounds like you have forgotten whether it rained or not. For facts, drop the flag: plain ても concedes reality just fine, and ため names the cause outright — more on that one below.

The te-form itself is not optional. Learners regularly produce `たとえ雨が降るても` — dictionary form plus も — and it simply is not a shape Japanese has. It must be {{furu-rain|te|降[ふ]って}}も. The same trap waits with i-adjectives: `高いても` is broken, because the final い has to become く first, giving {{takai-adj|te|高[たか]くて}}も.

Word order, happily, is fixed: たとえ always opens its clause. You cannot tuck it in after the subject or let it drift to the end of the sentence. Front of the clause, every time — which also makes it wonderfully easy to catch when you are listening to someone else use it.

> Watch out for a look-alike. Japanese has a word that opens with the same three kana as たとえ and means 'for example.' Same face, different job: one sets up a supposition, the other sets up an illustration. Mixing them turns 'even if it rains' into 'for example, it rains' — a very strange thing to tell a friend on the phone.

> And do not read たとえ〜ても as 'even though.' 'Even though' concedes a fact — it really is raining, and still. This pattern concedes a possibility: it might rain, it might not, and the second half stands either way. If you already know it rained, you have outgrown this sentence.

The second half carries your real stance, so put something there that can bear the weight:

```jp
たとえ{{shiken||試[し]験[けん]}}が{{muzukashii|te|難[むずか]しくて}}も、{{watashi||私[わたし]}}は頑[がん]張[ば]ります。
```

*Even if the exam is difficult, I will do my best.*

Nobody knows yet whether the exam really is hard — that is exactly why たとえ is standing at the front. The supposition is uncertain. The 頑[がん]張[ば]ります is not.

## Casual speech

In relaxed speech the ても half contracts, and it contracts hard. Verb te-forms become 〜ったって: {{furu-rain|te|降[ふ]って}}も turns into {{furu-rain|stem|降[ふ]っ}}たって. I-adjectives follow the same current: {{takai-adj|te|高[たか]くて}}も becomes {{takai-adj|stem|高[たか]く}}たって. And {{demo||でも}} after nouns and na-adjectives shrinks to だって: {{ame-v||雨[あめ]}}{{demo||でも}} becomes {{ame-v||雨[あめ]}}だって.

Through all of this, たとえ itself never changes. It just sits at the front of the clause, watching its partner get shorter.

```jp
たとえ{{hima||暇[ひま]}}だって、{{ano||あの}}{{mise||店[みせ]}}には{{iku-v|nai|行[い]かない}}。
```

*Even if I am free, I will not go to that shop.*

{{hima||暇[ひま]}}だって is the casual twin of {{hima||暇[ひま]}}{{demo||でも}}. You will hear 〜たって and 〜だって constantly in conversation, and they carry a relaxed, slightly blunt feel. Try listening for it the next time a character in a show refuses to back down — the たとえ at the front is the tell. In writing and in polite speech, stay with 〜ても and 〜{{demo||でも}} — the contracted versions can sound rough in the wrong room.

## Contrast

You already know ため, the formal 'because of,' and it lives in the same neighborhood — both patterns can hang on a word like {{ame-v||雨[あめ]}}. The difference is reality. ため reports a cause that actually happened:

```jp
{{ame-v||雨[あめ]}}のため、{{watashi||私[わたし]}}は{{ie||家[いえ]}}に{{iru-exist|masu|いました}}。
```

*Because of the rain, I stayed home.*

It rained. Fact. The rain is the reason, full stop. Now set たとえ{{ame-v||雨[あめ]}}{{demo||でも}} beside it: the rain is only a possibility, and the whole point of the sentence is that the possibility changes nothing. ため explains the world as it is; たとえ〜ても overrules the world as it might be.

限[かぎ]り — 'as long as' — is the mirror image, and the cleanest way to feel what たとえ〜ても is really doing:

```jp
{{hima||暇[ひま]}}な限[かぎ]り、{{maiasa||毎[まい]朝[あさ]}}公[こう]園[えん]を{{hashiru|masu|走[はし]ります}}。
```

*As long as I am free, I run in the park every morning.*

限[かぎ]り makes the condition everything: free mornings mean running, busy mornings mean no running, and the sentence lives or dies by that line. Flip it to たとえ{{hima||暇[ひま]}}{{demo||でも}}、{{hashiru|masu|走[はし]りません}} and the condition stops mattering at all — free or busy, the answer is no. One pattern chains the result to the condition. The other cuts the chain and walks away.

So: たとえ flags the what-if, ても concedes it, and the second half says what stands anyway. Keep this one close — soon you will meet でしょう, the 'probably' word, and it loves parking itself in the second half of these sentences, softening 'I will, no matter what' into 'I probably will, no matter what.'
caution_notes: たとえ only pairs with hypotheticals — for something that actually happened, drop it and concede the fact with plain ても or name the cause with ため.
The concession must be built from the te-form every time — 降っても and 高くても, never straight off the dictionary form.
Do not confuse たとえ with its look-alike that means 'for example' — same opening kana, completely different job.
In casual speech ても contracts to 〜たって and でも to だって, but たとえ itself never changes.
